This is because of the knowledge of one's own nature as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). In this state of awakened intellect, how, and in what manner, could there even be talk—that is, discourse—concerning the physical (*ādhibhautika*) body? How could it possibly exist?
It declares the unreality of the world, which has arisen from the lotus-born Brahmā who is devoid of a physical body, saying:
"The world is the kingdom of the mind; though it is the kingdom of a person called 'mind' who assumes various forms, it stands as if it were real. (MU 3.3.33)

Because it maintains various forms, it belongs to that which is called "mind"—to the one endowed with the name "mind. It belongs to the human being known as Padmaja, who is devoid of a physical, material body. "The kingdom of the mind" means a mental construction. "The world" means existing in the form of the world; it comes to be so. Of what kind is the world? It is as if it were of the nature of reality.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, because it consists of nothing more than mere conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*), it does not possess the nature of truth; thus the word "as if" (*iva*) is employed. Furthermore, the dream serves as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) here quite clearly, so no further effort is required in this regard. The term "the kingdom of the mind" (*manorājya*) for a person named Mind should be understood as a partitive genitive, like "the head of Rāhu."

[Objection: "But in the scriptures, it is stated that the four-faced one is the lotus-born [Brahmā] of a certain specific deity; how then can you say that it is the pure mind alone that is so described? To this he says: "Know that the mind itself is Viriñca (Brahmā), whose nature consists of volition (saṅkalpa). Having brought its own form to a state of expansion, this [universe] is spread out by the mind. (MU 3.3.34)

Know that you are the mind (*manas*), which consists of volitional construction (*saṅkalpa*) and whose nature is the self-reflection of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Know it as the pure mind, the lotus-born Viriñca. For, having brought its own body—its own essential nature—to a state of expansion and vastness, this world is spread out, extended, and produced by that mind; for such is the very nature of Viriñca.
This is precisely it: that which is produced as the world is produced clearly by the mind alone, according to the analogy of a dream;

therefore, it is logical that he alone possesses the nature of Viriñca. The conceptualization of him as a specific four-faced deity, however, is intended only for those of coarse vision—this is the underlying meaning.
It declares the absolute non-difference between Viriñca and the mind:
"Viriñca is the form of the mind; the mind is the body of Viriñca. Earth and the other elements do not exist here [in reality]; therefore, earth and the rest are merely imagined. (MU 3.3.35)
Viriñca is born from the lotus (*padmaja*). Of the pure mind—that is, of the mind—there arises its own form (*svarūpa*).
The pure mind is the mind; it becomes the body (*vapuḥ*) or the essential nature of Viriñca, who is born from the lotus, because they perform the single function known as "production.

In this context, neither earth nor other elements exist for these two, Viriñca and the mind, because, having arisen from pure consciousness alone, there is no departure from the state of being pure consciousness alone.

Therefore, for that reason, earth and the other elements—beginning with the ground—are imagined; they are conceptualized as existing within imagination, like a dream; this is the remaining sense of the statement.

[Objection: But how can the mind, which has the form of Viriñca, produce the world without a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*)? For even a skilled potter does not have the power to bring forth a jar without a material cause known as clay. To this, he says: "Within the lotus-eyed one, there exists a lotus-like [mind] that is pleasing to the heart; let it be seen. The mind and the vision of what is seen are never, in any way, distinct from one another. (MU 3.36)

The suffix *bhāva* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*), as is the archaic usage (*ārṣa*). Therefore, the meaning is as follows: "the visible" (*d�śyatā*) refers to that which is visible (*dṛśyam*). "In the heart of the mind" (*manohṛdi*) means within the mind (*manasaḥ antaḥ*). "Exists" (*asti*) means it remains. This is because [the world] arises in that very manner from pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) endowed with all powers; otherwise, it would be impossible for it to manifest as the nature of the visible. Like what? Like a lotus-pond (*padminī*). Just as a lotus-pond (*kamalinī*) [is contained] in a lotus-seed (*padmākṣe*), that is, in a lotus-grain (*padmabīje*).
"It exists within" means "it is so. Furthermore, the fact that the lotus-eyed one is within the lotus-pond is to be inferred from her emergence from it;

for that which does not exist within something cannot emerge from it, just as water cannot emerge from a waterless jar. Therefore, the mind is both the seer and the seen—the seer of the mind and the seer of the visible world. "At any time" (*kadācana*) means "ever"; "in the slightest degree" (*kiñcana*) means "even by a fraction"; "not divided" (*bhinne na*).

They belong to you [the opponent], because they exist in the relationship of material cause and its effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*). Therefore, the meaning is that there is no dependence here upon a material cause that is inherently distinct [from the effect].
He confirms this very point by means of another illustration:

"Likewise, in this case, your own dream and mental construction—the intellect that rules the mind—are themselves the illustrations through one's own experience; therefore, the realm of the visible exists within the heart. (MU 3.37)
This is clear.
Therefore, just as a piśāca residing within a mental construction destroys a child, so too does this [grasping] which takes the form of the visible destroy the internal observer.
The seer who has the form of the mind, the seer.
Just as a sprout situated within a seed manifests a radiant body according to place and time, so indeed does the intellect of the visible expand itself.
And these three verses occur at the end of the first canto; therefore, no further effort has been made [to cite them here].
He states the final conclusion with a verse at the end of the chapter:
"If that visible suffering does not subside, it can never subside while the visible world persists; nor can there be isolation for the knower while the visible world remains.
However, when the visible world is no longer possible, the state of being a knower subsides even while the knower exists; for that indeed constitutes his liberation."
They said: "MU 3.3.40" [is as follows].

This presently experienced suffering of the visible world is the suffering that takes the form of the visible. If it exists as a reality (*sat*), meaning as ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*), then it will never cease, according to the principle that "non-existence does not apply to that which exists. This is the meaning. As long as the visible world does not cease, there can be no state of isolation (*kevalatva*)—that is, the state of being isolated—for the knower, the seer; in other words, the nature of the non-knower [the subject] cannot come to an end.

Because that which is distinct from oneself exists as an object of cognition situated within the field of perception (*dṛśya*), [the author], having described the manner in which liberation would be impossible, now explains liberation itself. Regarding the word "in the visible" (*dṛśye*): it refers to the alternative case; that is, when the visible object is no longer possible—that is, when, according to the logic already stated, it is characterized by non-arising and arising in its true nature—then the state of being a cognizer (*boddhṛbhāva*) in the cognizer, the seer, shall be stilled and attain peace. For [the state of being a cognizer] does not exist for one who is devoid of the visible.

Does the seer possess some quality called "seership"? [The answer is: No, regardless of what state the object of sight (*dṛśya*) may be in—even if it remains present, even if it partakes in manifestation because it is appearing. Now, one might ask: "What will be accomplished by this pacification of the state of being a cognizer? To this, he says: "For that belongs to him. Here, *hi* signifies certainty. The wise know that pacification of the state of being a cognizer to be the liberation (*vimokṣa*) of this cognizer.
They say—that is, they declare—the distinguished liberation; for liberation consists precisely in the absence of orientation toward the visible world. Thus, may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the third canto in the section on Origination within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. Śrī Vālmīki speaks to Bharadvāja:
While the leader of sages was thus delivering his unrestrained discourse, and while the assembly remained as if silent, intent on hearing him with single-minded devotion.
The tinkling sounds of the networks of small bells were stilled; even the hārītas and parrots within their cages ceased their play, no longer fluttering about.
Even while the women remained there with their amorous charms completely forgotten, the entire royal assembly hall appeared as if fixed upon a painted wall.
When only a single *muhūrta* remained of the day, its heat became mild; all worldly activity, along with the rays of the sun, began to diminish.

When the leader of sages, the venerable Vasiṣṭha, was speaking in this manner— uttering words that were exalted yet profound in meaning— and while he remained as if in silence, as if engaged in the vow of mauna (the sage’s silence), the assembly of people became intent on hearing him alone, absorbed in that single flavor; likewise, without any movement, [he perceived] that which was performed by women and others who were his own support.

"Without vibration" means in the absence of movement produced by women and others who are one's own support. While the sounds of networks of tinkling bells were present; likewise, while the green parrots and parakeets situated within their cages had also ceased their play—that is, had abandoned their sport; and likewise, while the women remained with their amorous charms entirely forgotten—meaning they had completely lost all playful allure.

Thus, while the entire royal assembly and the whole palace were as if fixed upon a painted wall or depicted in a picture, the day— possessing a sweet, mild radiance— remained with but two *ghaṭikās* (two hours) of its duration left; likewise, worldly activity along with the rays of the sun began to draw toward its end.
In response to the expectation of what else occurred then, he says:
"Sweetly blowing breezes, rich with the intoxication of clusters of blossoming lotuses, blew as if they had come to hear [the teaching]. (MU 3.4.5)

The winds blew—indeed, they were blowing—with a sweet vibration and a gentle vibration. Of what nature were they? They were such winds as those that were intoxicated by the clusters of blossoming lotuses (*kamala*), which, because they caused [the flowers] to close, had risen up in form and were full-bodied. Like what were they? As if for the sake of hearing—the hearing of the words of the Sage.
As if they had arrived; even one who comes for the sake of hearing [the teaching] blows with a sweet vibration.
As if to contemplate what he had heard, the Sun abandoned his wandering through the arrangement of day and night; he went to a solitary spot on the slope of the Sunset Mountain and entered the void.

The sun, Bhānu, abandoned his wandering—the revolution for the purpose of creating the day—and likewise the void; for that very reason, he went to the slope of the sunset mountain, a solitary and uninhabited place. As if to contemplate—that is, to bring within the range of reflection—the multitude of the sages' words which had been heard—that is, brought within the range of hearing.
For even one who wishes to contemplate some teaching or instruction they have heard likewise abandons the delusion of action-form and goes to a solitary place.
In the forest lands, the onset of mist arose, darkening them like the inner states of tranquility that become cool upon hearing the teachings of true knowledge.
In the forest regions, those darkened by the onset of mist—darkened by the onset of the frost—arose, that is, they became manifest;
for indeed, at the close of day, mists arise. What are these things darkened by the onset of mist like? They are like states of tranquility (*śāntatā*), due to the absence of agitation;

just as "coolnesses" (*śītalāḥ*) are cool by nature because they destroy heat, so too are these states of tranquility. This is because of hearing the *Vijñāna* [section], namely, through hearing the *Vijñāna* spoken by the venerable Vasiṣṭha.
They arose within the minds of the listeners; that is the meaning of "so it was."
People in all ten directions became scarcely moving, as if they had abandoned all activity in order to listen with full attention.
At the close of day, the natural tendency of people to move about little was imagined as being caused by their abandonment of activity for the sake of listening.
The shadows grew long, as if they possessed long necks to hear the entire sequence of descriptions concerning the lineage of Vasiṣṭha.
For at the time of evening, shadows indeed lengthen; even he who wishes to hear something becomes long-necked. This is the statement regarding two natural properties.
The doorkeeper, bowing low before him, said to the lord of the earth: "O King, the time for bathing and the worship of the twice-born has indeed passed far beyond.

[Note: *Prahva* means having become bowed or humble. In response to the inquiry "What did he say?", the latter half of the verse provides the action; *deva* refers to the king. *Hi* is used here in the sense of certainty.]
The venerable Vasiṣṭha, having thus withdrawn his sweet speech, says: "Therefore, O Great King, let what has been heard up to this point suffice for you today."
Having said, "We shall speak another [matter] in the morning," he remained silent. Upon hearing this, the king said, "So be it," for the sake of increasing his prosperity.
With offerings of flowers, water for honor, water for the feet, respectful salutations, and the giving of sacrificial fees, he reverently honored the celestial rishis, the sages, and the brahmins.
Knowing that the listeners were eager to hear, he said, "In the morning"; that is, immediately upon hearing [the request], and not by offering a counter-argument. He was Daśaratha.
Then the entire assembly, including the circle of kings and sages, rose up, their faces surrounded by a halo from the mass of rays scattered by their earrings.
"Sabhā" means a multitude of people. He qualifies the assembly: "with earrings.

This refers to the mass of rays—the collection of light-beams—that is strewn and diffused on all sides by the earrings; the halo or circle formed by that [mass] covers the faces of the people, that is, the faces of those present at the assembly, in which [assembly]. Such is it.
The armlets and bracelets jingled as they struck one another’s shoulders, while the spaces between their breasts were covered by golden bands pressed down by the weight of their necklaces.

It was that [city] in which armlets and bracelets clashed against one another, meeting together and thus jingling; and it was that in which the spaces between the chests— the middle regions of the breasts— possessed the luster of golden bands, struck by the weight of necklaces.
With swarms of awakened bees resting upon the abandoned flower-crests, the upper parts of her head seemed filled with a humming sound, as if with falling locks of hair.
Upon the crests—the flower-crests of the members of the assembly—by way of their natural exuding of fragrance, they were rested, that is, endowed with repose;

likewise awakened, they were clever at smelling the scent. By the swarms, that is, the multitudes, of those bees (*madhupa*), the regions of the people's heads became filled with the *ghuṅghuma* sound. With which [swarms] of bees? As if with... [the rest of the simile follows].
By those falling, meaning having the nature of falling; by the hair of the head (*mūrdhaja*), because of their black color, as if they were [actual] hairs.

The quarters of the sky were turned golden by the radiance of their golden ornaments, while the activities of their senses were completely stilled through the meaning of the Sage’s words held within their intellects.
The sky-dwellers went to the heavens and the earth-dwellers to the circle of the earth; everyone performed their own daily routines in their respective homes.

The radiance and light of golden ornaments turned the quarters of the sky into gold; such were they. Likewise, by the meaning of the Sage’s speech—which dwells in the intellect and does not fade from it—the activities of the senses became completely stilled, having ceased their outward orientation toward their respective objects.
Those who were capable of such sensory functions—those moving through the sky, traveling in the atmosphere, went to the heavens;

those moving on the earth went to the terrestrial sphere. Then all of them together, including those moving in the sky and the rest, performed their respective daily routines in their own dwellings, in their respective homes.
In the meantime, the dark night appeared like a young woman in a house empty of the crowds of people.
In this interval, at this time, the night was dark; it was a nocturnal night joined with its watches, and [the place] was devoid of the throngs of people, abandoned by the masses of men.
The lord of the day departed to illuminate other lands; for it is the very nature of a virtuous person to act as a source of light everywhere.
The state of being a light-maker is the quality of being a light-maker; "connected with a true person" means belonging to a true person.
The twilight arose on all sides, bearing a multitude of stars, like the splendor of spring appearing with forests of blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees.
It arose; it became manifest.
The birds settled within the mango, nīpaka, and kadamba trees, at the village shrines, and inside the houses, just as their movements were now confined within his mind.

The birds, the winged ones, settled down; they became hidden. Where? In the interior of mango trees, *nīpa* trees, the tops of *kadamba* trees, village shrines, and the cavities of houses—namely, the mangoes, the *nīpas*, the tops of the *kadamabas*, the village sanctuaries, and the inner spaces of the dwellings. There, what were the birds? Like those modes of conduct; like those modes of conduct, which are the mental activities of the disciples (*śrāvaka-jana*). In the mind.
They dissolved; that is the meaning of "tathā."

The western mountain, adorned with fragments of clouds tinted by the light of the sun as it reveals the glow of twilight—appearing as if slightly stained with the hue of saffron—is clothed in yellow garments; joined with the sky, it possesses the beauty of a necklace of stars against the ocean of darkness.

The western mountain, the setting peak, is characterized by fragments of clouds— portions of cloud-masses— that are somewhat adorned, meaning they have been turned yellow by the light of the sun, which resembles the hue of saffron, like a design of saffron. [It appears] like the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who wears yellow garments, emerging from the ocean of darkness known as *tamaḥ*.
He was present; and he was clothed in yellow garments, for the fragments of clouds adorned by the radiance of the sun take on the form of yellow robes.
And it is indeed fitting that the ocean should be joined with the yellow-robed Śrī Nārāyaṇa. How was the western mountain?
It was endowed with the beauty of a necklace of stars; "tārāhāra" means that which has stars as its necklace, and it was "yuta" (endowed) with "śrī," meaning splendor.
"Endowed with Śrī": he is both Tārāhāra (having stars for a necklace) and endowed with Śrī; thus, "Tārāhāra-Śrīyuta. Furthermore, of what nature is he?
"Kha," meaning space or the sky; "sameta," meaning gone to or pervading. The sense is that he pervades the sky; otherwise, his state of being Tārāhāra would be impossible.
And the possession of the Tārāhāra by Śrī-Nārāyaṇa signifies his being joined with Lakṣmī and his pervasion of the sky through the conquest of Bali.
And it remains exactly as it is.

Having performed the twilight propitiatory rite and taken up his worship, he described the arising of darkness as the twilight departed the way it had come: "The glooms arose like a circle of vetālas."
This is clear.
A cool breeze blew, gentle and tender, stirring the droplets of dew and playfully shaking the sprouts; it whispered of the night-lotuses.
The sense is that it portends the appearance of night-lotuses because of its fragrance resembling that of the night-lotus.
Even the directions, with their stars clearly visible, fell into utter darkness, like widowed women with long, hanging locks of hair.
Those whose hair is long, that is, extremely long.
The ocean of milk, whose form consisted of elixir, came through the sky filling the world with a flood of radiant milk, like the moon itself.
The flood of milk is indeed brilliance; by means of that, his form consists of elixir, a form consisting of nectar.
Masses of darkness fled and vanished somewhere, becoming invisible, like the ignorance within the minds of kings when they hear the words of wisdom.

By whom the words of wisdom spoken by Vasiṣṭha—the utterances of knowledge—have been heard; from such a person [the ignorance] comes. The ignorance refers to the foolishnesses of kings, beginning with Daśaratha.
Sages, protectors of the earth, ascetics, and likewise brahmins, rested in their own abodes as if they were diverse objects within the mind.

The manifold meanings—various types of significances—pertaining to the words of the illustrious Vasiṣṭha, which possess diverse imports, found rest; that is, they attained repose within their own abodes, their respective homes.
Dark as a mass of thick gloom resembling a pair of black clouds, the dawn slowly approached them there, appearing like a mist.
"Resembling the body of Yama" means similar to the body of Yama; [this refers to] the dawn for those seers and protectors of the earth.
The bright stars in the sky became invisible, like showers of saffron powder swept away by the morning breeze.
This is clear.
Behold, Viveka-vṛtti (the faculty of discernment) has arrived, her eyes opened by the light of the sun; she is like a new dawn risen within the minds of the great.
The function of discrimination is the mental operation known as *viveka*.
Then the sky-dwellers and earth-dwellers returned once more to the assembly hall, having performed their morning rites in the same manner as the previous day.
The connection is that those who move through the sky and those who move upon the earth arrived at the assembly hall in the very same order as on the previous day.
With her former arrangement, she entered the vast assembly hall; she became motionless in appearance, like a lotus pond when the wind has ceased.

"By its former arrangement and former configuration" means that the immobility of the assembly should be understood as resulting from their eagerness to hear the instruction of the venerable Vasiṣṭha.
Then, seizing the opportunity, Rāma spoke with sweet words to Vasiṣṭha, the tiger among sages and the best of speakers.
The meaning is that having encountered this consequence (*prasaṅga*), otherwise there would be the consequence of the fault known as audacity (*dhārṣṭya*).
In response to the inquiry, "What did he say?", [the author] says:
"O Blessed One, tell me clearly what the nature of the mind is, by means of which this entire cluster of defects is stretched out. (MU 3.4.36)
"What is the use of describing the form of your mind? To this, he says: "Because by that mind... This [creation] has the nature of being created.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha replies:
O Rāma, no form whatsoever is seen of this mind, except for its mere name, like that of the void which is empty and inert in nature.

"O Rāma, apart from its mere name—that is, excluding the mere name—not even the slightest form of this mind is perceived. The sense is that the mind exists as a mere name alone, not as a form. Of what nature is this mind?

It is empty (*śūnyā*), meaning it has no form whatsoever because it cannot withstand investigation; it is inert (*jaḍā*), meaning it is endowed with the quality of insentience because its establishment depends upon being apprehended by the witness."

That whose form (ākṛti) is its own essential nature (svarūpa). Of what such [a thing] is it like? Like space (vyoman). The meaning is: just as space has a form that is empty and insentient, so too [is this]. //MT_3,4.37//
This very point he confirms:
"The mind does not exist as a real entity either externally or within the heart; know, O Rāma, that it is situated everywhere, just like space."

The mind does not exist as a real entity (sadrūpa) externally, because it is not perceived by the external senses; nor does it exist as a real entity within the heart—that is, even in the region of the heart—for nothing called "mind" is found in the region of the heart. O Rāma, you should know and understand that this mind is situated everywhere, both externally and within the heart. [This is so] because of that which is called volition (saṅkalpa).

This is because its effects manifest both externally and within the heart. For even volition takes as its objects external things such as jars and internal states such as pleasure. How is the mind? Like the sky. The meaning is: just as the sky is situated everywhere, so too [is the mind].
[Objection: Even so, its essential nature must be stated; for it is not logical that what is entirely non-existent should exist everywhere. To this, he says:
"This form of his, which has arisen as non-existent, is like the water of a mirage; hear now its nature in brief, which is comparable to the delusion of a second moon. (MU 3.4.39)

This mind of yours has arisen from non-existence and appeared falsely; therefore, it is like the water of a mirage and comparable to the delusion of a second moon. Listen briefly to this very form that is being experienced, which is its own true nature.
He explains the very nature of the mind:
"O virtuous one, know that this which has become the manifestation and appearance of an object—whether it be existent or non-existent—is the mind and nothing else. (MU 3.4.40)

O virtuous one, know that mind to be that which has attained expansion—that is, firmness—regarding an object or entity, whether existent or non-existent; that is to say, that which is intuition, a flash of insight, or the mental synthesis of an object as such. Any other [mind] conceptualized by logicians and others in the form of atoms and so forth is not the mind.
This was stated by relying on the distinction between proponents who hold that [the object] exists or does not exist.
Again and again he says this very thing:
that which is the manifestation of meaning is designated as "mind" (manas); there is never anything else whatsoever called "mind."
The manifestation of meaning is the appearance of the state of being an object within objects.
Know that the mind is volition; it is not distinct from volition. Just as water is inseparable from its fluidity, so too is movement inseparable from the wind.
This is clear.
Where there is volition, O dear one, there the mind is likewise situated; volition and the mind are never, for anyone, distinct.
In whatever state (*avasthā*) conceptualization (*saṅkalpana*) occurs— O friend— in that very state, that well-known mind (*manas*) exists in the form of what is called conceptualization. For some,
conceptualization and the mind are never at any time distinct, because they possess a single nature.
Whether it be real or unreal, know that the mind is merely that which appears as an object; that is Brahman, this Grandfather.

Whether it be real or unreal, that which is the appearance of an object—the manifestation of an object—exists. You should know, understand, that the mind (*manas*) is merely that appearance of an object. This mind, whose nature is the appearance of an objects, is declared in the scriptures to be the Grandfather (*pitāmaha*), another name for Brahmā.
Because it is the cause of all creation; for even in the scriptures, that which is the cause of creation alone is declared to be Brahman.
It describes the mind as having the nature of a subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), which is experienced by all during dreams and so forth:
"The mind is designated as the self of the subtle body; the material intellect (ādhibhautika-buddhi), however, is the long-enduring consciousness. (MU 3.4.45)

By the learned, the self (ātman) or essential nature of the body—which is of the nature of *ativāhana* (swift transport), meaning it reaches a destination within a moment that would otherwise take years, and which appears as a body in dreams, volitions, and the like—is designated as "mind" (*manas*). It is not, however, the atom (*paramāṇu*) as maintained by the logicians; for in the case of the latter, the aforementioned nature of swift transport is not tenable.

Because that [intellect] is not perceived when the gross body has begun [to function]. In this context, he establishes that the intellect of the material realm (*ādhibhautika-buddhi*) constitutes the material body by means of the term "material" (*ādhibhautika*). The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction. By the wise, the "intellect of the material realm" is understood as the intellect taking the form of the material body; that is to say, it is the very nature of the material body. It has attained firmness (*dārḍhya*) in the sense that the intellect persists for a long time.

It is always stated that the intellect has the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*) as its object. For it is precisely the intellect, whose nature is the mind and which has the subtle body as its object, that manifests through the state of the material (*ādhibhautika*) once it has attained solidity. There is no separate material entity called the "fleshly" body; for even if such a thing were to exist, it would be like a non-entity without being an object of the intellect.
But if it were an object of the intellect (*buddhi*), its nature as the intellect would not be lost; for that alone is called an "object" which appears as if situated within the subject (*viṣayin*).
Otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even a yellow substance could be the object of a cognition of blue. The second word *tu* is for the purpose of completing the meter.
To establish that the mind is an object of perception, he states its synonyms for "the perceivable":
"Ignorance, transmigratory existence, the intellect (citta), the mind (manas), bondage, impurity, and darkness—these, the wise know, are the synonymous names for the perceivable. (MU 3.4.46)
Therefore, the mind is indeed the object of perception; otherwise, it would not possess the status of being synonymous with "the perceivable."
[Objection: But how is it logical for the mind, which appears as the grasper of objects, to be synonymous with the "visible" (dṛśya)? To this he says:
"For there is no form of the mind whatsoever apart from the visible; moreover, I shall explain again that this visible has indeed arisen. (MU 3.4.47)

For this reason—because there is nothing whatsoever apart from the visible, that is, no form of the mind distinct from the visible—it is certain that such a thing does not exist. Therefore, the sense is that it is logical for the mind to be a synonym for the visible. [The opponent asks: "But what follows from that? To this, he says: "And the visible... This visible object, moreover, is not something produced, because it has already been stated so previously.

Therefore, the sense is that the mind (*manas*) is likewise unarisen. Now, one might object: "But previously, no certainty arose for me regarding the non-arising of the visible. To this he says: "I"—this [term] refers to the non-arising of the visible. He will explain this again later;
the sense is that it is difficult to understand.
He explains the very non-arising of the visible world:
"Just as the lotus bud exists within the lotus seed, so the visible world exists within the atom of the Great Consciousness."
Just as the lotus bud resides within the lotus seed—that is, within the *padmākṣa*—otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence that its emergence later on would be impossible;

likewise, the visible world—the world that has become the object of the act of seeing—resides within the great atom of consciousness (*mahācit-paramāṇu*). "Great consciousness" (*mahācit*) is consciousness that is undivided; it is called an "atom" (*paramāṇu*) precisely because of its extreme subtlety. It resides within—that is, in the midst of—that [atom]. Otherwise, [it could not emerge].
The sense is: from where could its emergence possibly come? Therefore, since the visible object lacks any separateness from the Great Consciousness (mahācit), it is simply unarisen;
this is the ultimate point.
This very point he states again and again:
"Just as light belongs to the lamp, just as motion belongs to the wind, and just as liquidity belongs to water, so too is visibility [inherent] to the seer. (MU 3.4.49)
Light is a specific quality that causes the manifestation of an object; motion is vibration. The intended meaning is that there is no existence of an object of perception distinct from the perceiver.
Just as the state of being a bracelet exists in gold, just as water exists in a mirage, and just as a wall exists in a dream-city, so too does the perception of the visible object exist in the seer.
This is clear.
By this same reasoning, he declares that even the fact established—that the seer consists of the seen—is to be wiped away as a stain:
"In the same way, whatever quality of being the seen resides in the seer as if it were non-different from him, I shall quickly wipe away even that stain from the mirror of your mind. (MU 3.4.51)

This being so: in the seer, the agent of the act of seeing, that which is non-different—meaning not distinct from him according to the logic already stated—namely, the state of being seen, the state of being the object of the act of seeing, exists as if it were "I. Even that impurity, existing in the form of impurity, is non-different from the seer; that state of being seen, too, I wipe away from the mirror of your mind, from the reflecting surface of your own consciousness.

The meaning is that by this means, there shall be no perception of the visible at all in your mind; for even a visible object appearing as non-existent causes suffering to some slight degree. If it is asked: "How can the state of being an object of vision (*dṛśyatva*) be a stain when it is non-different from the seer?
For a stain must be something distinct," [the reply is: True. Yet the state of being an object of vision is determined by the seer even as non-different from himself.
It also brings about difference from itself; for, without a counter-correlate (pratiyogin) termed "difference from itself," identity with itself cannot be established.
Thus, it is perfectly clear that the visible object which brings about difference from itself is a stain (mala), and so there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Now, one might ask: "Why do you wipe away the state of being an object of perception—even though it is of the nature of impurity—from that which exists as non-different from the seer? To this he says:

"Know that when this seer’s state of being a non-seer occurs by force due to the absence of the seen, that is the state of absolute liberation (kevalībhāva); therefore, [liberation] belongs to that which is both non-existent and existent. (MU 3.4.52)

Of this [Self] which exists as the Self; of the seer, the agent of the act of seeing; when the object of sight is absent; "by force," that is, by power, meaning without one's own effort; that state of being a non-seer might occur. For indeed, without an object of sight, there is no such thing as the "seer-ness" of a seer, because even for one who exists in the state of potentiality, the essential nature [of the seer] does not depart. You—that [state].

Know—that is, understand—the state of being a non-seer (*adraṣṭṛtva*) to be isolation (*kevalībhāva*), which is liberation (*mukti*). This is because liberation consists precisely in the seer’s mere lack of orientation toward the objects of sight. Of what kind of seer? Precisely for that reason, "of one who is both non-existent and existent": non-existent with respect to the state of being a seer, and existent with respect to the state of isolation. For it is not logical that there should be isolation for that which is non-existent; thus, it is of that which is inexpressible (*anirvācya*).
This is the meaning. Therefore, the sense is that for the sake of achieving the state of isolation (kevalībhāva), one must by all means effect the complete eradication of the visible [objects].

[Objection: Even if non-perceptiveness (*adraṣṭṛtva*) is established through the power of the absence of the visible, the state of isolation (*kaivalya*) is not yet established; for attachment and the like, which have the visible as their object, persist in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), just as in deep sleep. To this, he says:
"When the reality has been attained, the latent impressions of attachment, aversion, and so forth subside, just as the agitation caused by movement ceases when the wind is still. (MU 3.4.53)

When one has attained the state of reality— that is, the true nature consisting in the non-existence of the visible object and the resulting state of being a non-perceiver— then the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of passion, hatred, and so forth,

which were previously formed by the objects of perception that appeared as such, come to rest and attain quiescence, because of the absence of both the substratum and the object. However, in deep sleep, although the latent impressions are present in the form of the substratum and the object, the passion, hatred, and so forth that follow from them [do not cease].

Or rather, there is an abiding in the absence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). For in deep sleep, there is no destruction of the seer and the seen along with their roots; otherwise, it would follow that one who has awakened would again have attachment to them. Indeed, attachment is not appropriate when something has been destroyed along with its roots. However, for those who have ascertained the non-existence of the seen, attachment never arises even when the seen appears. In this regard, [the state of] one's own mind...
Thus, it is witnessed; enough with this elaboration. What is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of passion, hatred, and so forth? It is like the agitation of vibration.

Just as when the wind is no longer blowing, the agitation caused by the wind—which is of the nature of vibration—perishes; such is the meaning. Therefore, it is logical that the state of being a non-seer, produced by the absence of the visible, is the state of absolute isolation (*kaivalya*).
Such is the intended meaning.
Precisely this point, because it is extremely difficult to understand, he states again and again:
"When everything consisting of the directions, the earth, and space has ceased to exist, whatever form the stainless light would take in that which is to be illuminated..."
When the three worlds, as well as "you" and "I," have attained non-existence within the visible realm, there arises for the pure-souled seer that state of absolute isolation.

In that which consists of the directions, the earth, and space; in that which has the very nature of the directions, the earth, and space; when a multitude of objects—which are to be illuminated and are capable of being manifested—is present, yet remains impossible [to perceive] while assuming the agency of the act of manifestation, there may arise a form of light such as the stainless and pure light of the sun, which is beyond the reach of the senses. For it does not emerge from the solar disc.

Light that has not fallen upon a wall becomes perceptible to the eye; when the three worlds, "you," and "I"—that is, the visible world—have attained non-existence or absence, there arises for the seer, who remains as the illuminator of the visible, such a state of isolation (*kevalībhāva*), which is a state of stainless form. Of what kind of seer? Of one whose self is stainless—that is, of one whose nature is pure consciousness alone, untainted by objects of thought; otherwise, it would not be so.
The state of being stainless, which is another synonym for the state of a Kevalin, would be untenable.
For just as the nature of a mirror remains solely its own essential form, even when it contains the reflections of infinite mountains and all other things; ||| MU_3.4.56 |||

When the delusion of the visible world—in such notions as "I," "you," and "the universe"—has subsided, there arises that state of absolute oneness while the Seer remains established, no longer looking outward.

The word "praśānte" (when it has become tranquil), which belongs to the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*), should also be applied to the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*). Therefore, this is the meaning: *hi* signifies certainty; when all the infinite mountains and so forth have become tranquil within their reflection—that is to say, when the mirror, taken as the subject of the illustration, assumes the state of being a reflection—the mirror consists solely of its own essential nature.

It consists of the very nature known as the "pure mirror. Just as there would be the state of being a mirror when the delusion of the visible—the delusion in the form of the visible, meaning the visible itself—consisting of "I," "you," "the world," and so forth, has become completely stilled; and when the observer remains established without performing the act of seeing—that is, without looking—such purity would exist. It is just like [a mirror] that is pure in the absence of reflections.
The meaning is that just as only the mirror remains, so too, in the absence of the visible object, only the pure seer remains.
Considering the impossibility of the non-existence of that which is perceived, Śrī Rāma asks:
"If this does not subside, then there is no non-existence of what exists; yet we do not perceive non-existence in this visible world which bestows such defects."

The word *vā* has the sense of *yataḥ* (since). This visible world, if it were *sat*—that is, if it possessed existence (*sattā*)—then it would not cease. Since for that which is *sat*, possessing existence, non-existence (*abhāva*) does not occur, because that would entail the loss of its own nature (*svarūpa*).
Otherwise, even fire would lose its capacity to burn. [Objection: "In that case, let it then be simply non-existent (*asat*). To this, he says:

"And [the phrase] 'asattām' means: in that which bestows faults—that is, in that which bestows the fault consisting of the nature of passion and so forth. The point is that it is not logical for that which is non-existent to bestow a fault, because otherwise even the son of a barren woman would possess that quality."
He states the conclusion:
"Therefore, O Brahmin, how can this cholera of the visible world be pacified—this [cholera] which causes confusion through the arising of manifoldness and bestows a continuous stream of suffering?"
"Arising from various [causes]" means the production of diversity. "Delusion" is false cognition; she is such that she produces that.
In order to fulfill his vow, "I shall wipe it away," Śrī Vasiṣṭha speaks this reply:
"Listen to this mantra for the pacification of this demon of the visible world, by which, O Rāma, it will utterly perish and meet its death."

O Rāma! For the pacification of this demon of the visible world that manifests before you, listen to this mantra, which consists of the collection of words to be spoken hereafter; by means of which mantra this demon of the visible world shall undergo absolute death—the non-existence of all three times—and thereafter perish, passing out of sight. And it is indeed fitting that a demon should die by means of a mantra.
And non-perception.
He speaks of the mantra itself:
O Rāghava, that which exists can never be destroyed; for even when it has seemingly perished, it remains as a seed within the heart.
O Rāghava, whatever entity possesses existence, its destruction can never at any time occur;
for even if that entity is destroyed by some other [cause]— such as the destruction of its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*)—
it remains in the heart, within the mind, as a seed, or it persists in the form of a seed, that is, in the form of existence.
Thus it is said; for it is observed that even a lost object recurs again and again within the heart.
"Surely, what fault follows from that? To this he replies:
"The perception of the visible world, having emerged again in the space of consciousness from the seed of memory, spreads forth a vast defect in the form of the world, mountains, and the sky."

The cognition of the visible is that which has the seed of memory as its cause; it is a cognition possessing the form of the visible—meaning, the visible itself. Having arisen and become manifest in the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), it again expands—that is, specifically spreads out—the vast defect in the form of the world, mountains, and sky, by way of subtle phenomenal proliferation (*sūkṣma-prapañca*). This is because it is seen in dreams.
But what follows from that? To this he says:
"In this way, there would be the fault of no liberation, nor is its partial occurrence possible; for gods, sages, and seers are seen to be recipients of liberation. (MU 3.4.63)

This being the case, there would be the defect of non-liberation—a defect consisting in the consequence that liberation does not exist—because liberation is defined as the very absence of the visible world in its two forms, gross and subtle. [The opponent objects: "Let that defect be; what will it do to us? To this, he replies: "And not... That is to say, even in the slightest degree, the possibility of that defect of non-liberation does not exist, because...
The celestial sages and seers are seen to be vessels for liberation.
Furthermore, he says this very thing again:
"If this world had a beginning, then there would be no liberation for anyone; whether it resides outside or within the heart, the visible world leads only to destruction."

If this world were beginningless, it would possess existence; in that case, liberation—the release from the visible—for any cognizer whatsoever would not occur. This is because, even if the destruction of the visible were somehow brought about, the visible would manifest again in a subtle form due to the power of memory. For whether the visible exists as something external in a gross form, or as something internal in a subtle form within the heart, [the result remains the same].

Or let it be so: [the state] exists for the sake of producing the destruction known as bondage (*bandha*). The meaning is that there is no distinction in its capacity to cause agitation (*kṣobhakatva*).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and torpor (*taimilya*) and so forth are included, because these too are objects of perception (*dṛśyatva*).
"Now then, what should be done? To this he says:
"Therefore, O Rāma, listen to this most terrifying proposition, which you will surely understand through the subsequent text. (MU 3.4.65)
And the extreme dreadfulness of the proposition is to be understood from its being engaged in what is impossible.
For the purpose of awakening Śrī Rāma, he speaks this very subsequent passage:
"This world, characterized as being of the nature of ether, the elements, and so forth, and as 'I'—is it not the case, O Rāma, that there is no referent for the word 'world' at all?"

O Rāma! Indeed, in the sense of certainty, that which is characterized and determined as having the form of space, the elements, and so forth, as well as "I"—this is the meaning and the referent of the word "world" (*jagat*). From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), it simply does not exist; it does not possess existence at all. It is not the case that, having possessed existence, it perishes. And this being so, there is no consequence of the fault of non-liberation (*nirmokṣa*); for [liberation] does not concern that which is non-existent.
The sense is that its status as a bond is observed. Although space is also an element (*bhūta*), it is mentioned separately because of its predominance.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the effects of the elements are included.
Now, one might ask: "How is it logical for this world, consisting of 'I' and so forth, which appears manifest before us, to possess existence in every respect? To this, he says:
"Whatever web of objects is seen here appearing before one, all that is indeed Brahman alone—undecaying, immortal, and immutable. (MU 3.4.67)

This web of visible objects that stands before us—this collection of perceivable things such as blue, pleasure, and so forth—which is seen and experienced by us, all of that is ageless and immortal because it is devoid of a body; thus, it is imperishable, being free from destruction. It is Brahman itself, expanded in the form of the world; it is the pure consciousness-principle alone that exists as the state of the world. Thus it comes to be, and thus it is perceived.
For the manifestation of water in the form of waves occurs; and this being so, it is indeed logical that the world, though appearing, is non-existent.
The point is that the existence of a wave, even while appearing in water, has never been observed.
It further confirms that the visible world is nothing but Brahman alone:
"In the Full, the Full expands; in the Supreme, the Tranquil remains supreme. Space has arisen in space itself; Brahman abides in Brahman. (MU 3.4.68)

In the *pūrṇa* (full), which is independent; it "spreads," meaning it performs its movement. In the *para* (supreme), which is established in its own nature (*svarūpastha*) and transcendent; in *brahman*, the expanded reality.

Here, the description of the pure consciousness (*śuddhacittattva*) is given by means of words ending in the locative case, while that which possesses its form—the world—is to be understood by means of words ending in the nominative case. Now, one might ask: how can there be an abiding in the pure consciousness, which is endowed with qualities such as fullness?

This is logical, because we observe that the smaller resides within the larger. True; however, there is no "residing" here in the sense of being a supported object (*ādheya*), which would lead to the aforementioned fault. Rather, it exists by way of its identity with that [the larger], so there is no occurrence of the fault here.
Enough with these elaborations.

There is neither the visible object nor the seeing, neither the seer nor the act of seeing; there is neither emptiness nor insentience, nor even consciousness—this all-pervading reality is simply peace.

The visible object (*dṛśya*) is the object of the act of seeing; it does not exist and does not possess being. Seeing (*dṛk*) is the act of seeing; it does not exist. The seer (*draṣṭṛ*), the agent of the act of seeing, also does not exist. The vision (*darśana*), the fruit accomplished by the act of seeing, also does not exist, because all these have as their essence mere cognition (*pratītimātra*). [Objection: "In that case, does this non-existence itself exist? To this, he says: "It is not empty."

"Empty" means the non-existence of the visible and so forth; yet it is not [non-existent] either, for it is not logical that what is absolutely non-existent should appear, since that would entail the appearance even of things such as a rabbit's horn. [Objection: In that case, there would be mere insentience (*jaḍya*). For in the state of insentience, there is indeed the non-existence of all things. To this, he says: "not insentient. This is an expression emphasizing the state of being (*bhāvapradhānanirdeśa*); "insentient" means the state of being insentient (*jaḍatva*). It does not exist, because if that were the case, there would be the appearance of the visible and so forth.

"It would be improper. [Objection: "In that case, would it not then be consciousness (*cit*) alone? To this he says: "It is not consciousness" (*no cit*). Consciousness is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*);

it does not exist [as such], because its existence depends upon the object of cognition (*cetya*), and because, by the reasoning already stated, such an object of cognition is impossible. [Objection: "If so, what is there? For absolute non-existence cannot be apprehended by the intellect. To this he says: "It is tranquil" (*śāntam*). It is pervasive (*ātataṃ*).
This entire world of the visible and so forth, whose nature vibrates everywhere, becomes quiescent; it becomes pure consciousness alone, free from the agitation of the objectified.
Failing to reach a definitive conclusion on this matter, Śrī Rāma attributes to the sage the habit of propounding impossible propositions:
"A mountain is ground to powder by the son of a barren woman; a rabbit's horn is perceived. Stretching out his mass of arms, a stone performs the Tāṇḍava dance. (MU 3.4.70)
"Sands flow with oil, stone statues recite, and painted clouds thunder"—such, O Lord, are these words.

The word "tava" (of you) is to be supplied [at the end]. O Lord, this speech of yours becomes thus; it takes such a form. Why? Because of the phrase "by the son of a barren woman," and so forth. The meaning is that people proceed to cognize (*pramāyate*)—that is, begin to cognize—a rabbit's horn. The usage *pramāyate* is an archaic (*ārṣa*) form. In every respect, yours is indeed nothing but an expression of an entirely incoherent meaning.
The meaning is "the statement. The address "O Lord" (*prabho*) is intended to dispel the lack of discipline manifested through the false attribution of teaching an impossible matter.
The world consists of the sky-like mountain of suffering such as old age and death; why do you say to me, "It does not exist"? MU 3.4.72.
The sense is that it is not reasonable to deny the multitude of entities—such as those characterized by aging—that are directly perceived through experience.
The word "api" (even/also) is intended to indicate that Śrī Vasiṣṭha is unfit to be a proponent of impossibility. By the word "mama" (my), he illuminates his own status as a true disciple.
"If this is indeed true, then it is right that you should explain it. With this intention, he said:
"O Brahmin, tell me how this universe is neither established, nor produced, nor existent, so that this may become certain."
This is the absence of persistence and so forth.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha speaks the reply:
"I am not one whose speech is inconsistent; listen, O Rāghava, as this is being told: how this unreal world appears, like the son of a barren woman or a mirage in the sun."

"I am the one named Vasiṣṭha. I am not such a person whose speech is disconnected or incoherent. O Rāghava, listen! I shall describe to you how this world appears—how it manifests and flashes before you—as something unreal (asat). How is this? It is like a barren woman’s son who utters cries."
Like the son of a barren woman; the meaning is that it appears as something non-existent, just as he [the son] does.
He explains that very point:

"This [world] was unarisen at the beginning, at the start of creation; therefore, it does not exist as a reality. For this appears through the mind, just like a city in a dream and the like. (MU 3.4.75)

This visible world was unmanifest in the beginning—that is, at the very start, at the commencement of creation when pure consciousness (cinmātra) first turned toward the object of thought; for, in the ultimate sense, it did not deviate from its state as pure consciousness. Therefore, it did not rest upon a separate existence. Indeed, even in the case of a jar produced from clay, no existence distinct from the clay is observed even externally.

Therefore, for that reason, this world is "alam"—that is, it is excessive; it does not possess real existence (*sattā*), because its existence is obtained merely through its status as the witness of pure consciousness (*cinmātra-sākṣitā*), like a city in a dream. [Objection: "If that is so, then how does this appear? To this he says: "this. Indeed (*hi*)—meaning, certainly—this visible world appears, that is, it manifests as an object of sight, by means of the mind (*manas*) through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
What is it like? It is like a city; the meaning is that just as a city appears to the mind in dreams and so forth, so it is here.
"Is it not the case that the existence of the visible world, which appears through the mind whose own nature is real, is indeed logical? To this he says:
"And the mind itself was unproduced at the beginning of creation and is of an unreal form; listen to this as I shall explain how it is experienced."

At the beginning of creation, when the nature [of things] was first proclaimed at the onset of the world-process, the mind alone was unproduced; for that very reason, it possesses a non-existent form, having an unreal nature. Listen to this from me: I shall explain how this is experienced by you.
[Objection: But surely, setting aside the discussion of the non-existence of the visible world (*dṛśya*), it is improper to speak of the non-existence of the mind (*manas*). To this, he replies:

"The mind spreads this defect consisting of the visible world, which is of the nature of destruction; it is itself unreal, yet takes on the form of the unreal, just as one dream [leads to] another dream. (MU 3.4.77)

The mind expands—that is, spreads out—the defect consisting of the visible, whose nature is the visible; [a defect] which is this very thing appearing before one, consisting of destruction, having a perishable nature. How is the mind? It is indeed unreal (*asad*), because its form is merely a manifestation;
thus its very nature is unreal. How is the defect consisting of the visible? It has the form of the unreal, its nature is unreal—[unreal] by virtue of the unreal.

Because it is being expanded; for that which is non-existent is not capable of becoming existent through expansion, since even a web of words expanded by the son of a barren woman would result in [the fallacy of] existence. "Like what? "Like a dream. The meaning is: just as a dream, whose own nature is non-existent, extends another dream with a non-existent form, so too [is this]. For indeed, one dream within a dream is seen.
Thus, there is no dispute on this point.
It further states that this very [consciousness] is the cause even with respect to the body which serves as its own substrate:
"It itself spontaneously and swiftly conceives of a body; by that, this splendor of a magical illusion is spread out by means of what has been spread out. (MU 3.4.78)

That mind—this physical body appearing as the self—quickly, by itself without depending on the assistance of others, and at its own will, forms intentions and accomplishes them through mere volition. He speaks again of the very subject at hand with the words "by that, this": by that mind, this [world] which appears as an object of perception.
He summarizes the meaning already stated in a verse at the end of the section:

"The mind—whether it flashes forth, moves, leaps, begs, exists, sinks, or withdraws by itself; whether it even attains the state of being something else—it merely moves due to its flickering power. (MU 3.4.79)
And this is an illustration; therefore, whatever action occurs here, it is produced by the mind alone—this is the summarized meaning. May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the fourth canto in the "Chapter on Origination" within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus heard the determination regarding the mind as something that must necessarily be addressed, Śrī Rāma asks:
"O Blessed One, O tiger among sages, what indeed exists here in this mental delusion? How has the mind, which consists of illusion, arisen, and from whence does it come?"

O Blessed One, tiger among sages, O Blessed One, best of sages: in this delusion that takes the form of the world, what indeed exists as the mind? What is its essential nature? Likewise, how has it arisen? In what manner has it manifested?
From where does the mind, which consists of illusion and is of the nature of illusion, come to be?
Regarding that, with the intention that one should first explain the very origin, he said:
"O Lord, best among speakers, tell me in brief about the origin at the beginning; thereafter you shall declare the remainder of what is to be said."
"O Lord, you shall explain that which remains—the origin residing in the mind—after my question has been asked; for it is you yourself who remain," such is the sense. Śrī Vasiṣṭha gives the reply:
"When the great dissolution has occurred and non-existence has arrived, when the entire visible world has vanished at the beginning of creation, only the Peaceful (Śānta) remains. (MU 3.5.3)

When there is the attainment—that is, the fullness—of the great dissolution known as the fourth state (*turya*), or the time of the end of the great aeon (*mahākalpa*); and when, at the beginning of creation, the entire visible world—which consists of all objects of perception, their creation, their withdrawal, and their latent impressions—has reached non-existence, that is, invisibility; then [the Self], being peaceful, gradually emerges from the agitation known as the witness-consciousness of creation and its destruction.
Even when [the world] has emerged, there remains and persists only that ineffable reality (*tattva*).
Herein, creation bears witness to the collection of objects within its own domain; dissolution effects the non-existence of objects as its own goal;

and sublimation (*saṃskāra*) effects the sublimation of objects—that is, the sublimation of the non-existence of objects. Of these two, sublimation consists of the sublimation of objects and the sublimation of the non-existence of objects.
And thus the distinction is to be understood. // MT_3,5.3 //
He clearly states what remains after [all else] has been stilled:
"The unborn, undecaying, divine Lord, free from affliction, the all-maker, the all, the Supreme Self, the Great Lord, remains as the sun that never sets. (MU 3.5.4)

The Supreme Self (paramātman) is, in the ultimate sense, a certain internal reality that appears as the object of the "I-notion" (ahantā); it exists—that is, it persists—because it first exists as the witness of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), and subsequently remains as the witness of all inherent natures (svabhāva) however they may be conceptualized. Herein, the statement regarding the existence of the Self, which is eternally present, refers to its state of being in the present.

Because it is employed with respect to the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), it does not entail any fault. In response to the inquiry "In what manner is this Supreme Self (*paramātman*)?", he states the qualifying attributes, beginning with "unsetting" (*anastamita*). It is "unsetting" because, while remaining as the grasper even of that imagined self which has [otherwise] set, it is in effect devoid of setting. It is "resplendent" (*bhāsvat*) because, by virtue of being the witness, it illuminates everything.

He is the very nature of the sun; it is a marvel that the luminous one never sets. He is unborn (*aja*), meaning devoid of birth. For birth is indeed manifestation (*prādurbhūti*), and such [birth] is not possible for him, because he is eternally manifest as the Self (*ātman*). Indeed, it is never logical for the Self to be non-manifest, since even his own non-manifestation exists as its perceiver. He is the Divine (*deva*).

He is fond of play; otherwise, how could such a world come into being? For one who is not fond of play turns away even from the mere movement of a hand. He is free from affliction, having emerged from the disease called *māyā*. Otherwise, being seized by the disease called *māyā*, it would be illogical for him to be the impeller of *māyā*; for one seized by a disease does not become the impeller of that very disease. Always.

He is the doer of all, acting as the agent of everything in all places and at all times; otherwise, being experienced in this way, He would be the source of all at all times, which would be illogical. Everything has His own nature as its essence; otherwise, what would constitute the essential nature of things? Maheśvara is the supreme controller; otherwise, all things would not be restricted to their respective natures.
Furthermore, he qualifies that very same [Brahman]:
"From which words turn back, which is realized by the liberated; and for whom designations such as 'Self' and so forth are merely conceptual constructs, not born of intrinsic nature."

All words—both worldly and Vedic—turn back from that Supreme Self. For speech functions toward an object by presupposing a convention (*saṅketa*), yet it is impossible to establish a convention regarding the Supreme Self because it is beyond the range of both external and internal organs. It is only with respect to objects within the range of the senses that a convention can be established through direct apprehension, as if grasping it with the hand.

"It is seen; therefore, it does not exist. To this, he says: "By those who are liberated. That is, by those alone whose minds are unattached to the visible world, and not by worldly people. "That which is understood" means that which is known as the Self. For the liberated know some pure reality as the Self; otherwise, liberation would be impossible. And thus, its non-existence is not tenable.

[Objection: But surely, it is improper to state that words turn back from that [ultimate reality], because words such as "self" (ātman) and so forth denote it. To this he says: "And of which... The word "by those who know reality" is to be supplied. "Fictitious" means established by conceptual construction, like the name "oil-drinker" (tailapāyikā) and so on, without depending at all on a basis for application (pravṛttinimitta).

Now, if that [reality] is indeed one alone, then how is it that the Sāṅkhyas and others have spoken of multiple *puruṣas* and so forth? To this he says: "That which is the Person for those with the Sāṅkhya view, the Brahman for the Vedāntins, and mere consciousness (*vijñānamātra*) for the knowers of consciousness—[all these are] exclusively stainless. (MU 3.5.6)

"Of those with the Sāṅkhya view" means those who delight in the Sāṅkhya philosophy. For the Sāṅkhyas indeed describe the *puruṣa*—also known by the synonym *jīva*—as distinct from *prakṛti*, as the one who remains (*śeṣa*). Yet, when that [puruṣa] is investigated, it is logically concluded that it rests precisely in the nature of the aforementioned Supreme Self;
thus it is rightly said, "he who is the *puruṣa* for those with the Sāṅkhya view. This should be applied in the same way everywhere. And so, regarding the mere difference in names...

The intended meaning is that because [the Self] is established as such, the aforementioned fault does not follow. Now, if it is asked: "Upon what philosophical system (*darśana*) did the venerable Vasiṣṭha base this scripture?"—it is true. This scripture was composed by him relying upon the essence of all philosophical systems; otherwise, the acceptance of all doctrines would be untenable. Here, the discussion primarily concerns the Vedānta scriptures.
It is observed that, in comparison to that [ordinary knowledge], even the Śiva-śāstra—which is a great secret—is [superior] by a small margin; enough with this digression from the subject at hand.

Brahman is the tranquil essence of consciousness (*cittattva*), which has become both the locus and the object of ignorance. Pure consciousness (*vijñānamātra*) is formless knowledge whose objects are things such as jars and cloths.

He who is the illuminator of emptiness for the proponents of emptiness, who possesses the brilliance of the sun; he who is the speaker, the rememberer, the truth, the enjoyer, the seer, and the eternal agent.

The state of "nothingness" experienced in deep sleep is emptiness (*śūnya*). This is an illustrative indication; by it, one should understand that this very [state] is that reality which serves as the place of rest for all philosophical systems (*darśana*). Furthermore, what is its nature? To this, he says: "the illuminator" (*bhāsaka*). It is that which [illuminates] the splendors of the sun and other such things, namely, the splendors whose essential forms are the sun and so forth.

The illuminator becomes a manifester by resting upon the specific locus called the eye. Likewise, he who is always—that is, eternally—the speaker, rememberer, enjoyer, seer, and doer, exists as such because he abides as the self of all speakers and so forth. "Truly" (ṛtam) is an adverbial modifier of the action; it means "as truth," that is to say, from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ).
Though existing, it is non-existent; though situated within the body in this world, it is far away—this is indeed the light of consciousness, for it is like the radiance of the sun.
That Self, although existing and being the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for this entire delusion of the world,

is yet non-existent (*asat*), because it is not within the range of the external or internal organs. That Self, although residing in the body— since a body, which is like a stone, cannot otherwise be the locus of movement— is nevertheless far removed, unlike those things situated in space.

There would be no perception of the sun and other celestial bodies; for "hi" indicates certainty. This light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*) is a light whose nature consists of the awareness of objects.
Why is this so? It is like light. Just as light, which is the seeing of objects, arises from the luminous sun, so too [does this consciousness arise];
such is the meaning.
From whom Viṣṇu and the other gods emerge like rays from the sun, and from whom infinite worlds arise like bubbles from the ocean.

The gods are to be known as twofold: internal (ādhyātmika) and celestial (ādhidaivika). Among these, the celestial are well-known. The internal are as follows: the mind is Brahmā; the intellect is Viṣṇu; the ego is Rudra; and the senses and so forth are the gods. The worlds likewise are to be known as twofold; those that are celestial are well-known.
But the internal ones should be understood as mental volitions.
Into whom all visible multitudes dissolve like waters into the great ocean, and who illuminates both the self and objective entities like a lamp; //MU_3.5.10//

The meaning is that the multitudes of visible objects go toward Him, who is the form of the seer, and dissolve into Him; He whose nature is pure consciousness, who illuminates—like a lamp—both Himself, whose nature is pure awareness, and likewise all objects (the singular "padārtham" is used for the genus, implying "all objects"). // MT 3.5.10 //
He who is established in space and in the body, in visible things, in waters, and in creepers; in dust, in mountains, in winds, and in the netherworlds.

That Self which is situated in space and in the body, as well as in visible stones, in waters, in creepers, in dust, in particles of soil, in rocks, in mountains, in winds, and in the netherworlds—this is merely an illustration; by it, one should understand that the Self is situated everywhere, even in stationary things. How is it that the Self exists within stationary things?
If [you say], "True," then all stationary beings (*sthāvara*), when investigated, ultimately rest in ineffability (*anirvācyatā*) alone;

and since ineffability itself is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the Self (*ātman*), there is no contradiction whatsoever. Alternatively, stationary beings must either be endowed with a self (*sātmaka*) or devoid of a self (*nirātmaka*). If they were devoid of a self, what form could they possibly possess? But if they are endowed with a self, it is clear.
In this way, it should be understood that the self abides within them.
He who drowns the agitated city-of-eight (puryaṣṭaka) here and there, by whom the deluded have been rendered mute, remaining as if fixed in meditation upon a stone.

That which is the Self (ātman)—the "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*), whose nature consists of the three internal organs and the five subtle elements—is, by implication, the group of conscious beings. It causes them to float here and there, leading them wherever they go; that is to say, it causes them to act.
The "deluded" are the insentient; those who have been rendered mute—incapable of reflective awareness—by that Self which exists as their very essence.
Having performed [their duties], they abide in "meditation on stone"—that is, meditation like a stone. They become as if completely inert; that is to say, they become as if utterly dull-witted.
The word "as if" (iva) is employed because even those who are deluded are, in ultimate reality, of the nature of pure consciousness alone.
By whom the sky was made empty, by whom the mountains were made solid, by whom the waters were made fluid, and by whose power the sun blazes; //MU_3,5.13//

By which [power], through its state of possessing all capacities, having resorted to a nature devoid of substantial reality (*nistattvarūpatā*), space (*vyoma*)—that is, the ether (*ākāśa*)—was made empty, its very essence being without substantial reality; likewise, by which, having resorted to the state of clay and stone, through that very self, mountains—the peaks pervaded by it—were made solid, rendered dense and compact; and likewise, by which, having resorted to the state of liquidity...

By means of that Self (*ātman*) which has gone [into them], the waters—that is, the liquids pervaded by it—have been made liquid, being endowed with the quality called fluidity (*dravatva*). Likewise, the sun—the sun situated as the pervader—is illuminated by the power of that Self which has attained the state of light characterized by the nature of burning;
it is by the influence of that Self that it becomes radiant. And this is merely an illustration.
From which flow forth the various rains of the essence-less cycle of existence, like showers from a cloud filled with inexhaustible nectar.

"Imperishable" means free from destruction. "Amṛta" refers to the essence of bliss. From that which is "filled," meaning overflowing with it—from which Self (ātman)—the showers of the essence of saṃsāra, that is, showers in the form of torrents of worldly existence, "proceed," meaning they flow forth. Like what? Like rain-showers. Just as [showers] proceed from a cloud filled with imperishable nectar—that is, filled with indestructible water.
From the cloud, rains flow forth; such is the meaning.
In whom the waves of the three worlds, consisting of manifestation and disappearance, vibrate incessantly like rays of light from the sun.
The waves of the three worlds consist of manifestation and concealment; they are endowed with appearance and disappearance. In what?
In that which, by implication, has the form of an ocean, in which they flash incessantly. Like what? Like rays of light. Just as rays flash in the heat of the sun, so it is here; such is the meaning.
That which is of the nature of non-destruction, whose essence is indestructible, which dwells within all things, which is hidden though distinct, and which is established within all existents.

Just as it is of an indestructible nature, so too, because it exists as the witness even to its own destruction when that destruction is conceived, the Self is devoid of destruction; for the Self becomes the very form of destruction, since it exists even in the state of destruction. Otherwise, how could destruction—which is devoid of a self—be manifest in any form? Likewise, although distinct [from objects], it has a nature transcending all categories of existence by virtue of being pure consciousness alone.

Furthermore: that Self which abides within all entities because it exists as their essence—how could that which is indestructible possess the nature of destruction? Moreover, it is contradictory for that which is distinct from all entities to abide within all entities.
What is the nature of this Self? It is situated within all things; it stands within them as their internal controller. Therefore...
Thus protected, he is invisible from the outside.

By which wind does that creeper of primordial nature dance—nature which has grown in the sky, bearing the great cosmic egg as its excellent fruit, with the mind as its root and the senses as its leaves?

*Prakṛti* is a certain principle that constitutes the root cause of the universe; she alone is the *vratati*, the creeper. By which wind—that is, by which wind in the form of the Self—she dances, meaning she assumes agency through transformation into the state of an effect. Otherwise, since the inertness inherent in the category of effects could not otherwise be accounted for, [it follows that] for her, who is inert in nature, there must be a transformation into the state of an effect.

Because agency is impossible [for the Self]. Of what nature is the creeper of *prakṛti*? It has arisen—that is, it has become manifest—in the void, which is the very nature of space, the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) that possesses no form whatsoever. Likewise, it is such that the cosmic egg itself is its true fruit; it is such that the mind alone is its root; and it is such that the sense organs themselves are its petals.

That [prakṛti] is of such a nature; since it has been stated that prakṛti is established merely as a mental construct by virtue of its being rooted in the mind, one should not raise the objection: "How can prakṛti, which is the fundamental cause of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), have its root in the pure consciousness (cinmātra) of the puruṣa contained within it? MT 3.5.17.
That very jewel which shines within the casket of every body, wherein these rays of the web of worlds flicker like the light of the moon.

The "consciousness-jewel" (*cinmaṇi*) is consciousness itself as a jewel; it is a gem because of its luminosity. That which is the Self (*ātman*), whose nature is that [jewel], shines forth—manifests as the individual soul (*jīva*)—within every casket of a body (*dehasamudgaka*). Otherwise, what would be the form of the individual souls residing within bodies? And it is logical that a jewel should shine within a casket. These are the ones being seen before us.
The world-web is like rays [of light] that shimmer within that moon; otherwise, what support would their appearance have?

For the manifestation of a world-web without a support does not enter the intellect. Furthermore, the world-web's nature as a mirage should be understood through its being the object of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*), since it never departs from the state of being the light of consciousness.
