Indeed, that which is insentient (*acidrūpa*) is incapable of being an object of consciousness.
It occurs because, due to their mutual contradiction, it is impossible for that [other] to be present when this one is present.
In that dense mass of tranquil consciousness, which rains down nectar, all beings flash like torrents of water and clear visions appear like lightning bolts.

O showerer of nectar, showerer of bliss! In that [Self], which is a dense mass of tranquil consciousness, whose nature is like a cloud called "pure, independent consciousness," all beings—all objects—[are present]. The showers of water are the perceptions, which are the cognitions directed toward those objects;
they flash forth clearly and manifestly as lightning. And it is fitting that in a rain-cloud pouring down water, there should be showers of water and flashes of lightning.

And its throbbing, as well as its being a showerer of bliss, should be understood from the fact that the self is the object of supreme love; for one who does not shower bliss cannot be the object of supreme love, since we observe that the status of being an object of love belongs only to those such as sons who shower bliss.
Furthermore, the fact that the self is the object of supreme love is self-evident to everyone, so no further effort is required [to prove it].
When objects produce wonder by their mutual appearance, that through which the non-existent has become existent and that through which existence has attained its being—[that is the Self].

Objects—meaning the various classes of entities consisting of subjects and objects—mutually, that is, through the perception of one another; that is to say, by means of the state of perceiving one another, they experience wonder, meaning they experience bliss. The point is that the very act of perceiving them is the cause of their wonder. This was stated as a general negation with the word "falsely" (*mithyā*). The underlying sense is as follows: the subjects...

To that extent, having experienced desired and undesired objects of enjoyment, they become indifferent toward other objects of enjoyment; otherwise, the experience of the object of enjoyment presented at that time would not reach its conclusion. Furthermore, that state of indifference toward other objects of enjoyment at that time is not established without their experiencing a sense of wonder (*camatkāra*) regarding it. This occurs through what is being experienced in a single object.

Indeed, it is through wonder (*camatkāra*) alone that a person becomes indifferent toward other objects. And when that wonder is investigated, it is found to be the very nature of the Self (*ātman*), because it is the cause of indifference; for it is the Self, whose nature is the state of supreme rest, that is the cause of indifference. Thus, it is entirely logical that the cause of wonder—which consists in the perceiver’s vision of the objects of enjoyment—is the Self itself.

Thus, since this reality is accessible only through direct experience, those possessed of intuitive insight (*pratibhā*) should strive for it themselves; enough with further elaboration. Likewise, by that Self which stands as the witness, the non-existent arose as non-existent; and likewise, by that such Self, existence came to be existent. Without the Witness, there would be no states of being existent or non-existent, nor the actualities of existence and non-existence.
Because it is free from conceptual construction.
In the presence of that Supreme Jewel who abides in peace within himself, this inert body moves even though he has no desire for it.

Because it is devoid of the basis for desire for one who is desireless—that is, for one who is free from longing—and because it is therefore peaceful within itself, it remains for one who abides free from the agitation known as the desire to move. In the presence of that supreme jewel, this "iron"—namely, the body called the physical frame—is inert, being non-conscious by virtue of having the nature of a mere object of perception; yet it moves, it performs activity, [all] due to its being regarded as the cause of bodily movement.

Since the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is also endowed with the power of the self (*ātman*), it is logically impossible for it to be the ultimate cause of bodily movement. The term "supreme" (*parama*) is employed to indicate the absence of insentience inherent in external jewels. And it is logical that iron moves when in proximity to a jewel known as the magnet (*ayaskānta*).
Fate, place, and time, as well as movement, vibration, and actions—by him, who pervades all beings, these have been brought into existence.

*Niyati* is a specific power that brings about restriction among entities. *Deśa* is a particular entity that serves as the substratum for objects. *Kāla* is a certain particular entity whose nature consists merely of measurement (*kalana*), which is inferred from the movement of the sun and other such phenomena, and which acts as the cause of the transformation of entities. *Calana* is general motion. *Spandana* is effort directed toward action. *Kriyā* is action in the form of cooking and so forth.

And this is an illustration. That is to say: by that nature which approaches all beings—that is, which pervades the objects and categories within the entire domain of existence—it has attained existence. For it is only through the pervader that the pervaded attains existence.
Because it consists of pure consciousness, that which is space becomes so through the awareness of space; yet, through the awareness of objects, it remains as the object itself, without being fixed.

Because it consists of pure consciousness (*śuddhasaṃvinmaya*). "Pure" means not having reached a conclusion in any form whatsoever; that which is consciousness is the act of cognizing. Because its nature is that [consciousness], it is "unconcluded," meaning it has not reached a conclusion in any form. By virtue of being the consciousness of space—through the connection with the consciousness "I am space"—it becomes the void (*kha*), the sky (*vyoman*). The meaning is that it becomes something whose nature is the absence of objective entities (*padārthābhāva*).

By virtue of being the knower of categories (*padārthavit*), [the Self] is joined with the cognition "I am a category" (*padārtho ’ham*); thus, it "abides in" or "takes as its basis" (*avatiṣṭhati*) the state of being an object (*arthatva*), that is, the status of being a category.

By the force of the prefix (*upa*), the meaning of the root *sthā* is "taking as a basis. It is stated that it is "not fixed" (*aniṣṭhita*) because a jar, once established in the nature of a jar (*ghaṭatva*), does not go over to the state of a cloth (*paṭatā*).
He concludes the description of his own majesty with this verse at the end of the chapter:

"Even while performing the infinite vibration of the great worlds as if it were so, he never does anything at all; remaining alone, his mind has abandoned rising and staying in the changeless self-awareness that never sets. (MU 3.5.24)

The word "yaḥ" (who) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. He is the Self who, although—as it were—performing an infinite vibration regarding the great universe because the manifestation of the world would otherwise be inexplicable, yet at no time does he perform anything whatsoever, due to the absence of the conceit of agency in his supreme purity; for otherwise, the use of the word "iva" (as it were) would be inappropriate. Of what nature is he? He is one whose consciousness is without setting.

Just as there is no setting [of the sun], so too, because it abides as the witness even to the imagined setting of itself, that consciousness is, in the ultimate sense, devoid of setting. In its own nature—which is likewise changeless and free from modifications such as passion and hatred—one remains established in one's own self, in one's own true form. Furthermore, how is one characterized? One who has abandoned [the notions of] arising and abiding.

He whose mind [is directed] toward the arising and the persistence of the world—that is such a one. The meaning is that he is indifferent toward the arising and the persistence of the world, and by implication, its destruction. Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the fifth canto in the "Chapter on Origination" within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. Having thus established the true nature and majesty of the Supreme Self, and perceiving that Śrī Rāma was eager for its attainment, [the Lord] speaks of the easy means for attaining it:
"Only through knowledge of this Supreme Self, the God beyond gods, is the supreme perfection attained, and not through the exhaustion of ritual performance. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.6)

Of this one whose essential nature has been described—the God of gods, whose nature is unsurpassed play and whose nature is luminosity, the unsurpassed Supreme Self—attainment, which consists in reaching [Him], occurs through knowledge alone, that is, through the means called knowledge. His attainment does not consist in the exhaustion caused by ritual performance; it is not such that it "gives" (bestows) the fatigue that comes from ritual practice. It does not become so.

"But surely, how can there be fitness without practice? To this he replies: "In this case, knowledge itself is the practice; nothing else is required. It has the nature of perceiving the cessation of the delusion of water in a mirage. (MU 3.6.2)

In this regard, within this perfection consisting of the attainment of the Self, there occurs knowledge—the practice, the effort that accomplishes the goal of perfection. Any other practice, distinct from the practice called knowledge and known as bodily activity, is of no use. That knowledge is such that it brings about the cessation of the delusion of water in a mirage. It is by means of that [knowledge] which is of such a nature.
That which is cognition—form is like that; because it possesses this [cognition], it becomes "of such a kind. The meaning is that it becomes the nature of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).

"Now, where does such a Self reside? To this he says: "It is neither far away, nor in space; it is not unattainable, nor is it difficult to reach. Having the nature of the radiance of its own bliss, it is obtained from one's very own body. (MU 3.1.3)

This Self is not far away, because it exists within one's own body; by this, the suspicion that it might reside in great distant pilgrimage sites is dispelled. This Self is not in the sky; by this, the suspicion that it might reside in the worlds above is dispelled.
This Self is unobtainable, meaning it is impossible to acquire as something new; it is not so, because it is eternally obtained, for otherwise it would lack the fitness to be the Self.

By this, the doubt regarding its rarity is dispelled. This Self is "difficult" (viṣama), meaning hard to attain; yet it is not so [in the sense of being cruel], because it is the object of supreme love. Indeed, it is not fitting for that which is hard to be the object of love, and what need is there to mention such a thing for love characterized by its supreme nature? By this, the suspicion of cruelty—like that of a king seized by the intoxication of a mere fragment of sovereignty—is dispelled.

This Self (ātman) is that which, for a person, consists of the manifestation of its own bliss, having the nature of a self-arisen appearance of bliss independent of objects such as sensory enjoyments.
It is obtained from one's own body alone. By the phrase "consisting of the manifestation of its own bliss," the notion of its being something heterogeneous [to the self] is refuted.
By the phrase "from one's own body," the notions of its being distant or residing in space are refuted. By the word "obtained," the notion of its being unobtainable is refuted.
Now, it may be objected that some claim the attainment of the Self is achieved even through austerity and the like; to this he replies:
"In this matter, austerity, charity, vows, and so forth do not contribute anything at all; there is no means here other than resting in one's own true nature. (MU 3.6.4)

In this regard, with respect to this attainment of the Self (*ātmaprāpti*), asceticism, charity, vows, and so forth do not assist it even in the slightest; they provide no benefit at all, because they function as external limbs (*bāhyāṅga*) that contribute only indirectly. For through asceticism and the like, there is only the purification of the inner being (*sattvaśuddhi*), but not the attainment of the Self. In this attainment of the Self, apart from resting in one's own nature—that is, resting in one's true essence—nothing else is required.
Having abandoned [the means], it does not become a proof.
For those who are incapable of resting in the true nature of reality, he explains the means:
"In this matter, dependence solely upon the scriptures, the company of the virtuous, and authentic yogis is the means—the unartificial awakening that destroys the web of delusion. (MU 3.6.5)

In this regard, "here" means in this attainment of the Self (*ātmaprāpti*). "Scripture" (*śāstra*) refers to the inner science (*adhyātmaśāstra*), and that [scripture] along with the company of the good and true yoga constitute "scripture, the company of the good, and true yoga. In that context, "supremacy" (*paratā*) means single-minded devotion; it is not austerity and so forth. It "becomes" the "means" (*sādhana*), that is, the method. What is that means? That which pertains to the "net of delusion" (*mohajāla*) in the world—namely, that which is called the ignorance of the world's true nature.

For the person who is entangled in the snare of delusion—characterized by the proliferation of false knowledge and known as the cognition of "worldliness" regarding the world—the awakening that says "this is indeed Brahman" is uncreated and innate; such is that which effects this awakening.
He describes the primary status as a means toward the repose in the Self—which is the fruit resulting from devotion to the scriptures and so forth—as follows:
"Merely by the thorough recognition that 'This is indeed the Lord,' suffering no longer arises for a person, and he attains liberation while living. (MU 3.6.6)

This cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), consisting of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth, has the nature of manifesting before one as "I-ness" and "this-ness. It is well-known because, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), it exists as the very self-nature of all beings. This is the divine (*deva*), the principle of consciousness (*cittattva*) which is characterized by luminosity and playfulness. By this alone—by the mere fact of thorough comprehension, that is, by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)—[it is realized].

Suffering does not arise for the living being, because even suffering that comes by way of the stream of existence is known to be nothing but consciousness. That living being attains the state of liberation while alive (jīvanmukti), because he is liberated despite the presence of the body.

Unable to accept that asceticism and the like—which are established as means [to liberation]—are not actually the means, and doubting whether this Self is easily accessible or merely nearby, Śrī Rāma asks:
"Is it true that by the mere thorough knowledge of this Self within the self, faults such as death and so forth never again cause affliction? (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.6–7)

In the self— that is, in one's own self— by the mere thorough comprehension, meaning by its being correctly ascertained as the substratum of the world beginning with the "I," the defects such as death and so forth do not afflict [the self]. For when one has attained the state of pure consciousness (*cinmātratā*), the afflictions pertaining to the body, such as death and the like, are not capable of causing any harm.
"In that case, since the object of knowledge has already been known, you should simply maintain silence.
To this, the God of gods replied: "This Great One—whence is He reached from afar? By what intense austerity, or by how much hardship?"

By us, from how far away, or from what distance, is this God of gods attained? Likewise, by what intense austerity is he attained, or else by what degree of hardship consisting of breath-restraint and the like is he attained? For indeed, the attainment of such a God of gods is not possible without austerity and the like, nor without breath-restraint and the like.

For it would follow that everyone would attain it; yet it is not observed that all are possessors of its attainment. Furthermore, it is not logical for that which has not been attained to be an object of knowledge, since it is observed that only things like jars, once attained, become objects of that [knowledge]. This is the intended meaning.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha gives the reply:
"O Rāma, that Divine One is known through one's own human effort and through blossoming discernment, not by means of austerities, ritual baths, or religious rites."

O Rāma, that Lord is known by a person through his own effort consisting of mental exertion— that is, through an expanding inquiry in the form of discernment such as "Who am I? and "What is this world?"— but He is not known through austerities, ritual baths, or rites, because those are solely intent upon the purification of the mind and so forth.

By the phrase "it is known" (*jñāyate*), it is indicated that here only the cognition itself is to be established, not the attainment [of the object]. For in the case of one who, perceiving a mother-of-pearl shell lying before them as silver, desires the attainment of the shell, the attainment of the shell is not what is to be established; rather, it is only the cognition in the form "this is indeed a shell" that is to be established. Why [is it said] "from afar"? [This follows:]
Because this is absolutely unconnected [to the context], no further explanation is given.

It is quite evident that austerity and the like, when joined with passion and other such afflictions, are not means to the goal. However, even if they are means when free from those, it is logical that freedom from passion and the rest alone constitutes the means; with this intention, he says: "O Rāma, without the abandonment of passion, hatred, delusion, anger, pride, and envy, austerity and charity are nothing but suffering, for they lack reality. (MU 3.6.10)
Austerity and giving constitute that which is austerity-giving; it is real, produced by an innate disposition.
When the mind is afflicted by passion and the like, one acquires wealth by deceiving others; therefore, the fruit of that gift belongs to the one for whose sake it was acquired.
Then, from that word *dhana*, the suffix *tasil* is applied, which functions as all case endings (*sārvavibhaktika*).
Whatever vows and other such acts are performed when the mind is afflicted by passion and the like, that is called hypocrisy; its fruit is either negligible or non-existent.
The word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative position.

Since it declares that [the result] has been achieved, one should therefore, through human effort, employ the primary medicine for destroying the disease of cyclic existence: association with true scriptures and virtuous people.

One should acquire—that is, one should exert effort—meaning one should act; for the purpose of destroying the disease called *saṃsṛti*, that is, for the sake of destroying the disease known as cyclic existence (*saṃsṛti*).
In this matter, apart from a single human effort, no other means whatsoever is found to lead to the attainment of the destruction of all suffering.

In this regard, regarding this attainment of the self (*ātmaprāpti*), "human effort" refers to exertion consisting of the investigation of authentic scriptures and so forth; "the way" (*gati*) means the means (*upāya*); and "in the attainment of the destruction of all suffering" means in the attainment whose nature is the destruction of every single form of suffering.
"Now, what is that human effort like? To this he says:
"Listen to what that human effort is like for the sake of attaining self-knowledge, by which the cholera-like diseases of passion and hatred are entirely pacified. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.15)

Listen: what kind of exertion (*pauruṣa*) leads to the attainment of self-knowledge? It is that exertion by which the cholera-like diseases of passion and hatred are pacified without remainder; otherwise, it would not serve as the cause for attaining self-knowledge—this is the sense.

He proceeds to fulfill his promise to describe the true nature of the Self by means of such modes of expression as may be appropriate, provided they are not in conflict with worldly convention or sacred scripture; with a mind satisfied by contentment, he abandons all craving for enjoyments.

According to one's capacity, through diligent effort and with a mind free from agitation, one should first take recourse in devotion to the company of the virtuous and the study of the true scriptures.

By means of a livelihood (*vṛtti*) that follows what is possible according to circumstances, and not one achieved through strenuous effort; [he should abandon] greed for enjoyments (*bhoga-gardha*), that is, craving for enjoyments.
He who is content with whatever he has obtained, who disregards what is censurable, and who delights in the company of the virtuous and in the true scriptures, is swiftly liberated.
That which is censurable is wealth and so forth acquired through unjust means.
"Now, how is it that he is liberated so quickly? To this he replies:
"For the Great-minded One who has fully understood the nature of reality through investigation, these—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Śaṅkara—become objects of compassion. (MU 3.6.19)

By means of discernment—that is, by the investigation established through the power of association with the virtuous and so forth—he has fully understood, meaning he has ascertained his own nature or essential form as being distinct from the body and other such things. For such a person of great intelligence, who is endowed with wisdom, even these—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Śaṅkara—are objects of compassion. Of what sort are they? They are those whose nature consists in being intent upon activities such as the creation of the world.
They become objects of compassion in the form of thinking, "There is indeed calamity for them"; what more need be said? The sense is: how might their swift liberation come about?
"Now, you have first stated that association with the virtuous alone is the means; but who indeed might that virtuous person be with whom one should associate? To this he replies:
"He whom people generally call 'virtuous' because he is for the most part well-born—that is the distinguished one, that is the virtuous person; one should resort to him with effort. (MU 3.6.20)

"Consisting mostly of good people" (*sujanaprāyam*) means "for the most part good people. By the use of the word *prāya* ("mostly"), there is the exclusion of both goodness and badness in a person who, though actually good, is called "good" by relatives for some specific purpose, and in a person who, though actually bad, is called "bad" by wicked people whose sole delight is in slandering others. (MT 3.6.20)
Having established what is right, he now establishes the conclusion of the scriptures:

"Among all branches of knowledge, the science of the self (adhyātmavidyā) is the foremost; that scripture which takes its support from its discourse is called a true scripture (sacchāstra), and one who investigates it is liberated. (MU 3.6.21)

Among all branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), that is, among all forms of cognition, the inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*), which is the knowledge of the self (*ātmajñāna*), is preeminent. Therefore, the wise call a treatise (*śāstra*) that relies upon its discourse—that is, one which expounds the inner science—a "true scripture" (*sacchāstra*).
A person who possesses investigation into that, meaning a person endowed with inquiry into the aforementioned true scripture, is liberated from the bondage created by cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
One becomes liberated. Therefore, the implication is that only the inner science (adhyātmaśāstra) is applicable here.
Having clarified with a verse at the end of the chapter that discrimination arising from the study of authentic scriptures and the like is the primary means [to liberation], he states:

"By means of discriminations born from the company of the virtuous and the study of authentic scriptures, impurities are forcibly destroyed, just as the turbidity of waters is removed by contact with *kataka* nuts, or as the dullness of the ignorant is dispelled by the consumption of the *abhaya* herb. (MU 3.6.22)
The impurities consist of passion (*rāga*) and so forth; in the context of people, they consist of dust (*rajas*). *Kataka* is a specific substance that purifies water.

He states the second illustration: "Just as for the dull-witted" (*yathā jaḍānām*). "Dull-witted" means those who lack self-discrimination. "Through the employment of fearlessness" (*abhayopayogāt*): through fearlessness given by someone; the employment (*upayoga*) performed is that which is called consolation.
Therefore, the impurities—which take the form of fear produced by [the delusion of] a rope-snake and the like—perish; such is the meaning of "likewise.
For those who possess discernment, these perish through their own inquiry and become fearlessness; thus it is said, "[they perish] for the dull-witted. May there be auspiciousness! MT 3.6.22.
Thus ends the sixth canto in the "Section on Origination" of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Considering that the attainment of the Self could not be achieved without traveling to a distant land and employing a web of means, Śrī Rāma once again asks the very same question as stated before:
"O Lord, tell me where this deity who was mentioned—by knowing whom one is liberated—is situated, and how may I obtain him? (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.7)

Tell me: of this god whom you have described, and by knowing which god a person is liberated—that is, attains liberation—where does that god abide? And how, by what means, shall I obtain—that is, reach—that very god?
The venerable Vasiṣṭha speaks the reply:
"This deity who has been described does not abide at a distance; he is eternally situated within the body, renowned as pure consciousness alone."

This God whom I have described does not abide at a distance or in a far-off place, for He is renowned and well-known as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). He is eternally situated within the body; otherwise, the body—which would be like a stone—would lack the capacity for movement, just like a dead body. Furthermore, that which resides within the body cannot be said to be distant.
It is appropriate to say that even in the case of one's own hands, there is no conjunction because they are situated at a distance; such is the intended meaning.

"Is it not then the case that this [Self] must be of the same size as the body? And if so, like the body, it would also be non-eternal? To this he says: "This is all this universe; but the universe is not this. This alone exists as the one, omnipresent; there is no vision [of reality] that is designated as the 'universe'. (MU 3.7.3)

This Self is this entire universe, this entire world; it exists as the essence of all, because it abides as the core of everything. However, in the alternative view, that [Self] is all-pervading and, as the essence, pervades all objects; yet this [Self] does not *become* the universe, for it exists as one alone. "The vision named 'universe'" means the vision that has the name "universe"—that is to say, the vision known as the universe.

It does not exist; for even while the universe appears, its nature as that [Brahman] is not lost from the perspective of one who sees it thus. Indeed, when water is overtaken by waves, there does not arise a perception that designates it as "waves," because even while the waves appear, their nature as water is not lost from the perspective of a person possessing discernment.

[Objection: But surely Śaśibhṛt (the Moon-bearer) and others are also the very nature of the Great Deity; so why have you said, "He alone truly exists as one"? To this, he replies: "This Moon-bearer is pure consciousness alone; the Eagle-bannered One is pure consciousness alone; the Sun is pure consciousness alone; and the Lotus-born One is pure consciousness alone. (MU 3.7.4)
This one, renowned as the creator and destroyer, the moon-bearer Śrī Mahādeva, is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).

If it is asked, "How can this be so?"—the answer is true. Is the moon-bearer sentient or devoid of sentience? If he were insentient, being of the nature of stone, his state of security and well-being would be identical to that of the lowest beings in the world. But if he is sentient, then [his identity with consciousness] is clear.

It is pure consciousness alone that manifests in the form of those various states. If it is objected, "In that case, there would be total equality between the moon-bearing [Śiva] and a worm," we reply:
who has said that such equality does not exist? If it is argued, "A difference must be postulated because their effects are seen to be dissimilar," this is an improper postulation.
Indeed, one cannot postulate a difference between a spark of fire and a great mass of fire on the basis of the dissimilarity of their effects.

[The opponent] says: "It is logical. But surely there is no difference in the effects produced by a spark of fire and a great mass of fire, since we observe a single effect called 'burning' in both cases. [The author replies: "Then the same applies to the moon and a glowworm as well. What difference in effect exists between them, given that the action of cognition and the action of illumination are one and the same? As for the distinction caused by their greater or lesser magnitude, that exists in the case of the illustrative example as well."

There is no contradiction whatsoever; the same should be applied elsewhere as well. Garuḍadhvaja is the presiding deity over maintenance (*sthiti*). Tapana is the Sun, who effects the ripening of the objects within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). Kamalodbhava is Śrī Brahmā, the presiding deity over creation (*sarga*). When the internal meaning is intended, Śaśibhṛt is the ego (*ahaṅkāra*); Garuḍadhvaja is the intellect (*buddhi*); Tapana is the vital breath (*prāṇa*); and Kamalodbhava is the mind (*manas*).
Thus it should be applied. //MT_3,7.4 //
Śrī Rāma asks:
"If even children say that the world is merely consciousness, what indeed could be the purpose of instruction in this matter?"

If the world were merely consciousness, then it would simply be so; that is to say, this alone would be the truth. In that case, even children would say this, for everyone indeed speaks of the world as consisting of *jīva*, which is a synonym for consciousness.

Therefore, what could there be here that is called "instruction" (*upadeśatā*), since instruction consists precisely in making known what was previously unknown? In this context, "children" refers to...
By this, the Buddhist Vijñānavādins are included; for they alone assert that consciousness—of which "volition" (cetanā) is a synonym—is the self.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha replies:
That which you have understood—that the universe is pure consciousness and the conscious principle—is not at all that knowledge which brings about liberation from existence.

The conscious one is pure consciousness; that which is called consciousness is pure consciousness. The universe becomes [this]. Thus it is. You are that which you have known. By you, this—though even by a mere fraction—has not been understood: the means of crossing over, the deliverer from saṃsāra.
This is because of your lack of familiarity with the reality of pure consciousness. For indeed, by the mere knowledge of the reality of pure consciousness, saṃsāra [is transcended].
It perishes.
"How is this so? To this he says:
"That which is called consciousness is the cycle of existence; this living being is known as a bound soul (paśu). From this very source emerge the waves of old age and death."

The term *nāma* (name) signifies determination. Consciousness (*cetana*) becomes *saṃsāra* (the cycle of existence), because for that which abides in pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), the very orientation toward an object of thought (*cetyaunmukhya*) constitutes consciousness, and that same orientation toward an object of thought constitutes *saṃsāra*. For *saṃsāra* is said to be "wandering" (*saṃsaraṇa*), and wandering is rising up from one's own place. And at the moment when pure consciousness is oriented toward an object of thought, it departs from its own place, which consists of pure consciousness alone.

Otherwise, what indeed would "orientation" (*aunmukhyatva*) be, if there were no such thing as "arising"? By the wise, this transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), which is of the nature of consciousness (*cetana*), is called the "individual soul" (*jīva*). One who is like a beast (*paśu*) due to being devoid of knowledge of one's own true nature is called a "beast"; and the individual soul is traditionally defined as the agent of the activity of living. Furthermore, consciousness itself is precisely living. Therefore, by metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of that [consciousness] to that which possesses it, it is [said to be] of the very nature of consciousness.

The state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) arises; however, the recourse to metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) for that which possesses [the quality] is made here in order to eliminate the notion of any other means of action distinct from the act of living, regarding the living soul whose ultimate nature is pure consciousness alone. [Objection:
But what follows from that? [Response: To this he says, "Precisely from this": "the waves of old age and death" refers to the ripples of old age and death residing in the body and so forth.
From this very volition alone they emerge, depart, and—so to speak—manifest.
The meaning is that for the dreamer, there are no waves of old age and death belonging to the dream-body.
Furthermore, he says this very thing again:
"For the animal, though insentient and formless, is indeed a vessel for suffering; because of its sentience, it perceives this, and thus, remaining itself, it is established in extreme misfortune."

"Amūrtaḥ" means being distinct from the gross and subtle bodies. Likewise, "of suffering alone" means of that very suffering which takes the form of the manifold world (prapañca) produced by itself. He is "the vessel," meaning he has become a receptacle for it, because he arises from pure consciousness (cinmātra) in that very form; otherwise, even his arising would be purposeless. Similarly, "ignorant" (ajñaḥ) means devoid of the reflective awareness (parāmarśa) of one's own true nature, which is called pure consciousness alone.

For this very reason, even though he is a *paśu* (bound soul), being equal to a beast, this *jīva*—because he is conscious (*cetana*), that is, because his essential nature is pure consciousness—perceives (*cetati*) this world, consisting of egoity (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth, which is his own manifesting form appearing before him; he makes it the object of his own manifestation. For this indeed is the consciousness of a conscious being: that he perceives something whatsoever; thus it is said "because he is conscious. Now, [one might object]:
"What was accomplished by that volition? To this he replies: "It is *ati*. Therefore, the "great misfortune" (*atyanartha*) is the world-form;
it has "remained," meaning it has manifested, of its own accord and without his will. And in this regard, the dream serves as an obvious illustration, so no further effort is required.
"Now, might this suffering of this conscious being ever cease? To this he replies:
"That state which is freedom from consciousness, or rather, the orientation toward the unconscious—that is its state of fullness; having known that, one does not grieve. (MU 3.7.9)

The state of liberation from the object of thought (*cetya*) first occurs by becoming oriented toward the object through its own autonomy, then by means of inquiry, and finally by emerging from it. Alternatively, it is the state of being turned away from the object of thought, which is precisely the absence of orientation toward the object of thought.
This is the state of the conscious subject (*cetana*); it is the state of fullness, the state of plenitude, existing by virtue of its own nature as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).

Because of its fullness. Having known that state of being filled—that is, having ascertained it as the very nature of the ultimate reality—one does not grieve; one does not become a partaker of the suffering called saṃsāra. This is because, through the state of being filled, there is the knowledge of the unreality of the consciousness residing within oneself, and consequently, the knowledge of the unreality of the suffering described therein. And here, freedom from the object of thought (*cetya*) occurs in the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).
It occurs as an orientation toward the non-conceptual state in the condition of disembodied liberation (*videhamuktatā*); such is the distinction to be understood.
"But what will be the state of this conscious being at that time? To this, it is said:
"The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut away, and his karmas are exhausted when That, which is both the high and the low, is seen. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9)

When that [Supreme Consciousness], which is well-known for existing as the self of all, is seen— that is, when it is realized in its ultimate sense as one's own nature within the Great Consciousness (mahācinmātra), which consists of both the supreme form of pure consciousness and the non-supreme form of the conscious self— then, in this state of fullness once known, the "knot of the heart" (hṛdayagranthi) of this conscious being— the knots concerning objects such as enjoyments— is severed, meaning it perishes.

Because of being satisfied; likewise, all doubts—that is, all uncertainties concerning the true nature of things—are severed, due to the certainty that pure consciousness alone is the essence. Likewise, actions—those actions performed for the sake of maintaining the body—are exhausted, because they no longer produce any residual impressions (lepa).
[Objection: "In that case, I shall simply establish that very state of being turned away from the object of thought (*cetyonmukhatva*), which is the ultimate to be attained. To this, he replies:

"But its state of being turned away from the object of thought cannot be obstructed without the non-existence of the object of thought. How indeed can the visible world, which is the object of thought, be stilled? (MU 3.7.11)

The state of being oriented toward the object of thought (*cetya*)—which brings about the condition of being a conscious subject (*cetana*)—is the orientation toward that which is to be thought. Without the non-existence of the object of thought, this [orientation] cannot be obstructed; for fire fallen upon a bundle of cotton does not become extinguished by itself. [Objection: "In that case, I shall simply destroy the object of thought itself. To this, he says: "The object of thought" (*cetyam*). The visible, whose very nature is to be seen, is the object of thought.

How could it be pacified? It cannot be pacified at all, because that which exists cannot undergo destruction. This is the point: if there is an object of cognition (*cetya*), how could it be pacified? If it does not exist, then the absence of any inclination toward objects of cognition is established by itself. Therefore, an effort to bring about its removal is not appropriate except through mere knowledge; for no one ever contemplates the destruction of the son of a barren woman.
It is performed.
In this regard, Śrī Rāma asks:
"O Brahmin, tell me, what is that Supreme Self like which is seen through the company of the virtuous and the true scriptures as the one who carries one across the ocean of worldly existence?"

O Brahmin, by means of association with the virtuous and the study of authentic scriptures, a person [realizes] that saṃsāra itself is an ocean because it is so difficult to cross; therefore, tell me: what is that Supreme Self who is seen as the one who delivers from it?
What is He like?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha, disregarding Śrī Rāma’s question, reiterates the very point previously stated:
"Those who desire this conscious individual soul—which is shattered within the jungle of births—even if they are learned, are indeed ignorant."
This conscious being, which is born in the wilderness of saṃsāra and becomes fragmented and limited, is what is called the *jīva*.
Those who desire this as the Self are wise only in comparison to those who identify the body with the Self;
yet even they are ignorant, because they perceive the *jīva*—which is not the Self—as the Self.
How is this so? To this he says:
"In this world, the living self alone is the transmigrator because of its connection with the continuity of suffering; when this is known, nothing remains unknown anywhere. (MU 3.7.14)

The transmigrations (*saṃsāra*) are those distinguished by the divisions of waking and so forth. Because they cause the continuity of suffering, they belong to the individual soul (*jīva*) alone, since it experiences the continuity of suffering pertaining to the transmigratory state by virtue of being its own substratum. Therefore, when this soul, which is the substratum of transmigration, is known—that is, when it is reached through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—something is "cognized," meaning it has been made an object of knowledge and reached through figurative indication.
It does not exist.
"In that case, by the knowledge of what is something attained? To this he replies:
"O Rāma, if the Supreme Self is known, then the succession of sufferings comes to an end, just as cholera ceases when the influence of poison has subsided. (MU 3.7.15)

O Rāma, if the reality of the Supreme Self—which exists as the essence of the individual soul (jīva) that has been described—is known, or [in other words] attained through its defining characteristics, then the continuous stream of suffering in the form of saṃsāra goes to its end, that is, reaches destruction. The meaning is that at that very moment, something truly attained comes into being. Like what? Like the cessation of thirst upon obtaining water. Just as when one obtains water, the thirst that was previously present perishes; so too, when the Supreme Self is realized, the entire succession of worldly suffering is destroyed. Thus it is said: "When the Supreme Self is realized, the succession of suffering ceases. This is the sense. Furthermore, this is not merely a matter of words; it is established by the scriptures and by reasoning. For it is stated in the *Śruti*: "When to the knower of Brahman everything has become the Self, then what should one see and through what? And in the *Smṛti*: "When to the seer all beings have become the Self, then who is there to be seen and through whom? Therefore, the realization of the Supreme Self is the means for the cessation of the succession of suffering. Thus it is said: "The succession of suffering ceases when the Supreme Self is realized. This is the meaning. Furthermore, this is not a mere assertion; it is supported by scriptural authority and logical proof. Like cholera: the meaning is that just as cholera comes to an end once the onset of the poison has subsided, so it is here.

Śrī Rāma, filled with an intense longing to hear about the nature of the Supreme Self, asks again about the nature of the Self—though his question was previously disregarded by Śrī Vasiṣṭha as being unfit for discourse—saying:
"O Brahman, tell me truly the form of the Supreme Self, by seeing which a person shall cross over all delusion."
Form is its own nature; it is as it truly is, correctly.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha, having ascertained Śrī Rāma’s fitness for instruction through his intense longing, speaks the reply: "The form of consciousness that exists in the interval between the body of one who has traveled from one distant land to another, even in the blink of an eye—that is the nature of the Supreme Self."

From one location—that is, from a single perceivable form which has been made the object—[to another] distant [location], meaning extremely distinct; [to] another location, called "perceived by something else," which is being taken as the objective domain; in a mere blink of an eye, that is, in a single moment, and not having experienced any confusion in the interim; [this refers to] consciousness which has reached [that state] by way of becoming the object and thus apprehends it.
Of the consciousness (cit) which is oriented toward the grasping of the visible, in its intermediate state— interposed between the previously and subsequently perceived and colored by passion—
that very form which exists, that ineffable essential nature which exists, that alone, and not something else similar to it, becomes the form of the Supreme Self (paramātman),
the reality of the Supreme Self who is the essence of all individual souls (jīvātman), because of His being composed of all things.

This is because it transcends everything. Now, one might ask: when consciousness takes the previously experienced object as its support and simultaneously takes the subsequently experienced object as its support, what is this so-called "middle" state wherein the consciousness abiding therein is said to be the nature of the Supreme Self? It is replied:

for consciousness colored by the previously experienced object, its own stainless nature has not yet been attained; [this middle state refers to] that which is about to be produced by the subsequently experienced object...

Because passion is untenable, it must be understood that this intermediate state consisting of a stainless nature necessarily exists. Just as in the case of a cloth dyed with indigo, when one desires to apply a yellow dye, the washing away [of the blue] reveals the intermediate state consisting of the pure cloth; otherwise, it would be impossible to apply the yellow dye that is intended to be applied. [Objection: But [is there not] the object previously experienced...
The previous consciousness has already ceased, while a new one has arisen with the subsequent object of cognition as its domain; thus, that which is called the "middle" is indeed empty.

If it is asked, "Does the self exist as something whose nature is purely empty?", the answer is no, because at the time of grasping the subsequent object of cognition, the recollection of the previously cognized object is impossible. For [the self] does not exist in the middle in a pure form during the time of grasping the previously cognized object.

Without a single consciousness (*saṃvit*) that persists even at the time of grasping a subsequent object of cognition, memory regarding a previously cognized object would not be possible. By this, the essence of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*), when devoid of the coloring of objects of cognition and untinged by insentience (*jāḍya*), is declared to be the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
For those who practice here, the attainment of the Supreme Self will occur before long and without effort. And of this very [Self]...

There exists a state known as "entry into the middle abode"; enough with this disclosure of secrets. And in this regard, because the middle between two similar objects of cognition is extremely difficult to attain, it is described as being "far away."
The absolute non-existence of the cycle of existence and the world's condition exists within that great ocean of consciousness which is the nature of the Supreme Self.

In that great ocean called Awakening, within the vast sea known as enlightenment, there is the absolute non-existence—indeed, an absence throughout the three periods of time—of the world’s persistence, of the very nature of the world’s existence, and of saṃsāra, like a bubble. That is the form of the Supreme Self; this is the state of being. The seeker of liberation, through the means of authentic scriptures and so forth, first [realizes this] by means of the analogy of the rope-snake and other such examples.

Then, having ascertained through the analogy of the golden bracelet and so forth that there is no existence of the visible world apart from Brahman, and having attained certainty in the identity with the pure consciousness-principle (*śuddha-cittattva*), when one experiences everywhere only the pure consciousness-principle by the power of practice— just as a goldsmith perceives only gold in bracelets and other ornaments— then that which constitutes his own essential nature is itself the essential nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Thus [it is said]. Now, an absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) having the world as its counter-correlative (pratiyogin) is not possible; for since the world existed previously, even if the absolute non-existence of the world is ascertained, it must be admitted that the world was indeed appearing previously. To this we reply: this is incorrect.

For when a false appearance of an object in a prior time is ascertained at a later time, that constitutes its being the counter-correlative of an absolute non-existence across all three periods of time (traikālikābhāva).

It does not negate [the rope's nature], because it would follow that even when the rope previously appeared as a snake, the rope would be subject to the negation of the absolute non-existence of the snake.

However, in the case of a rope that previously appeared as a snake, everyone clearly perceives that the snake is the counter-positive of its own absolute non-existence throughout the three periods of time; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
That wherein the sequence of seer and seen, though present, has utterly set; that which is not space, yet is space—that is the form of the Supreme Self.

Even while remaining present and appearing directly, this sequence of seer and seen— consisting of the form "this is the seer" and "this is the seen"— comes to an end, that is, reaches dissolution, completely and perfectly, with respect to that reality (vastu). Now, how can the sequence of seer and seen, which persists [in ordinary experience], [be resolved] in another?
If it is argued that, because [the self] arises from dissolution (*layasambhava*), it is therefore improper to describe the nature of the Supreme Self by means of this [distinction], we say:

no. First of all, do the seer and the seen appear to some witness or not? If they do not, how then can their status as seer and seen be established? Even if their establishment occurs in whatever manner, how can there be a fixed distinction between them?

It is established: if it is realized that "this seer is indeed this very object seen," then their dissolution into that [Seer] is indeed easy. For it is not possible for the seer and the seen appearing in a dream to exist in any form whatsoever apart from the witness of the dream;
thus, there is no contradiction. Likewise, whatever object exists is without space (anākāśa), because its sole nature is that of the grasper.

Because it lacks the nature of being an object of perception (*grāhyatva*), although it is distinct from space which has the single nature of being an object of perception, it becomes "space" (*ākāśa*). The meaning is that, by virtue of qualities such as all-pervasiveness and transparency, it becomes denotable by the word "space. That very thing is that [reality] itself; it is not something else merely similar to it.
It is the form of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
That which is empty yet as if non-empty, in which emptiness the world is situated—that emptiness which exists even while the flood of creation persists, that is the form of the Supreme Self.

That entity which is empty—by virtue of being ungraspable by the external and internal senses—is not some kind of form whatsoever; yet it exists as if non-empty, as if it were something. Otherwise, it would be impossible for it to serve as the substratum for the delusion of the world's form. For a non-existent entity cannot function as the substratum for anything, as that would entail the absurd consequence that even the son of a barren woman could be the substratum for the delusion of Maitra.

Likewise, in that which is empty—of the nature of emptiness according to the logic already stated—in which the world resides as a possessor of existence, just as jars and other objects reside in clay; for otherwise, what would be the nature of the world? Such is the sense. Likewise, while the flood of creation—that is, the multitude of emanations—exists, whether by way of being governed or by way of being an effect, that which is empty [remains].

It exists as being devoid of any entity distinct from itself. Indeed, it is not possible to conceive that a rope is joined with a distinct entity by virtue of its state as a snake, nor that clay is joined with a distinct entity by virtue of its state as a pot. That is the nature of the Supreme Self.
That which is composed of pure consciousness, though vast like a great stone, is insentient on the outside yet sentient within; such is the nature of the Supreme Self.

Whatever object there may be—though it consists of the Great Consciousness (mahācinmaya), and though its nature is the light of Great Consciousness because otherwise the state of being the witness of the entire universe would be untenable—it remains like a massive stone; it becomes as if utterly insentient, because due to its extreme tranquility, it is averse to autonomous self-reflection even when such reflection occurs. But what is it like? Internally, in the ultimate sense...

In its own nature, it is indeed non-inert; the meaning is that the inert appears as if inert. These two qualifiers should be understood as supporting the meaning stated in the first half-verse by way of reversing their respective order. That is the form of the Supreme Self.
That form of the Supreme Self, by attaining union with which everything—both external and internal—attains its own essential existence, is that very nature.

The entire world— everything existing as external and internal, including both the exterior and the interior— having attained a connection or relation with that Reality which exists as the Witness; that is to say, having attained the state of being its object, it attains its own individual existence, the existence of its particular form, without [the act of] manifestation apart from the cognition of the Witness.
For even though blue, pleasure, and so forth exist, their existence is seen to be like that of a non-entity; therefore, that becomes the form of the Supreme Self.
Just as light belongs to illumination, and as emptiness belongs to the sky, so is this established wherein that is the form of the Supreme Self.

Just as light, which is luminous energy, is a specific quality called radiance that causes objects to become manifest, or just as emptiness is the state of being void in the sky— that is, in space— so too is this world situated within that invisible reality; that is the form of the Supreme Self.

This is the meaning: just as light, while appearing, is not described as being primarily itself—otherwise, it would be impossible to describe it as having the quality of illumination—and yet, when examined, that very illumination is found to be ultimately indefinable; so too this world, while appearing, is situated within some indefinable, essential primary principle.

It should be understood that that in which [the world] is established is indeed the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Now, one might object: by these [arguments], the status of the Supreme Self has been established for some entity accessible through inference (*anumāna*); thus, it should be known that this Supreme Self is merely conceptualized (*kalpita*), because whatever is accessible through inference is conceptualized. This is because only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is accessible solely through non-conceptual direct perception (*nirvikalpa-pratyakṣa*), possesses ultimate reality (*paramārtha-sattva*).

If this is argued, it is incorrect. Although the nature of the Supreme Self—which is the very essence of the one being instructed—manifests through direct perception at every moment during its intermediate states, it remains unknown as the Self; thus, your Self is like a kinsman standing before you who has been forgotten for a long time. Therefore, for those possessing discernment, there is no room here for even the touch of inference. As for those lacking discernment...
But in this case, there is no qualification at all; therefore, enough with deliberating upon the faults and virtues of others.
Śrī Rāma asks:
How indeed is this Supreme Self understood as being beyond everything? And from what cause does the non-existence of this visible world, known as the "universe," arise?

By us, how indeed can this Supreme Self—whose nature is distinct from the world—be fully realized in every respect, that is to say, in all places and in all states? For since this visible world, which pervades both the external and the internal, is impossible [in its ultimate reality], how could it exist? Indeed, in the waking state, the gross world manifests; [but] in the dream...

The dream state is the world; in deep sleep, there is insentience. There is no state apart from these. And this question was posed by Śrī Rāma, who always desires to attain the nature of the Supreme Self, without relying on an intermediate state that consists of the pure nature of the Supreme Self and which flashes forth every moment during the waking state.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha says in reply:
"If there were a firm conviction regarding the absolute non-existence of this worldly delusion, which has arisen like the color of the sky," ||| MU_3,7.25 |||
That form of Brahman is known through that [realization], and not by any other action; for there is no other auspicious path except for the absolute non-existence of the visible world.

Like the color of space—that is, for that which has arisen and appeared, this world which manifests before one—there is the awakening to its absolute non-existence, the knowledge of its absolute non-existence; it is not what is called "destruction. That [knowledge] in which there is power established through conventional usage—if such a thing were to exist, then at that time, it would be the form, the very nature, of Brahman, the Supreme Self.

It would have to be known by some other action distinct from this, such as austerity and the like; it would not [be achieved] otherwise. For, apart from the absolute non-existence of the perceptible—that is, without the absolute non-existence of the perceptible—there is no other auspicious state or auspicious means. And the absolute non-existence of the perceptible is established only through the gateway of knowledge, not through an absence that is produced by effort.

The statement "because it is a non-existence by way of destruction" (pradhvaṃsābhāvatvāt) is an explanation of how the cognition of absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva)—such as the absolute non-existence of silver in mother-of-pearl or the absolute non-existence of a jar in clay—serves as a means [to the realization of the ultimate].

[Objection: But how can the absolute non-existence of the world, characterized by its visibility, which is established through the gateway of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), serve as the means for attaining the Supreme Self? To this, he says:
"When there is the realization of the absolute non-existence of this visible world, that which remains in its true state is the Supreme Reality; it is then awakened to and known. (MU 3.2.7)
This refers to that which exists exactly as it is, and not to that which has been destroyed by effort. Regarding this visible world-form, which is itself visible:

when there is the attainment of its absolute non-existence—that is, when its absolute non-existence is established, just like the absolute non-existence of silver perceived in mother-of-pearl, or like the absolute non-existence of a jar perceived in clay—then that ultimate reality is the substratum of the visible.

Or rather, this Supreme Self is the essential core of all that is perceived; it remains as the residue, like the mother-of-pearl when there is the cognition of the absolute non-existence of silver, or like the clay when there is the cognition of the absolute non-existence of a pot. Since nothing else exists apart from it, it is understood by the person through the indirect cognition "it exists," and is thereby ascertained. Thereafter, immediately following that...
It is known; it is ascertained through the immediate cognition "I."

[Objection: "Granted that the absolute non-existence of the visible may not be established as a means to knowledge; nevertheless, the knowledge of the Supreme Self will arise through forgetfulness alone, which is accomplished by a web of means such as the restraint of breath (prāṇarodhana). To this, he says: "Consciousness never exists anywhere without the reflection [of the visible], apart from the absence of the visible. Where indeed does a mirror remain without a reflection? (MU 3.7.28)

The nature of consciousness (*cittattva*) exists as a witness; that is to say, it does not exist anywhere as something devoid of the reflection of the object, since it is established as its own witness only through the absence of the object. This means it does not fail to exercise the state of being a witness to the object, for that would entail the consequence of abandoning its very nature. To provide proof for this, he states an illustrative example: where...
He disciplines [the mind]. The point is that a mirror is never seen to exist as a mere substrate when devoid of a reflection. Now, one might object:

even when the object exists in another location, the mirror is indeed seen to be devoid of a reflection; likewise, let there be the existence of external objects. However, consciousness (*cit*), by means of the restraint of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, does not flow outward and is thus devoid of contact with the visible world.
If it is argued that [the seed] will [perish], this is incorrect; for without the knowledge of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), it is impossible to destroy the seed of the perceivable.

Otherwise, the manifestation of the manifold world of dreams would not occur within one who is asleep. If it is objected that dream-appearance occurs for such a person because they lack means such as breath-restraint (*prāṇarodha*), then [we reply]: consider those who, though devoid of the knowledge of the absolute non-existence of the perceivable and free from deceit, nevertheless practice breath-restraint and other such methods.

Ask them this: "Do you possess the manifestation of a dream, or not? Have we not indeed already asked those who are free from deceit and endowed with the knowledge of the absolute non-existence of the perceptible? They too have stated that they themselves experience the appearance of dreams. Let it be said; what is the harm? Just as the world appears while awake, so too do they possess the knowledge of its absolute non-existence.
Even in a dream, they do not perceive the visible object as something merely appearing as an object of sight; rather, they perceive it as Brahman. Enough with this elaboration.

[Objection: "Even so, do we not perceive the reality of the Self even without the absolute non-existence of the visible world? To this, he says: "Without the possibility of the existence of this visible world called the universe, the supreme reality is never understood by anyone at any time. (MU 3.7.29)

Without the existence— that is, without the absolute non-existence— of this world, which flashes forth before us, which possesses the name "world," and which consists of the multitude of objects that are the targets of the act of seeing, no person has ever, at any time, realized the supreme reality known as the Supreme Self; therefore, there is the absolute non-existence of the visible world.
The intended meaning is that it is to be accomplished by means of right knowledge.

Doubting the non-existence of the visible world, Śrī Rāma asks: "O Sage, how can there be non-existence for this entire web of the visible—the cosmic egg and the stability of the universe? Where is Mount Meru within the belly of a mustard seed?"

This refers to an exaggerated statement (*vaipulyakathana*). For example, when someone says that Mount Meru exists within the interior of a mustard seed, the meaning of that statement rests solely on its demonstration of an impossibility;
the same applies to you, who propound that the existence of the world does not exist. This is the intended sense.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha says in reply:
"O Rāma, if you remain for a few days with an undaunted mind, intent upon the company of the virtuous and the true scriptures, then in an instant—"
I wipe away your perception of the visible world, which is like a mirage; when the visible is absent, the state of being a perceiver also subsides, and pure awareness alone remains.
O Rāma, if you remain for some days— meaning, for however many days— with an undistressed mind (akhinnadhīḥ), that is to say, with a focused intellect,
being devoted to the company of the virtuous and the study of the true scriptures,
then at that moment, I shall in an instant wipe away from you— that is, before you— the visible world, which consists of the realm of the seen.

"I destroy" means that I bring about the state of being endowed with absolute non-existence by means of knowledge. What is it like? It is like awakening (*bodha*). Just as awakening, which is right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), wipes away the water of a mirage—such is the meaning.

By this, it is stated that association with the virtuous and so forth is the primary means for the knowledge of the absolute non-existence of the visible world (*dṛśya*). [Objection: But by the wiping away of the visible...

"What will be established? To this he says: "In the absence of the visible. When the absence of the visible is established by means of knowledge—that is, when the absence of the visible has been proven—the state of being a seer (*draṣṭṛtā*) is stilled and goes to dissolution. [Objection: "In that case, is it not the case that only non-existence remains? To this he says: "Consciousness" (*bodha*). Consciousness is the pure essence of mind (*cittattva*), which serves as the witness to the absolute non-existence of both the visible and the seer; it is what remains.
Something remains [to be explained]. Otherwise, even for a perceptible absolute non-existence that has been established, it would follow that it is a mere conceptual fiction (asatkalpa).

Now, one might ask: "How does the state of being a seer come to rest simply through the absolute non-existence of the seen? To this, he says: "The state of being a seer exists only when this seen object exists; the state of being the seen exists only when there is a seer. For duality exists only when there is unity, and unity exists only when there is the perception of duality. (MU 3.33)
While this collection of objects— which has the nature of appearing before one, which is the domain of the act of seeing, and which possesses existence— exists, the state of being a seer would,

from the perspective of ultimate reality, belong to the seer whose nature is pure consciousness alone; for it is possible for agency toward the act of seeing to arise only when there is the existence of an object,
just as, for instance, when rice and other such things exist, there is agency toward the act of cooking with respect to them.

Just as agency belongs to the person who performs the action, so too does the state of being a cook belong [to him]. It is not the case that the seer possesses the status of a seer solely through the existence of the object seen; rather, with the intention of showing that the object seen possesses the status of being seen also through the existence of the seer, he says "dṛśyatvam" (the state of being seen).
"Avekṣake" means in the observer—that is, in the seer—when he exists, meaning while he maintains his existence.

If visibility were real from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), then the state of being an object (*dṛśyabhāva*) would have to reside in the object that is essentially pure consciousness (*śuddhacinmātrasvarūpa*). For it is not the case that rice and the like, once made the object of the act of cooking by a cook, assume the state of being cooked (*pācyabhāva*), which is synonymous with the state of being boiled rice (*odana*). Therefore, since the mere object of sight absolutely does not exist through mutual dependence, the state of being a seer (*draṣṭṛtā*) is merely the domain of the seer.

The sense is that it simply perishes. In the context of explaining the mutual dependence (*anyo'nyāśraya*) between the state of being a seer and the state of being seen, he explains the mutual dependence regarding their unity and duality as well, starting with the word "unity" (*ekatvam*). Unity primarily resides first in the seer, who is the object of counting; duality, being secondary, subsequently resides in the seen, which is the object of counting. It attains existence only when [the former] exists.

It must exist; for in the absence of duality, counting itself would not occur. Indeed, counting proceeds only after observing duality and so forth. But in the absence of duality and the rest, for what purpose would it proceed? Furthermore, if the determination [of number] were self-established, then oneness—which is its very first constituent—would clearly be unestablished. The same applies to duality.

Duality resides in the object of sight. When there is the cognition of unity—that is, when there is a cognition in the form of oneness—meaning, when there is oneness residing in the perceiver, [duality] would exist. For it is indeed clear that a second thing only becomes an object of enumeration after one has first counted as "one";
thus, the impossibility of duality without unity is manifest.
It declares the result:
in the absence of one, the accomplishment of both occurs; for here, indeed, when the duality of subject and object—the seer and the seen—is destroyed, the Real remains.

"Hi" indicates certainty. Therefore, "here" means between these two—oneness and duality. "In the absence of one," meaning when there is an absence of either oneness or duality, "of both alone"—that is, of both duality and oneness—there is no establishment. [The opponent asks: "Well then, what will be established by that? To this, he says: "Duality, unity... [and so forth]. It is the cessation of duality and unity, as well as of the seer and the seen.

The destruction of duality, unity, the seer, and the seen occurs. When that has happened, the reality known as "Being" (sat), which remains as the witness of duality and so forth, persists; it is what remains, it is what is left over.
He makes his vow once again to wipe away the visible world that has been obstructed:
"I shall wipe away for you the entire visible world, such as the sense of 'I' and so forth—the impurity from the mind-ocean by means of the realization of its absolute non-existence."
"I" refers to the impurity consisting of egoism and so forth, headed by the sense of "I-ness"—that is, the entire world of the visible, which is of the nature of impurity.

From the mirror of your mind—that is, from the reflecting surface of your own mind—I shall wipe it clean through the realization of its absolute non-existence; that is to say, by generating the knowledge of the absolute absence of the objects of perception. And it is logical that the removal of impurities from a mirror should be performed.

[Objection: "But how can you effect the cleansing of this much of the visible world? To this he replies: "The non-existent has no being; the existent has no non-being. But as for that which does not exist by way of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), what effort is there in cleansing it? (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.36).

For that which does not possess existence (*sattā*) while performing the act of bringing about existence, there is no such thing as "being" (*bhāva*). This is because even a rabbit's horn would then incur the consequence of possessing existence. For that which possesses the act of bringing about existence while already existing, there is no such thing as "non-being" (*abhāva*). This is because it would entail the loss of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
And the loss of one's own essential nature is not logical, for it would entail the loss of the very nature of fire as fire. That which does not exist by way of its own essential nature—
What difficulty is there in wiping that away? Indeed, no one is ever seen making an effort to snap off the horn of a rabbit.

[Objection: "Even so, what relevance does this have for [the world's] manifestation? To this he says: "That which was unarisen at the beginning of the world, and that which is seen spread out here—this is Brahman itself, expanded by its own consciousness within its own stainless self. (MU 3.7.37)
At the very beginning of the world, it is indeed unarisen; therefore, the sense is that there is no affliction in the cleansing of the world.
Now, if the world is unarisen from the very beginning, then what is this that appears?
To this he says: "And that which is this. And that which is this—that which is seen as something with an extended nature (*tataṃ*)—is perceived.

That very Brahman is the reality known as Brahman itself. Within its own stainless self—that is, upon its own ground which is the nature of pure consciousness—it becomes "bṛṃhita," meaning it undergoes an exceeding expansion. Otherwise, its status as Brahman would be impossible; for Brahman is defined precisely by its connection to *bṛṃhā* (expansion). Furthermore, in the case of a reality, what is called "expansion" cannot be said to be the production of another entity.
Furthermore, because water possesses fluidity, there is the undesirable consequence that the swelling [of waves] appearing as waves would be the production of a separate entity;

yet even a fool does not admit that waves are distinct from the water. Since it is observed that the very Self, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), swells into the form of dream-objects, it is said: "because of its being consciousness" (*cittvāt*).
Again and again he says this very thing:
that which is called "the world" has never arisen, does not exist, and is not perceived; it is like the state of being a bracelet and so forth in gold—what is the point of the effort to polish it?

The word "nāma" (by name) is used for the sake of emphasis. The world (*jagat*) has not arisen, nor does it exist, nor is it perceived; for it exists as the very form of Brahman. What is the world like? It is like the state of being a bracelet and so forth. Just as the state of being a bracelet appearing in gold does not exist [as something other than gold], because it exists as the very form of gold—such is the meaning. Therefore...

What effort is required for its cleansing? Since it is cleansed by the mere knowledge of its being Brahman, the state of being a bracelet or the like appearing in gold is not something impossible to cleanse; for it is cleansed by the mere knowledge of its being gold.
Having recognized that the disciple is thus devoid of consolation,
we shall here explain in detail, through many logical arguments, how to provide him with consolation, so that it may indeed be experienced by him personally as something uncontradicted.

We shall explain this aforementioned matter in detail here in this treatise through many logical arguments; indeed, with certainty, so that it may be experienced by you yourself as something uncontradicted.

He speaks precisely on the subject at hand: "How can there be existence here for that which has never arisen from the very beginning? How can there be a river of water in a desert, or a planet in the second moon? (MU 3.7.40)

The word "hi" indicates certainty. Regarding that entity which does not arise even at the very beginning, how could its existence—its being present here—come to be? To this, he states two examples, beginning with "how," and so forth.
Just as the son of a barren woman does not exist, just as there is no water in a desert, and just as there is no tree in the sky, so too the delusion of the world does not exist.
The delusion of the world (*jagadbhramaḥ*) means the delusion whose form is the world; that is to say, the world itself.
If so, what is this that appears? To this he says:
"O Rāma, that which is seen here is indeed Brahman itself, free from all affliction. We shall explain this to you through reasoning, and not by mere words."

That which is seen by us here is free from affliction—that is, devoid of the affliction known as existence and non-existence—and is indeed Brahman. We shall explain this to you beforehand, at the outset, through reasoning—that is, by means of logical arguments. We shall not speak of it by words alone; [here] *tasil* functions as a suffix applicable to all case endings.
With a verse at the end of the chapter, he declares that the rejection of reasoned speech should be abandoned:

"O noble-minded one, it is improper for a person of exalted intellect to show contempt for that which those who know the truth proclaim here through reasonings. For they know him to be truly ignorant who, out of a deluded mind, disregards what is consistent with reason; such a person brings about his own misery. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.4)

The word *nāma* is used in the sense of certainty. *Avahelanam* means disregard or indifference. *Kaṣṭāvahaḥ* means one who brings about suffering or bestows hardship. "By means of impossible efforts" refers to oneself; this is the ellipsis. Thus may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the seventh canto in the "Section on Origination" within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Śrī Rāma asks:
By what reasoning is this known, and how is it established? Once this principle has been experienced, nothing remains to be known.

This is the unreality of the visible. Now, why do you ask for the reasoning here? To this he replies with the word "nyāya" (reasoning). Because when this principle (*nyāya*) has been experienced through reasoning, nothing remains to be known, since everything becomes known by hearing the reasoning.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha, intending to fulfill his promise to speak in detail, says in reply:
"This chronic cholera of false knowledge, known by the name 'the world,' does not subside except through the mantra called inquiry."

Having ascended to the intellect, it flashes forth as reality; however, the world should be understood as being of the nature of false cognition, like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. Furthermore, the destruction of cholera by means of a mantra is logical.
He strengthens Śrī Rāma for the purpose of hearing the instruction that is about to be given:
