"O Rāma, I shall tell you these narratives for the sake of attaining realization; if you listen to them, O virtuous one, you will indeed be liberated and wise. *Ākhyāyikāḥ* refers to narrative accounts that provide instruction. *Bodhasiddhaye* means for the sake of attaining the realization of the absolute non-existence of the visible world (*dṛśya*).
The liberated one is untouched by the visible world.
He speaks of the punishment for not listening:
"If, out of a habit of agitation, you rise from the midst [of the discourse] and depart, then nothing at all will be accomplished for you today, for you are behaving like an animal."

If you do not listen to us, or if, out of a habit of agitation, you rise from the midst [of the discourse] and depart—then, for one who possesses the nature of an animal and is like a beast, nothing at all will be accomplished.
Indeed, if nothing is accomplished even by listening with firmness, what then is to be done? To this he replies:
"Whoever strives for a certain goal in that manner, he necessarily attains it, provided he does not turn back out of weariness. (3.8.5)

Whatever person desires whatever object— that is, makes it the object of their longing— and strives for it accordingly and not otherwise, they will certainly attain it, provided that they do not turn back when exhausted.
"Now, what kind of effort shall I make regarding this desired object? To this he replies:
"O Rāma, if you are devoted to the company of the virtuous and to the sacred scriptures, then in mere days or months you will attain the supreme state."
The distinction is that [one] with unsurpassed eloquence [attains it] in days, whereas otherwise [it takes] months. // MT 3.8.6 //

Śrī Rāma, having become certain of Śrī Vasiṣṭha’s saintliness, asks for a scripture as a means to awaken self-knowledge: "O best among those who know the scriptures, what is that scripture which is preeminent for awakening self-knowledge, by knowing which one no longer grieves?"
For the awakening of self-knowledge, for the manifestation of self-knowledge; one does not grieve—that is, the grieving consisting of attachment to the visible world is no longer experienced.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha says in reply:
"O Great-minded One, for those for whom self-knowledge is paramount, this very work titled the Mahārāmāyaṇa is the supreme scripture among all scriptures."

For those for whom self-knowledge (*ātma-jñāna*) is primary— that is, the essential core as that which is to be expressed— for such [people], this history (*itihāsa*), titled *Rāmāyaṇa* and known as the *Mahārāmāyaṇa*, exists. Now, in the *Śrīmahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the venerable Vālmīki himself, an instruction given by the venerable Vasiṣṭha to the venerable Rāma has been recorded in the context of narrating the life-story of Śrī Rāma.

If it is argued that since this [work] was extracted from the *Śrīmahārāmāyaṇa* by some compassionate person, how could the venerable Vasiṣṭha refer to the *Śrīmahārāmāyaṇa*—which occurs subsequent to the time of the instruction—with the words "this" (*idam*), for by this [reference] the authorship of the *Śrīmahārāmāyaṇa* by the venerable Vasiṣṭha would be revealed? To this we reply: we have already established this conclusion at the very beginning. What [is there further to discuss]?

You ask again and again because it was stated therein that those possessed of *pratibhā* (creative intuition) understand this matter by themselves, whereas for those devoid of it, a lack of qualification (*anadhikāra*) has been declared. Therefore, simply ask about *pratibhā*. If *pratibhā* does not exist, then due to a lack of qualification, one must remain silent; enough with this prolixity.
He praises the Śrī Mahārāmāyaṇa itself:
"From this, the best of histories, supreme awakening proceeds; this is declared to be the essence of all histories."
From this [work] called the Rāmāyaṇa.
Since the state of liberation while living arises spontaneously upon hearing this verbal scripture, it is therefore exceedingly purifying.
In the scripture consisting of speech.
Through inquiry, the world of appearances, though seemingly established, comes to its end—just as when a dream is recognized for what it is, the mental impression of the dream-objects vanishes.

It remains exactly as it is, not brought to destruction by blows from hammers and the like. Here he states an illustration with the word "just as" (*yathā*). *Bhāvanā* means the cultivation of [the realization of] reality. The particle *eva* is for the purpose of completing the meter. This is the intended meaning: just as when the waking state is fully known to be unreal in a dream, joy and resentment are no longer experienced toward the presence or absence of things encountered therein.

Otherwise, just as with the past states of existence and non-existence experienced while awake, there would arise joy and resentment due to the states of existence and non-existence belonging to that [dream] state. Likewise, when it is known through the investigation of the *Mahārāmāyaṇa* that the visible world is unreal,
joy and resentment are no longer produced by the states of existence and non-existence regarding the objects of perception.

"But surely there are other treatises as well; so how can you say that this alone is the unique cause? To this he replies: "What is found here is found elsewhere; what is not here is found nowhere. The wise know this to be the treasury of all the sciences of knowledge. (MU 3.8.12)

Whatever exists here in this *Rāmāyaṇa* in its entirety—that is found elsewhere in other treatises, though only in a scattered manner; this is the meaning. Whatever is not here is not found anywhere at all in any treatise. Therefore, the wise—those who know the essence of all scriptures—regard this glorious *Mahārāmāyaṇa* as a treasury of all branches of knowledge.
They know—that is, they understand—the treasury of all the inner sciences (*adhyātma-śāstra*).
He describes the fruit of listening to the *Śrī Mahārāmāyaṇa* whose characteristics have been stated:
"Whoever should listen to this constantly, the intellect of that person of noble wonder—even if he be a child—attains supreme awakening; of this there is no doubt."
The meaning is "even of a child" or "even of a fool"; the implication is: "what need is there to speak of a wise man?"

He tells this to one who is averse to what ought to be done, for this does not please one who is unfit due to the arising of evil deeds; let such a person investigate whatever treatise consists of the expression of knowledge.
To one who is unfit and possessed of a demonic nature; [the teaching] consisting of knowledge and speech, overflowing with the words of wisdom.
"Surely, for me who desires liberation, what is the use of hearing this? To this he replies:
"But upon hearing this, the state of being liberated while living (jīvanmuktatva) is experienced by oneself, just as freedom from disease is felt when a potent medicine has been drunk."
By itself, indeed, without effort.
For when this scripture is being heard, the listener understands it within himself: "This has been stated by us exactly as it is, and not like a boon or a curse."

This is the matter spoken by me. Now, one might ask: "If some obstacle or the like should arise for one who has engaged in listening to this, what then should be done? To this he says: "This [is] like a boon and a curse. That is to say, it is accompanied by both boons and curses; the word "like a mantra" is to be supplied as the remainder.
With a verse at the end of the chapter, he declares that self-inquiry is the unique cause for the knowledge of the absolute non-existence of the visible world:

"This suffering of worldly existence is stilled by the great discourse of self-inquiry alone; not by wealth, gifts, austerity, sacred learning, or the Vedas, nor by hundreds of efforts devoid of the effort to discourse upon it. (MU 3.8.17)
O [Lord], this visible nature of yours—the suffering of saṃsāra, the suffering known as birth—is pacified only by the great discourse on the investigation of one's own self;

that is, by the great mutual conversation concerning the investigation of one's own self. This suffering of saṃsāra is not pacified by wealth, charity, austerity, sacred learning, or the Vedas. Therefore, [it must be investigated]—this is the ellipsis. For this reason, by a person...
Of that inquiry into one's own self; "that discourse" means mutual discussion with virtuous people;

"for the sake of that," [discourses] have been "abandoned," meaning hundreds of efforts other than such discourse have been relinquished. By whom? By him. He should become such a person. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the eighth canto in the "Chapter on Origination" within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. He clearly explains the meaning of the verse at the end of the previous section:
"Those whose minds are fixed on Him, whose life-breaths are absorbed in Him, who awaken one another, and who constantly speak of Him—those people are contented and find delight."
For those who are solely devoted to knowledge, through the investigation of self-knowledge, that state of liberation while living arises, which is indeed liberation from the body.

Those whose minds are fixed on that—on that investigation of one's own self—are such [as they are described]. Likewise, those whose vital breaths—the external senses—have reached their culmination in that investigation of one's own self are such [as they are described].
Furthermore, those virtuous ones who mutually awaken one another to that investigation of the self, and likewise those who speak of that investigation of the self, find contentment.

They become endowed with contentment; likewise, they delight others and bring them to a state of being endowed with contentment. For those men who are solely devoted to the knowledge of the Self and solely intent on the inquiry into the Self, that state of liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatā*) arises and manifests from their investigation of the knowledge of the Self; it is indeed the very same as disembodied liberation (*videhamuktatā*), because there is an absence of identification with the body in its entirety.
Śrī Rāma asks:

"O Brahman, tell me the characteristics of one liberated after death (videhamukta) and one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), so that by means of that knowledge, I may strive accordingly with an intellect guided by the vision of the scriptures."

In the phrase "of one liberated while living" (*jīvanmuktasya*), the word "and" (*ca*) is to be supplied. "I make an effort" (*yate*); *yatna* means I exert myself. A "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is a quality that establishes one's true nature (*svarūpa*).

"By the intellect" (*dhiyā*) means by the understanding (*buddhyā*). Of what kind? That which has the scripture itself as its vision or eyes; such [an intellect], meaning one that follows the scripture. // MT_3,9.3 //
The venerable Vasiṣṭha says in reply:
He for whom this world, as it exists, has set like the sky—even while engaged in worldly affairs—and yet remains [as the sky], is called one liberated while living.

Even for that person who, though engaged in worldly activity, performs their dealings among all objects of the universe—for such a person, this world which habitually manifests before them remains exactly as it is, in this very manner; its essential nature has not been destroyed by any effort. It has "set," meaning it has gone to destruction; therefore, it becomes like space (*vyoma*), having the nature of emptiness. By the wise, he [is recognized].

He is called "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta). The meaning is that the defining characteristic of one liberated while living is the perception of the manifest world as unreal, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
He who, having attained exclusive steadfastness in awakening, remains even while awake as if in deep sleep, and continues his worldly activities—he is called one liberated while living.

One who has attained that state— namely, the condition of being one whose sole steadfastness is in awakening, which consists of self-knowledge preceded by the knowledge of the absolute non-existence of the visible world— and who, even while in the waking state itself, and even while engaged in worldly activity as it flows along, remains as if in deep sleep; such a person [is liberated].

He remains as if entered into deep sleep; that is to say, he remains without any mental synthesis (*niranusandhāna*). He is called "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*) by the wise. And it is observed that for a man who is devoted to women and other objects, even while engaged in the activities of the waking state, his condition remains like that of deep sleep; thus, no effort is required [to realize this].
He whose facial radiance neither rises nor sets in the face of pleasure or pain, remaining as it is naturally obtained—he is called one liberated while living.

For one who abides as they have attained it, reaching the culmination through the natural flow [of practice], whose countenance shows neither radiance nor gloom in pleasure or pain due to the absence of elation and resentment— he is called by the wise a "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*).
He who remains awake while in the state of deep sleep, for whom no waking state exists, and whose consciousness is free from latent impressions—he is called liberated while living.

The person who remains as if in deep sleep (*suṣupta*) while being awake— that is, while maintaining awareness directed toward external objects— is such because, through the certainty of pure consciousness alone (*ekacinmātratā*), he is devoid of any mental engagement with the external phenomenal world (*bāhyaprapañca*).
Likewise, for that person, the worldly waking state (*jāgrat*) does not exist, because he consists of the fourth state (*turyamayatva*).

For one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), perceiving everything in the waking state as consisting of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), remains indeed established in the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*).

Likewise, he whose awakening (*bodha*)— the knowledge of external objects such as the body— is free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*), meaning devoid of the impressions consisting of the notions of "I" and "mine," is called liberated while living by the wise.
Even while acting in accordance with passion, hatred, fear, and the like, he who is inwardly as utterly transparent as space is called one liberated while living.
That person, even while acting in accordance with passion, hatred, fear, and the like; even while enjoying attachment toward a son or others who are the basis for passion;

even while turning away from an enemy who is the basis for hatred; and even while moving away from lions and other sources of fear—remains within the mind as utterly transparent and exceedingly pure as space, despite the force of the flow of attachment and other emotions directed toward objects such as sons.

Because of the absence of mental continuity (*anusaṃdhāna*). For it is only when there is continuity in the mind that impurity arises. By the wise, such a person is called "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the body and other objects, as well as egoism (*asmitā*) and so forth, is intended.
He whose state of being is free from egoism, whose intellect is not defiled—whether he acts or does not act—he is called liberated while living.

That person whose state is devoid of egoism—that mental modification consisting of the sense of "I"—because he perceives Brahman as the agent in all things; and likewise, that person whose intellect is not smeared—that is, it is not made stained by sins in the form of passion and so forth (this is the ellipsis)—he is called liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) by the wise. Of what sort is he? He is one who acts for the sake of maintaining the body's existence.

Whether one performs action that has come forth spontaneously in the natural flow, or likewise does not perform it for some reason, one should understand that there is an absence of the stain of ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva-dhīlepa*); for at the time of acting, one acts without subsequent mental attachment (*niranusandhāna*), and at the time of non-acting, one abides in the realization of pure consciousness alone (*śuddhacinmātra-parāmarśa-niṣṭhatva*).
He who perceives the dissolution and creation of the three worlds through the opening and closing of his eyes, being equal to space, is called one liberated while living.

"Equal to space" means like the sky. As for the person: through the opening and closing [of the eyes]—that is to say, by the manifestation known as the orientation toward the object of thought (*cetyonmukhatva*) and by the closing known as the non-orientation toward the object of thought (*cetyān-unmukhatva*)—there occurs the creation of the three worlds externally, such as the earth and so forth, and the creation of the three worlds internally, such as waking and so forth, of the *puruṣa* who is determined to be the Supreme Self, the essence of consciousness.

By concealing its own nature, it perceives dissolution and birth—that is, withdrawal and manifestation—and likewise it perceives disappearance and appearance. He is called "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta) by the wise. Alternatively, self-reflection is *unmeṣa* (opening), and indifference toward that is *nimeṣa* (closing). Thus, through *unmeṣa* there is manifestation, and through *nimeṣa* there is dissolution; this is according to their respective order.
One should indeed act while abandoning all attachment.
He who is neither an enjoyer nor as if an enjoyer, having attained oneness with pure consciousness, remains inwardly like one asleep; he is called liberated while living.

The person who has attained oneness with pure consciousness through pure consciousness—being awakened, that is, endowed with enlightenment—remains as if sleeping within, because he is free from mental preoccupation. Like what? As if he were a non-enjoyer, even while actually performing the act of enjoying, by virtue of his knowledge of his own state as pure consciousness.
Due to the absence of the conceit "I am the enjoyer," he is called by the wise one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
He who is always a seer yet appears as a non-seer, who is alive yet like one dead, and who engages in worldly affairs yet is as immovable as a mountain—he is called one liberated while living.
He who, while being a seer and indeed maintaining the agency of the act of seeing—rather than remaining like a blind man—becomes a non-seer;

likewise, he who, while living and indeed maintaining the agency of the act of living, becomes like one dead, resembling the dead, as if dead due to the absence of desire for enjoyments and the like; likewise, he who, while being a transactor and indeed performing worldly transactions...
Thus, he becomes like a mountain because he is truly free from agitation; by the wise, he is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).

"He from whom the world does not tremble, and who does not tremble from the world; liberated from joy, envy, and fear—he is called one liberated while living. (3.9.13) "World" (*loka*) refers to ordinary people. "From whom the world does not tremble" means that because there is no cause for agitation, the world does not experience agitation toward him. Likewise, "who does not tremble from the world" means he is not agitated by it because it serves no purpose for him; for he is solely intent upon his own true purpose.

He trembles before those things from which he perceives no purpose for himself. Of what nature is he? He is liberated from joy, resentment, and fear—that is, devoid of joy, resentment, and fear—due to his knowledge of the oneness of pure consciousness within himself. By the wise, such a person is called "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta).
He for whom the fluctuations of saṃsāra have been stilled, who, though possessed of parts, is partless; who, though possessing a mind, is mindless—he is called one liberated while living.

He for whom the mental constructs of saṃsāra have become tranquil and dissolved through the vision of pure consciousness within the self— he, such a person, though possessed of *kalās* (even being endowed with the *kalā* called knowledge), becomes *niṣkala* (devoid of parts) by virtue of knowing his own partless nature as pure consciousness. Likewise, he who is *sacitta* (possessed of mind)— that is, endowed with a mind whose true nature is pure *sattva*.
Moreover, he is "without mind," having emerged from the mind due to the absence of a defiled mind; by the wise, he is called one liberated while living.
He who, though engaged in all kinds of worldly affairs, remains cool as if toward the interests of others, and whose self is full, is called one liberated while living.

The "full self" (pūrṇātmā) is one whose soul is satisfied by being pure consciousness alone, free from dependence. He remains cool—devoid of the feverish anxiety as to whether "this will be accomplished or not"—regarding all objects that come into the stream of experience and regarding the entire collection of purposes. In what way? Like [one indifferent] to the interests of others; the meaning is that just as an ordinary person remains cool toward the affairs of others, so does he.
He is called "liberated while living" by the wise.
Having described liberation while living (jīvanmukti), he now speaks of the liberation of the disembodied (videhamukti) which follows in due order:

"When the body has perished through the power of time after the state of one liberated while living has been relinquished, consciousness attains the state of disembodied liberation, just as the wind [loses] its vibration. (MU 3.9.16)

One who has attained the state of pure consciousness through the secondary sense (*lakṣaṇā*) is a *jīvanmukta*. When the body—the physical frame—is worn out or destroyed by the power of time, that is, by the force of destiny, the *jīvanmukta* leaves behind the state of being liberated while living and attains bodiless liberation (*videhamukti*).
Just as what? Like the wind leaving its vibration. For example, just as the wind leaves behind its vibration, which is the performance of movement.
"He abandons" means "in that manner. Alternatively, there is a reading: "as the wind [abandons] its vibration."

He describes the characteristics of that [state] as being similar to those of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), though only briefly: "The one liberated from the body (videhamukta) neither rises nor sets, nor does he cease; he is neither existent nor non-existent, neither far away, nor 'I', nor anything else. (MU 3.1.17)

The person who has attained disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*)—one who, through the absence of the sense of "I," has reached liberation from the body which was once grasped as such—does not arise, because he abides in the state of eternally risen pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Likewise, he does not set, because that which was imagined as having set arises from that very source; otherwise, it would be impossible. Similarly, he does not cease, for that would entail the non-existence of the appearance of *saṃsāra*.

It is not existent, because it is beyond the range of both external and internal sense organs. Likewise, it is not non-existent, because if it were of such a nature of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it would follow that it could not manifest at all; for a hare's horn cannot manifest in any form whatsoever. Likewise, it is not something situated at a distance, because it abides as the core of the "I-sense" (*ahaṃtā*) for everyone. Likewise, it is not the "I," because it is not limited.

The subject does not exist, because it abides as an unlimited subject. Likewise, the other, the limited object of cognition, does not exist, because it abides as an unlimited state of being the object of cognition.
Having spoken of its transcendence of the universe, he now describes briefly its identity with the universe:
"Becoming the sun, He shines; as Viṣṇu, He protects the three worlds; as Rudra, He destroys all; and as the Lotus-born, He creates all. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.18)

Having attained the state of pure consciousness alone, he becomes the sun; having reached the nature of the sun, he blazes, exercising the agency of heating. Likewise, having become Viṣṇu, he protects—that is, guards—the three worlds. This should be applied everywhere in the same manner. It should be understood that these [entities], such as the sun and others, are twofold, being both external and internal. For, externally...

That which is seen as the sun in the sky is, internally, the *prāṇa* (vital breath); for like the sun, it effects the digestion of the body. Likewise, Viṣṇu is the intellect (*buddhi*); for like him, it effects the maintenance of volitions (*saṅkalpa*). Likewise, Rudra is the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*); for like him, it causes all volitions to dissolve into itself. Likewise, the lotus-born Brahmā is the mind (*manas*); for like him, it generates volitions.

Thus, this should be applied everywhere according to the circumstances. Now, one might ask: "How is it that the disembodied liberated one (videhamukta), having assumed the state of moving and non-moving entities such as the sun and so forth, performs all the activities inherent in them? This is true. In that regard, first, the moving beings are clearly perceived as being presided over by the inner controller (antaryāmin) and the pure consciousness-principle (śuddha-cittattva); otherwise, even when they have entered the state of death, [the activities would not cease].

Because, as before, it would follow that [the body] is merely a substratum for action. But surely, in that action, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) itself is seen to be the impeller, since motionless bodies devoid of breath are observed to be inactive. This is incorrect; for here, what is called "breath" is not perceived as any conscious entity capable of being an impeller. Rather, it is by the impulsion of some other independent conscious being.

Just as a ball is seen to move in and out when impelled by Devadatta, so too the pure consciousness alone (cinmātra), acting as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of moving beings, is known to be the agent of the actions residing in those moving beings. Furthermore, the action of remaining that is observed even in non-moving things must be understood as being produced by that [consciousness] alone, because it is an action, just like the actions residing in moving beings. This is because, in cases where [beings] appear directly as conscious entities—

Mobile beings lack the capacity for their own activity; what then can be said regarding immobile things, which appear directly as insentient, in their capacity to perform action? Therefore, just as pillars and the like remain when placed in a certain position by a presiding agent such as Devadatta, so too do immobile things remain, established by some reality inherent within themselves.

This is to be understood as follows: in that case, Devadatta’s existence outside of those [elements] is perceived directly; therefore, his inclusion within them is not postulated there. In this instance, however, because no gross entity is seen outside, his inclusion within them is postulated. Let it rest at this point that his external existence is not contradicted either. And thus, in pure consciousness alone...

When he has attained identity with That, the agency of all actions is indeed established as having come to an end; just as a drop of water merged in the ocean is characterized by the qualities of the ocean. It should be understood that the remaining dead body is also implicitly included [in this state]. Now, even so, it is only established that the one liberated while in the body (videhamukta) performs all actions.

But it is not established that "everything having come into being" [is the case]. If one asks, "What then is the state of affairs there?"—it is true. In this regard, the following is the state of affairs:

when investigating what the nature of moving and non-moving entities consists of, their essential form, because it cannot be grasped by the hand, rests in nothingness (*anirvācyatā*). And this very nothingness is the essential nature of pure consciousness (*śuddha-cittattva*); thus, [one realizes] its state as the form of pure consciousness.

For one who has departed and attained liberation from the body (videhamukta), it is entirely logical that all phenomenal existence ceases; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. Furthermore, this nature of pure consciousness is established by direct perception for those who experience it. However, this effort has been made for the sake of those who do not yet know it; enough with further elaboration.

Having become space, it supports the masses of wind along with the stars, gods, and asuras; having become the range of the principal mountains, it serves as the abode for the cities of the world-protectors.

The connection is that, having become the host of the principal mountain ranges (*kulācala*), it becomes the abode of the cities of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), together with the *sarkṣasurāsura*—that is, accompanied by the stars, gods, and asuras.
Having become the earth, she sustains this unbroken stability of the world; having become grass, shrubs, and creepers, she yields a continuous succession of fruits.
This is clear.
Bearing the forms of both water and fire, it blazes and yet melts; as the moon, it exudes nectar, and as the *hālāhala* poison, it brings death.

Assuming the form of water, it flows, endowed with the quality of fluidity; assuming the form of fire, it blazes—so it should be understood. Having become the moon and having become the *hālāhala* poison, this should be connected [to the previous].
It manifests as brilliance, spreads through the quarters, becomes the darkness of blindness, and being empty, it attains the state of space; being a mountain, it completely obstructs.
It obstructs; it performs an obstruction.

In its state as consciousness, it makes the mobile immobile, and in its immobile form, it makes the immobile mobile; having become the ocean, it encircles the woman Earth just as a bracelet encircles the wrist.

Having remained in the state of consciousness—that is, having become endowed with the nature of consciousness—he makes the moving stationary while being in a stationary form, and he makes the stationary moving. Having become the ocean, he encircles the woman who is the earth—the earth itself as a woman—enveloping her on all sides at its boundaries. How? Like a bracelet; just as a bracelet [encircles] a woman, that is to say, the arm of a woman.
It encircles; that is the meaning of "tathā."
Having become the supreme solar form, spreading its light within, it remains perfectly tranquil, [encompassing] the entire multitude of motes in the three worlds.

Having become the body of the supreme sun—the body of the sun of consciousness—he spreads out, that is, extends, the mass of atoms known as the three worlds within his own "wall" (bhitti), which is of the nature of light. Yet, because he remains in the state of a witness, he abides as utterly tranquil, free from any agitation caused by that [world]. And it is logical that the spreading of a mass of atoms occurs within the light of the sun.
And the state of peace.
Knowing that it is impossible to calculate its specific distinctions, he describes it in general terms:
"Whatever this appears, has appeared, or will appear—whatever is visible throughout the three periods of time—all that indeed is this. (MU 3.2.5)

Or, in another sense: whatever this world is—whatever was manifested (*bhātam*) and vibrated (*sphuritam*) in the past, likewise shines (*ābhāti*) and vibrates (*sphurati*) today, and likewise will shine and vibrate (*bhām sphuraṇam*) in the future—that entire visible universe existing throughout the three times is called that "one liberated while disembodied" (*videhamukta*). He becomes such.
On this point, Śrī Rāma asks: "O Brahmin, why do you speak thus? For my vision of this is indeed difficult; it is certain that this [vision] is hard to attain and hard to ascend."

O Brahmin, speak; tell me how one becomes, or how one attains such a state, by a person endowed with these qualities who is liberated while in the disembodied state (videhamukta). For this is my firm conviction. Thus it is. What is it? This aforementioned view, which consists of liberation in the disembodied state, is difficult to attain—uneven and hard to reach.
And she becomes difficult to overcome.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha speaks the reply:
"O Rāma, this is called liberation; this is declared to be Brahman; this is described as nirvāṇa. Listen now to how it is attained."

O Rāma, the wise call this state "liberation while disembodied" (*videhamukti*), because liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) is not yet complete liberation, as it still rests upon the mind whose nature is *sattva*.
The wise have described this as "Brahman," because it possesses the quality of expansion (*bṛṃhaṇa*) through the existence of all objects.
The wise have called this "nirvāṇa," because the limited sense of ego has dissolved in every respect. Listen to this.
How is this attained by a person?
This visible object of perception, which is associated with notions such as "I" and "you," is attained through the intellect by means of its non-origination, even though it appears to exist.
By us: this visible world, which is joined with "I-ness," "you-ness," and so forth, is seen and experienced.

Even though this world exists in such a manner, by means of the non-arising—that is, by the very knowledge of its non-existence in the form of the cognition that "this is indeed unarisen"—it is [realized]; that is to say, by the knowledge of the non-arising of that world as its object. This is the point.

The state of disembodied liberation (videhamuktatva), possessing the qualities described, is "attained," meaning it is reached. The two particles *api* and *vā* have the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*.
By this, it is stated that the absolute non-existence of the visible world (*dṛśyātyantābhāva*) is the cause for disembodied liberation.
Śrī Rāma asks again:
"O best among those who know what is to be known, when those liberated while in the body (videhamukta) attain the three worlds, I think they have merely entered the state of creation."
O best among those who know the knowable, I think that when those liberated while in the body (videhamuktas) enter the three worlds,
they have then attained the state of creation itself; they have indeed entered the condition of creation, because they manifest solely through the nature of objects contained within creation.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha says in reply:
"If the three worlds exist, let them attain that state wherein not even the slightest meaning of the word 'the three worlds' can possibly occur."
In that case, since [the word] has attained the status of referring to the three worlds, how could there be an understanding of the meaning based on the word "Brahman"?
Therefore, no other conceptualization of the referent of the word "jagat" (world) is possible for us.

If the creation of the three worlds exists as a reality, then let those who are liberated while in the body (videhamukta) truly attain that state of being the three worlds; in whatever place there might be any object denoted by the term "the three worlds"—
that which is designated as the triple world.

"Sound and its object"—that is to say, [the former] does not occur. "Therein" means in that place. "The cognition of the expressed meaning of such an utterance" means a cognition having the form of the expressed meaning of an utterance of such a kind; that is to say, an utterance of such a kind and an object of such a kind. Why does it occur? Because of the impossibility of sound and object in the three worlds. The meaning is that it does not occur. What is this "iti"? It is Brahman.

By way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇayā*), he is one liberated while in the disembodied state (*videhamukta*). He has gone to the state of the three worlds, the state of emanation (*sargatā*); thus he makes a concluding summary with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

"Therefore" means for that reason. The conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) of the meaning of the word "world" (*jagacchabdārtha*)—the conceptualization whose form is the meaning of the word "world"—is no longer present as something other than Brahman. It does not exist as something distinct from Brahman.
In this context, he repeatedly declares the very identity of the world and Brahman:
"To those who have realized the truth, it is the truth that the world is indeed Brahman—non-different, peaceful, a mere appearance, and as pure as space. (MU 3.9.32)

The creator of the world; non-different, because it exists as the form of all things and is devoid of any entity separate from itself; tranquil, resting in its own nature; consisting of mere appearance, having the nature of mere appearance; pure as space, as clear as space—it becomes Brahman itself. This is precisely this. For one who realizes the truth, for one endowed with the knowledge of reality, it is the Truth.
It comes to be.
Regarding this, he provides an illustration:
"For just as the nature of a bracelet is not seen even when examined, anywhere at all, apart from pure gold. (MU 3.9.33)

The phrase "yathā hi" (just as) indicates an illustration. By us, even after investigating—having thoroughly examined—a golden bracelet (*hemakaṭaka*), that which is called "bracelet-ness" is not seen anywhere except in stainless gold (*nirmalahāṭaka*). Just as the bracelet is nothing but gold, so too the world is nothing but Brahman; thus the two subsequent verses are to be construed as illustrations for the preceding verse.
He tells the second illustration:
"Apart from water, I do not perceive anything at all in a wave; for that which is seen by people like you as 'waveness' does not exist there at all."
In the expanse of water, amidst the waves, I see nothing other than water; in the expanse of water, there is nothing else.
He tells the third illustration:
"Motion is never, at any time or place, anything other than the wind; the wind is always nothing but motion. Therefore, the world does not exist [as something separate]. (MU 3.9.35)
At no time, anywhere, and at no place, does vibration exist as something other than wind;

for wind is indeed vibration itself. He states the result by saying "the world" (*jagat*); since there are three illustrative examples for the world's nature as Brahman, therefore the world does not exist. And thus, for one who is liberated while in the body (*videhamukta*), there is no coming into the state of creation.
The meaning is: "How does it come to be? //MT_3,9.35 //
Furthermore, he explains the very same point mentioned previously by means of an illustration:
"Just as emptiness is space, and heat itself is water in the desert; just as light is itself radiance, so too the triple world is Brahman alone. (MU 3.9.36)
This is clear.
Śrī Rāma asks:
O Sage, instruct me in that supreme method by which liberation from the visible world arises through the attainment of its absolute non-existence.

O Sage! By what reasoning—through the attainment of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), that is, by the production of absolute non-existence—does liberation arise for this world-appearance, this visible world which has the nature of the world? Teach me that supreme, unsurpassed reasoning. How does the absolute non-existence of the object "world" possess the capacity to establish liberation? Regarding this point:
The meaning is: "State the logical justification."
To the question, "Why do you ask about logic again and again?", he poses another question preceded by an answer:
"When the seer and the seen, having come together, undergo the destruction of one, and when both are absent and have reached a state of non-existence, Nirvana remains. (MU 3.9.38)
Therefore, tell me how one understands that the visible world has an absolute non-origination, and how Brahman thus abides in its own nature.

According to the principle already stated, since this was said by you yourself—this being the ellipsis—the meaning is: since it was stated by you that when, between the seer and the seen, which have mutually come into existence (as established by the aforementioned principle) through mutual dependence, there occurs the destruction of one, and consequently both having ceased to exist, they reach a state of non-duality, then Nirvana, which is absolute liberation, remains. Therefore.

For that reason: the absolute non-arising—that is, the nature of absolute non-existence and absolute non-origination—of the visible world, of the world whose very nature is visible; by whatever reasoning it is understood or known, in that same way Brahman—the pure reality of consciousness expanded (*bṛṃhita*) into the state of the world—is thus situated in its own nature, abiding in its own essence, in the form of the world. Just as...
He awakens; therefore, speak and tell it to me in that manner.

Intoxicated by the immersion in aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), he asks once more for the reasoning that establishes the absolute non-existence of the perceptible and the reasoning regarding the abiding nature of Brahman:
"By what reasoning is this known, and how is this established? O Sage, if this is proven, nothing remains to be accomplished."

This is the absolute non-existence of the visible world and this is the abiding of Brahman in its own such nature. [The opponent asks: "But for what purpose do you ask these questions again and again? To this, he says: "In this [being established]," O Sage. When this is established, nothing remains to be accomplished—that is, there is nothing left remaining—because only liberation itself is desired.
And because that [point] is established by this very [argument].
The venerable Vasiṣṭha replies:
"This chronic cholera of false knowledge has been deeply rooted for a long time; it will surely be eradicated by the mantra of inquiry."

"Surely" (*nūnam*) indicates certainty. This "cholera of false knowledge" (*mithyājñānaviṣūcikā*) is a specific kind of cognition consisting of the thought, "This visible world exists within pure consciousness alone. It has taken root in the mind and appears as a reality. And it is appropriate that the cholera be pacified by means of a mantra;
here, "investigation" (*vicāra*) should be understood as the inquiry into the nature of this visible world: "What is the form of this visible world? MT 3.9.41.
"Indeed, at this very moment, an investigation has already been conducted by me even in part; so how is it that this visible world is not stilled? To this he replies:
"It cannot be eradicated all at once in a single instant, for in climbing up and descending down a mountain, one must exert equal effort. (MU 3.9.42)

"To completely cut off" means to destroy. He establishes this with the second half of the verse: "It accords. Just as someone who has climbed to the peak of a mountain and wishes to descend from there cannot descend all at once, so too the perception of the reality of the visible world, having been established for a long time, cannot be removed instantaneously; therefore, investigation must be carried out over a long period.
Such is the intended meaning.
He promises to state the reasoning by way of its result:
"Therefore, listen as this is being told—how, through the yoga of practice, by means of reasoning and logical justifications, the delusion of the world may be pacified. MU 3.9.43.
Therefore, for that reason—by means of the practice of cultivation through the method of practicing investigation; by such reasoning produced by one's own intellect;

and likewise by logical arguments (nyāyopapatti) as stated in the treatises on logic (nyāyaśāstra)—in whatever manner the delusion of the world, the worldly error regarding the nature of what is perceived, may be pacified, in that manner this web of words (vāgjāla) which is about to be described [is offered].
I shall speak; you should listen and bring it within the range of your hearing.
"Surely, what will be achieved for me by hearing that? To this he says:
"O Rāma, I shall tell you this narrative for the sake of attaining awakening; if you listen to it, O virtuous one, you will indeed be liberated and enlightened. This is clear.
Fulfilling the promise he made immediately after it was formed, he begins the detailed exposition of what was promised at the start of this treatise:
"Now, O Rāma, I shall tell you this chapter on Origination, by which one who is indeed born becomes liberated."

The word *atha* (now/then) signifies immediate succession; it indicates that this follows immediately after the concise exposition. [An objection is raised: "For what purpose is the section on origination (*utpatti-prakaraṇa*) explained first? To this, he says: "As for the one who... Since we have set out to explain liberation (*mukti*), it is precisely the explanation of the section on origination that must be undertaken. Otherwise, an explanation of liberation would be untenable, as it would be without a basis.
The sense is that it "might be."
"If this section on origination is to be explained in detail, what will you say? To this he replies:
"In this section on origination, I shall now explain how this delusion of the world appears as something unborn, having the nature of space."

This delusion of the world—the error appearing in the form of the world—is of a nature that flashes forth before one. In this manner, by means of this reasoning, it is indeed unborn and unproduced; therefore, being of the nature of space (khātmikā), it shines and manifests.
This is what is now being stated by me in this section concerning origination.

Intending to explain the section on origination itself, and for the purpose of revealing the pure consciousness alone—which is the root cause of origination—according to the maxim of "driving in a pillar," [the author] first describes the dissolution of the phenomenal world that obscures it:
"This entire world, whether stationary or moving, which is seen here in all its various forms, including gods, asuras, and kinnaras. (MU 3.9.47)

When that great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) arrives—which involves the transformation of Rudra and the other deities—that [reality] becomes non-existent and invisible; it goes somewhere, perishes, and its nature is indescribable. It is enriched with all modes, endowed with every manner of existence, non-existence, and so forth. During the great dissolution, which is a particular state called the Fourth (*turya*), and at the time of the end of the great aeon (*mahākalpa*), it is characterized by the transformation of Rudra and others, being joined with their dissolution.

Here, Rudra is to be understood as the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*), the Lord Mahādeva who holds authority over dissolution. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of Viṣṇu and others who hold authority over the creation and maintenance of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest. "Invisible" means beyond the range of the external senses. Now, one might ask: how can it be invisible? To this he says: "somewhere" (*kvāpi*). It goes somewhere—that is, it attains oneness with that indefinable essence of consciousness (*cittattva*). It manifests as something else [only] through differentiation.

...up to this point: "For this very reason it perishes, that is, it goes out of sight. For the total destruction of something that is appearing is not logical; otherwise, it would follow that even the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell would be totally destroyed. But the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is not totally destroyed; rather, it manifests as the nature of mother-of-pearl."

[Objection: "If this world that is appearing were to perish, what would remain? For when the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—which was appearing—perishes, the mother-of-pearl remains. To this, he replies: "Thereafter, there remains something existent that is still, profound, neither light nor pervading darkness, indefinable, and unmanifest. (MU 3.9.49) "Thereafter" means immediately following the destruction of the visible world. "Something" refers, by implication, to the nature of the witness of the destruction of the visible.

There remains some indefinable reality; it persists as the residue. Otherwise, where would this entire world, which appears in such a manner, abide? For the destruction of that which is appearing is not logical, as it would be like the destruction of the very nature of a jar. Nor is it like the destruction of silver in mother-of-pearl, because its nature consists merely in its manifestation in another form. And manifestation in another form is not possible without a primary substratum.

Thus [it is said]. Of what nature is it? It is "stilled and profound" (*stimitagambhīra*). "Stilled" (*stimita*) means devoid of the vibration called "outward-directedness" (*cetyaunmukhya*). "Profound" (*gambhīra*) means that which cannot be fathomed, both because its own nature is one of plunging into its own object and because it lacks the state of being an object for the act of plunging. And it is such, and it is such. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is not light (*tejas*), because its form is pure consciousness alone (*śuddhacinmātra*).

The meaning is that it is distinct from worldly consciousness (*laukikacetana*) such as the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth. Likewise, "it is not darkness" means it is distinct from insentient objects (*jaḍapadārtha*). Alternatively, since its nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), it should be understood as being distinct from external light and darkness, which are of the nature of the cognizable (*cetyasvarūpa*). Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "pervading everywhere. Again, of what nature is it? It is "inexpressible" (*anākhyam*), because it does not abide as an agent of expression.

The meaning is that because it is not an object of verbal designation (*ākhyā*), it is impossible to describe. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is unmanifest, its true form being unrevealed because it is not within the range of the external or internal organs. Since the causal relationship (*hetuhetumadbhāva*) between these preceding qualifiers has already been established as a linked chain, no further effort is made here.
He further specifies in detail that which was described as the remainder:
"It is neither empty nor space, neither the visible object nor the act of seeing; nor is it the multitude of real entities—that which exists by virtue of its infinity."

That entity which exists as infinite, by virtue of its infinitude, is not empty; for if it were [empty], its status as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the world would be untenable. Indeed, an empty thing is never observed to be the substratum of anything, because in those cases where things such as a peacock-feather fan appear, they are based upon the rays of the eye. Likewise, that entity is not space, because according to the logic already stated, it is distinct from emptiness.

And because space consists solely of emptiness, it is not that which is seen; because its nature is that of the seer alone, it is not an object of vision; because its establishment is independent of both seer and seen, it is not a flood of real entities—for in reality, it would be insentient.
It is something whose nature is indefinable, a form more full than the full; it is neither being, nor non-being, nor both being and non-being, nor is it non-existence or becoming.

From that which is considered full, such as space and so forth, there arises a reality whose form is even more full—that is, one whose configuration is more complete. This reality is something indescribable in nature, something whose essential character is ineffable. Likewise, it is not "existent," because it cannot logically serve as the substratum for the world; nor is it "non-existent," because that would entail the faults associated with both positions. Thus, it is neither existent nor non-existent, as both [extremes] would lead to logical fallacies.
Likewise, that which is not non-existent persists by way of being the absence of its opposite.
It is pure consciousness alone, devoid of any object of thought, infinite, undecaying, and auspicious; it is without beginning, middle, or end, free from mental affliction, and beyond all disease.
In response to the inquiry, "What is that which is of such a nature? Of what kind is it?", he says, "Pure consciousness alone" (*cinmātra*), and so forth.

It is pure consciousness alone, having the nature of consciousness itself. For this very reason, it is devoid of objects of cognition (*cetyarahita*), yet it is not stained by objects of cognition (*acetyārūṣita*). It is infinite (*ananta*) because it stands as the witness even of one's own mind. Indeed, it is without beginning, middle, or end, for it illuminates space and time, which establish the distinctions of beginning, middle, and end.

It is devoid of beginning, middle, and end; it is free from the afflictions based upon it because of the non-existence of the afflicted mind; it is stainless, being free from the diseases of the nature of existence, non-existence, and so forth.
In whom the world vibrates like a swan amidst a flight of pearl-like visions—he who is both this and not this, the God whose nature is both being and non-being.

In which object the world vibrates—that is, manifests as that which is to be presided over—how so? Like pearl-oyster swans in the vision. "Pearl-oyster swans in the vision" refers to pearl-oysters and swans shimmering within the vision; it is just like those. For, due to the influence of a disease, the rays that constitute parts of the vision flash in the sky in the form of pearls and in the form of swans. It is thus both existent and non-existent in nature.
He whose nature is both being and non-being—that is to say, the indefinable—He is the God who is playful by nature and radiant by nature.

He is that from whom this entire collection of phenomena (*bhāvajāta*), which is made an object through the "this-ness" (*idantā*) of perception, comes into existence, because it exists as its essence. That God is not "this," because he exists as the essence of the "I-ness" (*ahantā*).
Though without ears, tongue, nose, skin, or eyes, he always and everywhere hears, tastes, smells, touches, and sees.

One who is earless and tongueless is devoid of the sense organs of hearing and taste; likewise, one who is noseless, skinless, and eyeless is devoid of the sense organs of smell, touch, and sight. Such a person, everywhere—in all places—and at all times—in all moments—hears, performing the act of hearing all sounds; tastes, performing the act of tasting all flavors; and smells, performing the act of smelling all odors.

He acts; he touches—that is, he performs the act of touching all objects; he sees—that is, he performs the act of seeing all forms. This is because he exists as the essence of all sense-faculties and all clarity pertaining to all places and times, or because he exists as the state of all subjects (pramātṛ) throughout all places and times who are possessed by the conceit of being the agents of acts such as hearing. Furthermore, for one who exists as the essence of the sense-faculties, dependence upon other sense-faculties is not logical. [This applies] to the sense-faculties.

Because it is illogical for that essence (*sāra*) to depend on those [other senses] even while being independent of other senses; and because even if they were postulated, they would result in having no nature at all without this essence. However, if this [consciousness] is the essence, then since it exists even as their very state, there is no dependence on other senses, even when existing as the state of every perceiver (*pramātṛ*). By means of those senses...
Because, by the mere existence of one faculty, the other faculties would be rendered useless.

That very light by which the form of existence and non-existence is perceived—that is the beginningless and endless variegated creation, as well as the nature of the Self, which is devoid of attachment.

He alone, being of the nature of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), has attained the state of the seer; it is he alone, and no other whatsoever. By which light—that is, by which essential nature—the variegated picture of creation, the form of the world, is perceived or seen through the illumination of consciousness. For without the light of consciousness, the perception of the world by a seer is impossible. Of what nature is this variegated picture of creation? It is of the nature of both the existent and the non-existent (*sadasadrūpa*). Consequently...

It is indefinable as either existent or non-existent. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "without beginning or end," meaning it is devoid of beginning and end because its essence is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) that has no beginning or end. Again, of what nature is it? It is "of its own form" (*svarūpa*), meaning it is of the nature of space (*ākāśarūpa*) because its form consists of mere appearance, like a dream. Again, of what nature is it? It is "unstained," by the stains of existence and non-existence that appear [to it].
The meaning is that, by virtue of its purity, it is liberated from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*). The word "also" (*api*) is for the purpose of completing the meter.

He who perceives the world—whose pupils are like the points between the eyebrows with eyes half-closed—as being of the nature of space itself, ever-shining, and identical with his own true self; MU_3.9.56.

He who perceives—that is, brings within his own range—the true nature (*svarūpa*) known as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is his own essence (*svabhāva*), [and] the world (*jagat*), which consists of perishable objects of cognition;

how is that world? It is of the very nature of space (*vyomātman*), because in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) it lacks the form of a world, being indeed of the nature of nothingness. Furthermore, how is it? It is "always appearing" (*sadābhāsa*), meaning it appears as if it were existent (*sat*); yet in the ultimate sense, it is not existent.

This is the meaning. How does one see? Like the pupil appearing in the middle of the ground of the eyebrows with the eyes half-opened. One by whom the eye is half-opened is "one with half-opened eyes. The eyebrows themselves are the *bhū*, the place; the middle of that is the "middle of the ground of the eyebrows" (*bhrūbhūmadhya*). It is like the pupil (*tārakā*) shining in the middle of the ground of the eyebrows for one whose eyes are half-opened; thus, [the practitioner] has his eyes half-opened.
The meaning is: just as a person perceives the very ray of his own vision in the middle of his eyebrows in the form of a star; such is the sense.
And this meaning is to be understood through a physical gesture (*abhinaya*).
For that Lord, there is no other cause, as [there is none] for a rabbit's horn; yet this world is His effect, like a mass of waves from water.

The meaning is that for that Lord there is no cause. [Objection: But how is it that he has no cause? [Reply: True. That cause would have to be either of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) or of the nature of non-consciousness (*acidrūpa*). It cannot be the latter, because it is impossible for something of the nature of non-consciousness to be the cause of that which is of the nature of consciousness. As for the first case, how could that very same thing of the nature of consciousness be the cause of itself, which is also of the nature of consciousness? Thus, the entire world is its effect.
He says: "Of whom this [is the effect]"—it should be understood that the world is an effect of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), like a dream-world.
The light of that lamp of pure consciousness, which blazes incessantly on all sides and abides within the vessels of the mind, illuminates the three worlds.

Of that lamp which is pure consciousness alone—the nature of this lamp being understood through its quality of illumination—by its radiance, the light of consciousness issuing forth through the doors of the senses, the three worlds, appearing throughout the three states, the triple phenomenal expansion, shines and vibrates.
Of what kind [is it]? "Everywhere," meaning in all places; "blazing," meaning capable of manifesting everything.

Furthermore, of what nature [is it]? It exists within the vessels of the mind—that is, within the receptacles that are the forms of the mind—abiding as its essential substance (*sāra*). And it is appropriate for a lamp to be situated within vessels; even though the mind indeed dissolves during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), it is nevertheless described in this way because it remains there in the form of a seed (*bīja*). Likewise, externally, there is that which is called *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*.
The three worlds appear by means of the mind alone.
Without whom even these luminaries such as the sun would be like darkness; and in whose presence the three worlds proceed like a mirage.

Without which [the eye] these things being seen would remain as if lacking the essence of the visual faculty; even the sun and other luminaries would be like cataracts, resembling darkness. For indeed, when not illuminated by the eye, the sun and others are clearly just like darkness. "When it exists" means, for example, that mirages arise only in the presence of the sun.
Likewise, the meaning is: "in whose presence the three worlds [exist]."
In that [consciousness] in which this fortune of the world arises as if in motion and subsides as if motionless, it is like the circularity of a whirling firebrand.

When that [consciousness] is in motion—possessing the movement known as the orientation toward the visible—the splendor of the world arises, as it were; when it is motionless, it becomes as if withdrawn within, as if contained therein. In reality, however, it neither arises nor withdraws;
thus the word "as it were" (iva) is employed. Within what? As in the case of a firebrand: just as when a firebrand is moved with vibration, the state of being a wheel [appears].
The state of being circular arises when there is no vibration; it becomes as if situated within a firebrand—that is the meaning.
The pervasive and great one, whose nature is pure and imperishable, consists of both movement and stillness, and finds its delight in the creation and dissolution of the world.

The play of the creation and dissolution of the universe is the play of the world’s emanation and withdrawal. Whose [this play is]—it is whose that is imperishable, devoid of destruction; stainless, untainted by the impurity of duality; great, endowed with magnitude; and for that very reason, all-pervading. His very nature, his essential form itself, becomes this; nothing else. How so? As the play of creation and dissolution, whether being perceived or unperceived.

Since this [world] is thus like an unreal construction (*asatkalpa*), enough with worrying about it; for, because it is an object of consciousness and is contained within consciousness, it is of the very nature of consciousness, and thus there is no contradiction. Of what nature is it? It consists of both movement (*spanda*) and non-movement (*aspanda*).
Among these, the play of creation (*sṛṣṭivilāsa*) consists of movement, while the play of dissolution (*saṃhāravilāsa*) consists of non-movement.

The existence of that [Self], which consists of both vibration and non-vibration, is all-pervading like the wind; it appears as if divided merely by name for the sake of conventional usage, but not in reality.

That whose existence consists of both vibration (*spanda*) and non-vibration: existence joined with the orientation toward the object of thought (*cetyaunmukhya*) is "consisting of vibration," while that devoid of it is "consisting of non-vibration.

They are "as if distinct" merely by name—that is, by a name created solely for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). Of what nature are they? "All-pervading" (*sarvagā*), meaning they reside within the universal reality and its transcendent essential nature (*svarūpa*). Like what? Like the wind. For the wind, [existence] consists of vibration.

Existence (*sattā*) is that by which trees and other things tremble; it consists of both vibration and non-vibration, and its nature is like space. [Objection: But how can there be unity in existence, which consists of both vibration and non-vibration? [Response: True. Just as the unity of water—whether moving or still—is determined by those who are skillful, so it is here as well; thus, there is no contradiction.
He who is always awakened and yet always asleep; he who is neither deeply slumbering nor awakened, being so at all times and in all places.

He who is always, in all conditions, awakened—because he abides as the witness, he is indeed endowed with supreme knowledge; yet he who is always asleep—because he is devoid of that reflective awareness, he has entered a state of slumber;
and he who everywhere, in all places, at all times, and in every particular state, is never fast asleep.

Because it is eternally of the nature of awakening, it does not become a Buddha; for even when there is self-reflection through equanimity (*upekṣā*), it remains turned away from such conceptualization.

That which is motionless is the peaceful Śiva; that which is its vibration is the existence of the three worlds. He who is the single one, whose form is full, consists of the playful manifestation of both vibration and non-vibration.

Thus: that which is non-vibration (*aspanda*) and devoid of orientation toward the object of cognition (*cetyaunmukhyarāhitya*) is *śānta* (quiescent), free from agitation; it is *śiva*, bliss. That which is vibration (*spanda*) and possesses orientation toward the object of cognition is the existence of the three worlds (*trijagatsthiti*), the reality of the three worlds.

He who is the one whose nature consists of the play of both vibration and non-vibration, whose essential form is both endowed with and devoid of orientation toward the object of cognition, is [the ultimate reality].
Of what nature is he? He is "of filled form" (*bharitākṛti*). His form (*ākṛti*)—that is, his essential nature (*svarūpa*)—is "filled," meaning it consists of everything. Such is he.
For a single entity to simultaneously possess the nature of vibration (*spandamayatva*) brings about manifold variety (*vaicitrya*).
Like fragrance in flowers that perish, it does not vanish; though present before the eyes, it is nevertheless ungraspable, like the whiteness in white cloths.

That which does not perish among perishing objects— because it persists in a subtle state as their material cause even upon their destruction— is like fragrance. Just as when a flower has perished, its fragrance does not perish for some time, continuing to waft through the air.

The meaning is "so it is. That which is ungraspable—meaning it cannot be grasped by any external or internal sense organ—is such even though it is present before the eyes, even though it exists in direct perception;
for one's own self is never imperceptible, as in the thought, "I am not here. How so? Like whiteness; just as [whiteness] existing in a cloth...
Whiteness, although perceptible, cannot be grasped by the hand; such is the meaning.
He who speaks like one mute, he who thinks like a stone, he who enjoys while remaining eternally satisfied, and he who acts while possessing nothing—[he is a sage].

He who is the speaker, because he exists as the nature of all speakers; and of what kind is he? Even one resembling a mute, for his state of being like a mute is due to his freedom from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*). He who is the thinker and the knower—for indeed, without him, there could be no other so-called "thinker";
he is like a stone, because, having the nature of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), he is devoid of the stain of being a thinker.

He who, though eternally satisfied—being always satisfied by himself alone due to his nature as supreme bliss—is yet the enjoyer, for the state of being the enjoyer never departs from that very nature. He who, though the agent—having attained agency by bestowing power upon all agents—is yet "possessing nothing" (*akiñcana*); here, "something" (*kiñcana*) is to be understood as the agent; thus, the meaning is that he does not become an agent.
And its state of being a non-agent should be understood precisely through its state of possessing nothing; for agency consists in having some [specific] form.
He who, though without limbs, possesses all limbs, and has a thousand hands and eyes; by whom, even though he does not occupy any space, this entire world is pervaded.

He who, though bodiless—that is, devoid of limbs because he consists of pure consciousness alone—becomes possessed of all limbs. How is he so? He is "thousand-handed and thousand-eyed. Here, the word "thousand" signifies infinity; thus, the meaning is "infinite-handed and infinite-eyed.
This state of having infinite hands and eyes should be understood as existing within his infinite bodies by virtue of being their very self. This is indicated through the qualifying term "thousand."
This is the reason: likewise, by that [which] pervades all this; otherwise, what would this consist of? Such is the sense. By what kind of thing?
Even by one that is not established, nor existing anywhere. How? In the sense of even slightly (*kiñcit leśenāpi*). Or rather, because its state of being unestablished cannot be grasped.
Even though he is devoid of the power of the senses, all sensory functions belong to him; even though he is without a mind, these modes of mental emanation belong to him.

He whose activities of all the sense-faculties (*indriya*) occur—of what sort [is he]? Even though he is devoid of the power of the sense-faculties, his state of possessing the activities of all sense-faculties arises from the fact that they have the nature of the essence of the sense-faculties. Even though he is without a mind (*manas*), because he consists of non-conceptual pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), even while having the form of a mind, the modes of mental emanation (*nirmāṇa*) occur. Otherwise, from what source would these [emanations] arise when they appear in this or that form?
It may be so.
Because it is not contemplated, the fears of the serpent of saṃsāra appear; when it is seen, all calamities flee in every way and for all time.

"Because of non-contemplation"—that is, due to the absence of correct knowledge regarding its object—the "fears arising from the serpent of saṃsāra," which are the fears produced by the snake called saṃsāra, "appear" or manifest. The intention behind the word "serpent" (uraga) is this: just as fears of a serpent flash forth due to the absence of correct knowledge of a rope, so too it is precisely through ignorance of the Supreme Self that saṃsāra and the fears thereof appear within it.

When that Supreme Self is seen—that is, when it is experienced as one's own true nature—all calamities (*ītayaḥ*), which are afflictions existing in every way and in every manner, flee and go far away at all times and in all moments. The fleeing of these calamities is nothing other than the knowledge of their identity with the Supreme Self, through the reversal of their nature as calamities; for even they, in the ultimate sense, possess that very same nature.
In that witness, which is a vast and steady radiance like a lamp, all activities proceed—those various mental efforts preceded by movement—only while it exists.
In that which is the witness (*sākṣin*)—the witness being the subject that perceives all states of stillness and movement; in that which is expansive (*sphāra*) and all-pervading (*vyāpaka*);

in that which is manifestation (*ābhāsa*), whose sole essence is radiance; in that which is constant (*dhruva*) and indifferent (*udāsīna*)—when that exists, by its mere presence, the various activities of the mind (*citrehāḥ*) proceed. Of what nature are they? They are bodily movements preceded by vibration (*spanda*). They proceed.

The meaning is that they are accompanied by that [consciousness]. The sense is that if there were no internal principle of consciousness (*cittattva*), the arising of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and bodily movements would not be possible. What is it like? It is like action, such as worldly activity; just as worldly activity proceeds of its own accord when a lamp merely provides its presence, so too is the case here. This is the meaning.
For from it arise hundreds of rows of objects in the form of jars, cloths, and so forth, just as the ocean produces waves, droplets, surges, and billows.

From that which serves as the material cause (*upādāna*); from which there arise hundreds of rows of objects in the form of jars and cloths—that is, collections of hundreds of objects whose nature consists of jars and cloths. Although others have asserted that atoms and the like alone possess the status of material cause, nevertheless, because such things lack the status of a material cause with respect to sentient beings, some material cause must exist that possesses both a sentient and a non-sentient nature.
There is no dispute that [these] are to be conceptualized. What are they like? They are like ripples, droplets, surges, and waves. The meaning is: just as these arise from the ocean, so it is here.
That very same reality arises as something else through the delusions of hundreds of objects, just as gold appears as bracelets, armlets, neck-ornaments, and anklets.

That very one called consciousness (cit), while existing in its own unprecedented form, arises—that is, goes to its rising—as something else, by way of another nature. The meaning is that it assumes, as it were, another nature. By means of what? By means of the delusions (*bhrama*) in the form of a hundred objects; that is to say, by means of those hundred objects. And here, the word "hundred" signifies infinity. Like what? Like gold.
"Just as gold appears in the form of bracelets, armlets, neck-ornaments, and anklets—such is the meaning. // MT_3,9.72 //
You who are the self-luminous essence, I who am this, and these people who exist; and that which is not you, O one whose nature is unawakened, nor I, nor these people—that [is the Self].

O you whose nature was previously unawakened, who have not yet known the reality of the Supreme Self; you who are of the nature of a single manifestation, whose essence is pure knowledge—you who exist as the one to be instructed, meaning you appear as "thou"; you who exist as the instructor, meaning you appear as "I"; and these people who exist, meaning they appear as "that."
Because it exists as the essence everywhere. [Objection: "In that case, is it not then limited? [Reply: He says, "And which...
The meaning is that, in ultimate reality, it exists in the form of pure consciousness alone, free from conceptual constructions such as "you-ness" (tvattā) and so forth.

In that [reality] in which the world of appearances flashes forth—like a series of waves upon the water—it is both non-different and yet different from it, and it is itself as well as not itself, and is transitory.

"Bhaṅgurā" means having a perishable nature. "Dṛśyabhūḥ": the "dṛśya" (the visible) is the multitude of entities that are the objects of the act of seeing; that itself is the "bhūḥ" (ground), because it is the substratum for various arrangements, and thus a "bhūmi" (plane). That [visible ground] "sphurati" (throbs) or "vilasati" (shines forth) within which substratum. The fact that the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*) is the substratum of the visible should be understood through the analogy of a dream. How is it? It is indeed non-different from that; there is no difference from it.

It has not entered [into anything else] at all; it is "other" only in the sense of being like something else. The meaning is that it appears as such. The appearance of otherness in that which is non-distinct brings about variety.

Anticipating the doubt that there might be an absence of identity between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) despite the lack of distinction, he states "that very same [consciousness]" to express its identity with it.

It is that very same [consciousness], and not even in the slightest degree does it have the nature of something else. It is like that itself, appearing as if it were not that. Like what? Like a series of waves.
Moreover, it is established by universal experience that even when the water of the Gaṅgā possesses the nature of those [waves], it appears as if it were not of that nature.
From which comes the reckoning of time, from which comes the visibility of the visible, by which comes mental construction, and by which comes the shining forth of lights.
Since the reckoning (*kalanā*)—that is, conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)—of time occurs when it is devoid of adjuncts such as the present and so forth;
for the meaning is that the conceptualization of time is not tenable without an internal conceptualizer. Since the visibility of the visible occurs;
for the visibility of the visible is not possible without a seer. By means of which mental reckoning...

It exists; for even the mind is not established without a witness, by whom there occurs the manifestation—the flashing forth—of appearances, such as the cognitions of jars and so forth. Indeed, cognitions do not arise without a knower.
Action, form, taste, smell, touch, sound, and consciousness—whatever you perceive is that God; and that by which you perceive is also He.

By the word "action" (*kriyām*), the term "you do" (*karoṣi*) should be connected in place of "you know" (*vetsi*). Therefore, the meaning is as follows: that action which you perform is the instrument (*karaṇa*); moreover, that aforementioned god is the one who performs the play (*krīḍākārī*). Furthermore, that by which you act, the organ of action (*karmendriya*), that too is the god; likewise is form (*rūpa*).

That which you perceive as taste, smell, touch, and sound—that is the Divine. That by means of which you perceive through the five sensory organs—that too is the Divine. Likewise, that which you perceive as consciousness, volition, and so forth—that is the Divine. That by means of which you perceive through the internal organ—that too is the Divine. By this [it is shown] regarding the fruit of action...
And it has been stated that the instrument of that [action] consists of that [same material]; as for the agent, however, its being composed of that [material] is established beyond dispute.
Having thus described its essential nature by means of its qualifications, he states the means for entering it:
"O virtuous one, among the seer, the seeing, and the seen, that which exists as the act of seeing—you shall realize your own Self through focused attention upon that. (MU 3.9.77)

O holy one, worthy of the realization of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), you perceive—that is, you know—your own self, which is the Supreme Self existing as your true nature (*svarūpa*), by means of focused attention through the application of concentration upon that.
