Where? In the midst of the triad of the seer (*draṣṭṛ*), the seeing (*darśana*), and the seen (*dṛśya*).
That which remains as the act of seeing (*darśana*) is the conclusion here. All worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) for its part...

It is established within this very triad: therein, the seer is the agent; seeing is the action; and the visible object, which serves as the objective support (*ālambana*), is the action-object (*karman*) upon which the action arises. As for the instrument (*karaṇa*), which consists of the uncommon cause, it is not distinct from these [other factors], because the totality (*sāmagrī*) itself constitutes the instrument. In that context, for the seer who is seized by the conceit "I am the seer," there arises [cognition] directed toward the visible object, which has the nature of being solely the graspable.

Vision arises; otherwise, the relationship between those two as seer and seen would be impossible. Because it is seized by the conceit of being the seer, it cannot be purified instantaneously. But the seen, due to its extreme insentience, shares the same fate as that [seer]. Therefore, setting aside both of them, attention is prescribed toward vision alone. [Objection: But is not vision also corrupted by the defects of its locus and its object?

It cannot be purified at all. It is true that it is impossible to eliminate the "I-ness" residing in the seer and the "insentience" residing in the seen. However, for vision—which is tainted by contact with both even in the slightest degree—it is indeed possible to eliminate the two defects existing as its constituent parts. In this regard, the method is as follows: vision is not of my nature.

It is evident that [the seeing] is distinct from me; and because it lacks the nature of a seer, it does not possess the form of the seen. Since it is the grasper, nothing distinct from those two can be grasped. Thus, there exists an indefinable vision called "seeing" which is distinct from them; therefore, the identity of seeing with the Supreme Self is established. Consequently, it is also [identical] to the seer and the seen.
It is indeed more established: for when the connection with seeing has dissolved, the existence of the seer and the seen is not possible;
because the seer is a seer precisely by being the locus of seeing, and the seen is a seen precisely by being its object.
Alternatively, "seeing" here should be understood as occurring at the time of the desire to see; for at that time, it is [the seeing] due to the absence of the coloring of the locus and the object.
It manifests as pure alone; subsequently, however, it attains grossness.
He summarizes what was previously stated with a verse at the end of the chapter:

The unborn, undecaying, non-inert, eternal, constant Brahman—auspicious, stainless, beginningless, and beyond reproach due to its objects of knowledge; devoid of all mental constructions, the cause of causes, experience itself, unknowable yet the very act of knowing, and consciousness within. (MU 3.1.78)
"Knowing" means that it knows; "it becomes the end" means it becomes the final limit of the entire class of visible objects;

that is to say, it remains at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). Of what nature is it? It is unborn (*aja*), because it exists at all times; undecaying (*ajara*), because it is distinct from the body; unclouded by dullness (*ajāḍya*), because it is distinct from the mind; and eternal (*śāśvata*), because even though it is the self of the universe, it does not deviate from its own essential nature.

It is *acyuta* because it does not fall away; *brahman* because it expands (*bṛṃhaṇāt*) the world; *nitya* because it does not perish throughout the three periods of time; *śiva* because its sole nature is bliss; *amala* because it is devoid of the impurity of duality; *anādya* because nothing exists as prior to it; *anindya* and *akadarthita* because it is not defiled by the existence or non-existence that reside within it, which are [merely] objects of futile knowledge for those whose understanding is barren; and it is empty of all conceptualization.

Because its essential nature is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*). It is the cause of those causes—Brahmā and the others—who are considered to be causes; for even they possess form and are therefore themselves caused. Experience is the very nature of experience, because it is within experience alone that the previously mentioned specific qualities can exist. Even though its nature is experience, fearing the possibility of it being defiled by the object of cognition, he says "incognizable" (*avedya*). Incognizable means untainted by contact with an object of cognition.
Feeling; that is to say, having the nature of being neither conscious nor unconscious. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the ninth canto in the "Section on Origination" of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ! Here, as if having fallen into a state of delusion, Śrī Rāma asks:
"Regarding that which remains when the great dissolution has occurred—let it be called 'formless'; there is no doubt about this."

There is no doubt regarding this; this is the reality. It is formless, devoid of characteristics. Let it be so; the sense is that I too have conviction in this. What is this? That which is the existent reality remains as a residue when the great dissolution has occurred and all phenomena have perished.
He explains that it is not tenable to deny its nature as a real entity—such as emptiness (*śūnya*) and so forth—which is devoid of any externally perceived form:
"How could it not be empty? How could it not be luminosity? How could it not be of the nature of darkness? Or how could it not be of the nature of space? (MU 3.10.2)

How could that not be empty? The meaning is: let that very thing be so. This should be applied everywhere in this manner. *Prakāśa* is the manifestation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*). *Khātmaka* means having the nature of space (*ākāśa*).

Or how could it not be of the nature of consciousness? Or how could it not be the individual soul (jīva)? How could it not be the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva)? Or how could it not be the mind (manas)?
This was stated because even the nature of consciousness is excluded from that state as being ultimately real.
Or how could it be that nothing exists, or how could everything exist? By this turn of phrase, a kind of delusion has arisen within me.
Nothing does not exist in any form whatsoever, because even "nothingness" itself is negated; otherwise, how could it not also be the case that "everything" exists?
The venerable Vasiṣṭha replied:
"This question posed by you is exceedingly difficult; yet I shall resolve it with ease, as the sun dispels the darkness of night."

The word *ati* is displaced [in the compound]. This question has been posed by you as being extremely difficult and most hard to understand; however, [the particle] *tu* indicates a distinction. "I split this with ease and without effort"—this statement that "I split it" is used because the question is of the nature of a mental knot (*manogranthi*). How? Like the sun, the possessor of rays (*aṃśumān*); just as the sun [dispels] the nocturnal [darkness], that which pertains to the night.
It pierces the darkness; such is the meaning.
It resolves the very question:
that which remains as the existent at the conclusion of the great dissolution—that, O Rāma, is not empty; listen now as this is being explained.

Whether at the perfection of the end of a great kalpa, in the fourth state (turya), in the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), or at the completion of the time of the great dissolution—that which is well-known cannot be denied by anyone. O Rāma! That is the existent reality denoted by the word "that" (tat). In what manner it does not become void—explain that very manner; this is what is being stated immediately hereafter.
Listen, for it is being told by me.
He explains that very point:
Just as a carved figure remains within a pillar though it has not been carved out, so does the universe abide therein; therefore, that state is not empty of it.

It has not been carved out by a woodcarver, nor has it been manifested after being hewn; its state of residing within the pillar is due to its manifestation at the very front [of it]. Its existence within the reality of the universe is because it is manifest even this very day—this, however, is the distinction. That "place" (pada) is the station known as the Supreme Self (paramātman). If that were empty, then where would the world abide?
The sense is that an error without a substratum is untenable; thus it is said that [the object] appears as distinct, even though it is not carved out [as separate].
He explains this in detail as follows:
"This world, known as the 'living beings,' appears thus with great abundance; whether it be real or unreal, where in that [world] could there be emptiness?"
This expansion being experienced— let it be real, let it be of the nature of existence, that which is called "the world" (*jagat*),
possessing great enjoyment and great extension; whether it be unreal or of the nature of non-existence,
in whatever substrate, in whatever entity, it appears and manifests— where [is it]?
The meaning is that emptiness is not logical.
Just as a pillar that has not been carved with figures is not empty of those figures, so too, my dear, the world is Brahman; therefore, that state is not empty of it.
"Without the carved *sālikā* [bird] and without the carved *putrikā* [doll]," he applies this to the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the word "so" (*tathā*). O dear one, O venerable one!
By this "so," the two words "not" (*na*) and "empty" (*śūnya*) found in the preceding sentence are drawn in. Therefore, the meaning is this:
likewise, Brahman does not become empty of the world. He states the conclusion with the word "therefore" (*tena*).
Just as a wave in gentle water neither exists nor does not exist, so this world within Brahman has reached a state that is both empty and non-empty.

In the "somya" water—that is, in water free from agitation—it does not exist, because at that time it is unobtainable; nor does it not exist, because it will become manifest later on. He states the application to the example with the word "tathā" (so too). It should be understood that because it appears, it has reached the state of being non-empty, and because in the ultimate sense it has no form whatsoever, it has reached the state of being empty.
"Is it not then the case that the existence of the world in Brahman is already established through its similarity to a carved doll and the like? To this he replies:
"The carving of a doll on a tree is possible because [the tree] is limited by space, time, and so forth; but in the unborn element (aja-dhātu), by whom could one not be deluded within? (MU 3.10.11)
In a tree, by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the fashioning of a statue occurs upon a pillar; this is possible depending on the place, the time, and the agent and so forth.

But in the specific case—referring to the primary cause called Consciousness (*cit*), which is devoid of any new manifestation within the non-material realm (*aja-dhātu*)—within the inner mind (*antaḥ* = *manasi*), by what person would one not be deluded? Rather, everyone indeed becomes deluded.

The meaning [of the verse] is as follows: Why is there delusion? Because space, time, and so forth are quiescent (*śānta*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), agents and other such factors are included; thus, the meaning is "because of the quiescence of space, time, agent, and so on. Furthermore, this quiescence here should be understood precisely as pure consciousness alone (*śuddhacinmātratā*). And delusion should be understood as the notion: "How does the world appear within Brahman, which is devoid of contact with space, time, and the like?"
He states the conclusion:
"That [world], consisting of pillars, statues, and so forth, is a simile that resembles the ultimate state of the world only in part, not in every respect."

Since the fashioning of a figurine on a pillar is appropriate due to the occurrence of place, time, and other such factors, it is not appropriate for that same [fashioning] within the element of consciousness (ciddhātu), which is characterized by peace. For that reason, immediately after this, the "pillar-figurine" and so forth were mentioned; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), waves and water are included. This refers merely to the refutation of emptiness as a partial aspect of the way the world exists in ultimate reality.
The object of comparison (*upamāna*) is similar [to the subject], but not in every respect; that is to say, it is not similar in every way. This is the meaning.
Having refuted its emptiness by virtue of being the substratum of the world, he now refutes it by demonstrating its true nature:
"This never arises from another, nor does it ever cease; this form is solely the existent Brahman, established within its own self. (MU 3.10.13)

"From the other," that is, from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). [Objection: If the world neither arises nor ceases, then what is this that appears? To this he says: "This. It is merely the non-dual; *sat*, which is the nature of Being; *brahma*, the expanded reality.
It remains established within its own self, within its own nature. Of what nature is this? It is of the form of "this," accompanied by both cessation and arising.

The world—whose nature is form—is such [as described]. The state of Brahmanhood of the world, which is accompanied by both quiescence and arising, is to be understood as being the object of the expansion that has Brahman as its locus. For the object of expansion is indeed the very nature of Brahman itself.
Thus, the implication is that it is not logical for Brahman to be a void (śūnya).

He states the refutation of emptiness by means of the impossibility of non-emptiness: "Since non-emptiness is impossible, the conceptualization of the meaning of the word 'empty' depends upon non-emptiness; therefore, from where could both emptiness and non-emptiness arise? (MU 3.10.14) The phrase "depending upon non-emptiness" (*aśūnyatvāpekṣayā*) means depending upon some form of non-emptiness—that is, depending upon that [non-emptiness]. [This refers to] the conceptualization of emptiness (*śūnyatva-parikalpanā*). Of emptiness...

Regarding the state of being nothing (*nakiñcidrūpatva*): *parikalpanā* means conceptual construction (*kalpana*). What follows from that? To this he says: "because of non-emptiness" (*aśūnyatve*). This means that because non-emptiness is impossible—due to the impossibility of having any form whatsoever according to the reasoning already stated—both emptiness and non-emptiness, as well as being nothing and not being nothing, do not exist.
Why? The meaning is that they do not exist; the point is that when one of two interdependent things perishes, both perish. Thus, there is an absence of any form whatsoever.
And it should be known as being nothing but pure consciousness, free from any support.

Having set aside emptiness, this [proponent] sets aside the nature of luminosity in Brahman, for this light cannot possibly arise from the elements; how indeed could the sun, fire, moon, stars, and so forth exist there in that which is imperishable?

This light, which is perceived by the eye, is born of the elements—produced from fire and other elements—and is luminosity (*tejas*). Indeed (*hi*), it cannot exist in Brahman, the all-pervading reality, because [Brahman] transcends that [light] by being pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Regarding this, he states the latter half of the verse as the reason, beginning with "sūrya-". The particle *kila* is used to indicate the reason. [It does not exist] in the Imperishable (*avyaya*), which is devoid of destruction, because the sun and other luminaries possess form (*ākṛtimattva*).
Because destruction occurs, stability here is not logical; what then can be said of its having that very nature? This is the intended meaning.
He refutes the nature of darkness as follows:
"Darkness is said to be the absence of the light of the great elements; therefore, there is no darkness here anywhere that is produced by the absence of the great elements."

The meaning is that proponents have established that darkness (*tamas*) is simply the absence of light (*tejas*). He states the conclusion: "arising from the absence of the great elements" (*mahābhūtābhāvaja*); the word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction. [It is] born from the absence of the manifestation of the great elements by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), which is to say, it has that as its nature;
[this refers to] darkness. Here, regarding an existing entity (*sad-vastu*), by that reason—namely, being the absence of the manifestation of the great elements—it does not exist.

Where? In some part, in any locus of the persistence of the great elements (*mahābhūta*). Since the non-existence (*abhāva*) that is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the great elements is impossible, even darkness (*tamas*) is not tenable here; what then to say of its specific form? This is the intended meaning.
[Objection: But how can that [space] be manifested in the absence of light? To this he replies:
"The manifestation of this, which has the nature of space, is solely its own self-experience; that which exists within is experienced by that alone, and not by anything else. (MU 3.10.17)

Of this existent reality, which has the nature of space and is of the form of "nothingness," there is self-experience (*svānubhūti*). This experience, being its own essential nature, is that very experience; it is self-experience. That itself is the light—the radiance that constitutes the act of manifestation. The meaning is that it shines by means of self-experience alone, and not by external light. To the question "In what manner?", he says here: "That which is within" (*yo 'ntar*). That which is within...

It exists; it is experienced by that very person through that same [consciousness] which is not a separate instrument, and is brought within the range of one's own cognition, but not by another, because it is impossible for another to enter therein. This experience itself is the experiencer, the act of experiencing, and the object of experience; the meaning is that there is no dependence on anything else in this regard.
He connects the subject at hand:
"That which is liberated from darkness and light—know this undecaying state to be the very sheath of space, the sheath for the existence of the world. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.8)
In this manner; this being described by way of remainder; "undecaying" means free from the defect of old age; "pada" means the state or station;
it becomes "freed from darkness and light," that is, from both darkness (*tamas*) and light (*prakāśa*). He begins to preclude its nature as being merely space (*khātmakatva*):
"the sheath of space" (*ākāśakośa*), meaning the midst of space. You [should know] this Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as such.
Know—that is, understand—the treasury, the storehouse, of the world's existence.
He confirms this very point with an illustration:

"Just as there is no difference whatsoever between a wood-apple (*bilva*) and that which is called a wood-apple, so too here, there is not even the slightest distinctness between Brahman and the world. (MU 3.1.19)

Just as there is no difference whatsoever in the *bilva*— that is, in the fruit called *bilva*, or in the object which is the cause for applying the name "bilva"— so too, in this manner, in these three worlds, there is not even the slightest difference between Brahman and the universe; that which is Brahman is that very same [universe].
The world; the meaning is that whatever is the world, that indeed is Brahman. There is also a reading: "of the *bilva* [fruit], of the interior of the *bilva*."
"Even so, what relevance does this have to the present case? To this he says:
"Just as a wave exists within water, and just as a jar exists within clay, so too, where the existence of the world resides, how could that [reality] be of the nature of space? (MU 3.10.20)

Just as there are waves within water, so too, in that manner, that entity in which the existence of the world resides— being the substrate of appropriation— how could it be of the nature of space, having the character of the ether?
He begins the systematic exposition for the purpose of removing [any notion of] having the nature of consciousness:
"The beauty of the analogies such as clay and water possesses form here; it is not equal [to Brahman]. But Brahman is as clear as the sky; that which resides within it is likewise so. (MU 3.1.21)

The beauty of analogies such as clay, water, and so forth, is not appropriate—that is, suitable—in this case regarding Brahman. When the question arises as to why this is so, he says: "Because it possesses form. Since [Brahman] possesses form (sākāra), being endowed with form, how can it be fit for comparison with clay, water, and the like? To this he replies: "Brahman," with the particle *tu* used for emphasis. Brahman is as clear as the sky and is formless (nirākāra).

The sense is that it is not logical for something with form, such as clay and so forth, to serve as an analogy for Brahman, which is formless. He states the conclusion: "Of that" (tasya). "That" means for that reason. "Situated within that" (tadantaḥstha) means existing inside it. The meaning is that the world likewise becomes formless.
Furthermore, under the guise of a summary, he establishes the formlessness of the world:
"Therefore, just as the space of consciousness is clearer than even physical space, so too is that which exists within it—the referent of the word 'world'—exactly like that. (MU 3.10.22)

The purity of the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) is to be understood as being even more stainless than the physical ether (*ākāśa*), due to its lack of insentience (*jaḍatva*). The universe resides within it;

likewise, it remains formless. Even though it possesses the portion that constitutes the meaning of the word "universe"—the term *bhāva-pradhāna-nirdeśa* (an expression where the abstract state is primary) indicates this—meaning that although it appears in the form of the universe, it nevertheless possesses the status of being the referent of the word "universe."
Just as pungency within a pepper is not perceived without a taster, so too is pure consciousness in the supreme space not perceived without the element of the object of thought.

Just as the pungency and bitterness residing within a peppercorn—within the interior of the peppercorn—is not perceived or seen by anyone except the eater, yet when there is an eater, it is perceived by that very person; such is the meaning. Likewise, the state of pure consciousness (cinmātratva) residing in the supreme ether, which is the Supreme Self, is not perceived without the "particle of the object of thought" (cetyakalā), that is, without the objective aspect, because [consciousness is only manifest] through the relishing of the object of thought.
For in this way alone is the pure consciousness of pure consciousness itself known.
He states the conclusion:

"Therefore, even though consciousness is of the nature of the non-conscious, because it is not distinct from itself, this world-existence is exactly like that, by virtue of being essentially nothing but that."

Therefore, for that reason—by virtue of being devoid of the object of consciousness (*cetya*), that is, by being free from the object of consciousness—the *cit* (consciousness) itself becomes as if non-conscious (*acid*) within the Self, which is one's own essential nature called pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). This is because, according to the previous method, the capacity to firmly establish the state of pure consciousness has been applied precisely to the object of consciousness, and that [object] is absent here. Furthermore, its absence here should be understood as being Brahman itself, since it exists within Brahman.

He extends the state of being non-conscious even to the world that is non-different from Brahman, saying "the world-nature" (*jagattā*). This world-nature as well, by virtue of its non-difference from Brahman whose nature is consciousness, is itself of a non-conscious nature. He states a qualification here as the reason: "under the sway of having that alone as its essence" (*tādṛṅmātrātmatāvaśā*). Because it is under the sway—that is, dependent—upon having that alone as its essence, which is the nature of Brahman alone who is non-conscious; thus, it has the nature of Brahman who is non-conscious.

The meaning is as follows: by this, the absolute non-difference between Brahman and the world is also established. It is not that Brahman consists merely of the insentient form, because that [point] will be proven later as well.
Now, if the world is entirely non-different [from consciousness], what is the nature of form, light, and mental attention? To this he says:
Form, light, and mental attention consist of that [consciousness] alone and nothing else. Therefore, the universe as it exists is either deep sleep or the fourth state (turya).

[The three factors are] form, light, and mental attention (*manaskāra*). Form refers to blue, yellow, and so forth. Light is that which sees it, or the illumination serving as the instrument. Mental attention is the mental apprehension. These have those [three] as their objects; they consist of nothing other than them. He states the meaning of the word "only" (*eva*) by saying "not anything else. Furthermore, their consisting of those [objects] is due to their being like non-existent things in the absence of having those as their objects. He states the conclusion with the words "just as."

For this reason, the entire universe (*viśvaṃ jagat*), existing in its actual state—that is, persisting in this very manner and not having been rendered invisible by any power whatsoever—becomes as if in deep sleep (*suṣupta*). Anticipating the concern regarding the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of duality within deep sleep, he says "the fourth" (*turyam*); the meaning is that it becomes one with the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) whose nature is the fourth state.
He states that because the world is Brahman in its fourth state (turya), the yogi possesses the nature of Brahman even during worldly activity:

"Therefore, the yogi, though engaged in worldly affairs, remains with a mind at peace as if in deep sleep; he abides in the non-manifest Brahman, which is the casket containing all manifestations. (MU 3.10.26)

For the reason stated previously, the yogi is absorbed in the oneness of the world and Brahman; he abides as Brahman, that is, in his own true nature as Brahman. Why does he abide in such a form? Because, even while being engaged in worldly activity (*vyavahārin*), performing worldly transactions, his intellect is tranquil, free from agitation. Why is he even like this? Because he is one whose self is as if in deep sleep (*suṣuptātman*), with his internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) asleep toward the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

For one whose mind is asleep toward conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it is indeed appropriate that their intellect be at peace. Of what nature is Brahman? It is "without appearance" (*nirābhāsa*), meaning it has emerged from various appearances; that is to say, it transcends them. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is the "receptacle" (*samudgaka*)—the source of emergence—for all appearances, that is, for all cognitions of jars, cloths, and so forth.
Furthermore, he explains the very non-difference between Brahman and the world that is under discussion:
"Just as the property of fluidity resides in clear water which possesses form, so does the universe reside in the Supreme, which is formless, being similar to it. (MU 3.10.27)

Just as the sequence of motion exists in water—which possesses form, is characterized by a nature graspable by the external senses, is gentle, and is free from agitation—so too does the entire universe exist within the formless Supreme, the Parabrahman; how so? It exists in a manner similar to that [water], being formless.

The meaning is as follows: just as the quality called fluidity (*drava*), though it is only slightly manifest, becomes clearly evident in gentle water and thus consists of that [water], so too the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), though it appears as something distinct, consists of Brahman—this is the intended sense.
Having stated their non-difference, he now explains the reality itself:
From the Full, the Full flows forth; from the formless, the formless. The universe has appeared from Brahman, yet it is devoid of the objective reality of the universe.

From the Full Brahman, the world, which is of the nature of fullness, emanates and shines forth. Here, "emanation" is employed for the sake of a disciple whose intellect has been overcome by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). From formless Brahman, the world, though formless, emanates. Therefore, that universe which has appeared—that manifestation which has come into being—from Brahman, is devoid of the objects of the universe, such as jars, cloths, and so forth.
It becomes devoid [of duality]; the meaning is that it becomes solely composed of Brahman.
From the Full, the Full flows forth; that which is established remains the Full itself. Therefore, the universe is unarisen; and whatever has arisen, that too is precisely that.
From the full Brahman, the world, which is of the nature of the full, flows forth and manifests; its flow becomes established.
However, by that flowing forth, no fragmentation whatsoever arises in it—this is the meaning. He states the conclusion:
"Therefore" (ataḥ); for this reason mentioned above, the universe remains unproduced, because it is eternally [identical] with Brahman.

Because [Brahman] is eternally established. To one who cannot tolerate the non-arising of the universe, he says "And that which... and so forth. The meaning is: that which arises is precisely that very Brahman; for even that which has arisen is not inconsistent with being Brahman.
By this process, it is established that Brahman is insentient in nature;
therefore, how can there be any sense of sentience in that state? Just as there can be no pungency in a pepper for one who lacks the capacity to taste it.

The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is to be supplied [as the beginning of the sentence]. Therefore, for this reason; because of the impossibility of an object of consciousness (*cetya*). Because of the impossibility of the world, which is the object of consciousness (*cid-viṣaya*). In that state, in that state which is the very nature of Brahman, what possibility is there for the status of being consciousness (*cid-arthatā*), that is, for being the ground for the application of the word "consciousness"? The meaning is: none at all. For it is only by virtue of taking an object of consciousness as its domain that the name "consciousness" (*cit*) is appropriately applied to *cit*.

But in the absence of an object of consciousness (*cetya*), that [consciousness] is not tenable. And the absence of an object of consciousness has already been established in detail previously. Furthermore, the negation of consciousness having an object here should be understood as being due to its transcendence of that [object], and not due to its insentience (*jaḍatā*). To provide a supporting illustration for this, he says "āsvādakā-," meaning "like a taster.
The sense is: "like what? Like nothing at all. This means: "due to the impossibility of a taster" (*āsvādakāsambhavataḥ*), that is, by virtue of the non-existence of a taster.
Furthermore, this very point is stated:

"This [world] arises in the consciousness of another [the Supreme], whether it be real or unreal; since there is no reflection [of an external object], how can there be the capacity for a reflection? (MU 3.10.31).

The "consciousness" (cit) belonging to the intellect (citta)—that is, the state of consciousness—is, in the Supreme Self (para), truly non-existent in its ultimate sense (paramārtha), being by nature unreal; yet it appears as if real. Regarding this, he states an illustration: "Because of its absence" (abhāvāt); the word "of the mirror" (darpaṇasya) is to be supplied.
Just as the capacity of a mirror to reflect is known only through a reflection, but in the absence of that [reflection], it is not known.
In this way, another's mind is known only by means of its object; the point is that in the absence of that object, how could it be known?
To exclude the nature of the individual soul (jīva) and so forth, he qualifies the reality of the Supreme Self:
"That is subtler than even the subtlest atom; it is pure, subtle, supreme, and more tranquil than even the interior of space. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.7)

That Brahman is subtler than even the atom; it is exceedingly subtle. Subtler than what? Subtler than even that which is minute, namely, the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth. Its subtlety is to be understood by its being ungraspable by the external senses. That Brahman—of what nature is it? Pure, undefiled by the dust of passion and the like; subtle; supreme.
It has transcended; it is peaceful and empty of all mental activity; it is beyond anything whatsoever, even the interior of space.
Because its nature is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, it is exceedingly vast; it is without beginning or end, a manifestation devoid of anything to be manifested.

That Brahman is exceedingly extensive, meaning it is vastly expanded. Why? Because its nature is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), material objects are included; the meaning is that it is devoid of the three kinds of limitations. Now, one might ask:

how can this [Brahman] be devoid of limitation by space and the like? And even if it were so, how could there be such vast expansion? [The answer is: Space, for its part, is that which is perceived...

Or rather, it is not [perceived]. If that is so, then since it is itself unestablished, how could it delimit another? If it is being perceived, then it is delimited by consciousness alone; how then could it delimit that [consciousness]? The same should be understood for time and the rest as well.
An object is delimited precisely by being delimited by space and so forth; in the absence of those, however, it would simply be infinitely extended.
It remains in a state of extreme vastness. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is without beginning or end;
even though a beginning and an end might be conceptually imagined, it is devoid of beginning and end because it is the witness to them. Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is "devoid of that which is to be manifested," meaning its essential nature is knowledge free from objective appearances and objects of cognition.
By relying on the previously mentioned qualifications, he negates its nature as a living being (jīva) and so forth:

"Wherein only the form of consciousness (cidrūpa) is found, how could there be the state of a living being? How could there be the form of mental impressions (vāsanā), which are like the wind, within that state of pure consciousness? (MU 3.10.34)

In that Brahman, which is thus distinguished by such qualities, even the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*)—the term being used with the abstract suffix to denote the state of being—is not obtained; that is, it is not experienced according to the logic previously established. In such a Brahman, how could there be "living-ness," the state of being a living soul (*jīvatā*)? Of what nature would it be? It would be of the form of "cittatā" (the state of being mind); for "mind" (*citta*) is the state of being mind (*cittatva*) that has entered into the bed of the object of cognition (*cetya*). Thus, [the soul] would be of that very form.

The meaning: Furthermore, of what nature is it? It has the form of the wind of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Latent impression is the conceptualization of an object; that very thing, by virtue of its movement, is the wind.

It has that as its form. The sense is: where even the state of pure consciousness (*cidrūpatā*) does not exist because it is occupied by the bed of objects to be cognized, what talk can there be of "living-ness" (*jīvatā*)?
By the very absence of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatva*), it simultaneously negates the state of being a living soul (*jīva*) and so forth;

precisely because the nature of consciousness does not arise there, the state of being a living soul does not exist at all, nor is there the state of intellect (*buddhi*), nor the essence of mind (*cittattva*), nor the state of the senses (*indriyatva*), nor the latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

"Precisely because of the non-arising of the form of consciousness (*cidrūpa*)," that is, because of the non-manifestation of the very nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*), and not due to any other cause.

This non-arising of that form has been explained previously. The latent impression (*vāsanā*) is the conceptualization of an object of cognition (*cetyabhāvanā*) that persists in a subtle form. [Objection:

But how is it that, through the non-arising of the form of consciousness, there is no state of being a living soul (*jīva*) and so forth? [Response: True; for it is only through the swelling (*ucchūnatā*) of consciousness itself that there is the state of being a living soul and so on, and thus, in the absence of the arising of that form, [the state of being a soul does not exist].
It is indeed logical that [the self] lacks such states as being alive; thus, there is no contradiction.
He states the conclusion:
"Thus, this state remains—though it is full of the commencement of dissolution, yet it is undecaying; from our perspective, it is peaceful, empty, and more vast than space."

The state characterized by the supreme self—that abode which is full of dissolution yet remains undecaying, being devoid of the bodily attributes known as old age—is more tranquil than space when compared to space; likewise, it remains as empty, having the nature of nothingness. How so? The meaning is: "in this manner," that is, by means of the reasoning previously stated.
Having realized that the nature of the Supreme Self is difficult to comprehend, Śrī Rāma asks again:
"What is the form of that ultimate reality, which has the infinite consciousness as its shape? Explain this once more skillfully for the increase of my understanding."
You, however, for the sake of increasing awakening—that is, for the increase of knowledge regarding the Supreme Self—should explain this thoroughly and correctly; that is, you should tell me this:

what is the nature of that well-known Supreme Self, whose form is infinite consciousness, whose essence is consciousness unconditioned by space and so forth, and whose nature is ultimate reality? //MT_3,10.37//
The venerable Vasiṣṭha spoke this reply:
"Listen as I describe that Supreme Brahman which remains when the great dissolution has occurred—the cause of all causes."

At the occurrence of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), in the fourth state (*turya*) or beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), or at the time of the end of the great aeon (*mahākalpa*), that which remains—the cause of causes, the root cause, the Supreme Brahman which has expanded into the form of the universe, the reality characterized as the Supreme Self—remains as the witness of the great dissolution; it is that which is left over. That I shall describe here; therefore, listen to it.
He describes the very nature of the Supreme Self:
"When one's own self has been dissolved through the cessation of the mind's fluctuations, that form which is inexpressible is the true form of that Reality. (MU 3.1.39)

Of that reality—which is synonymous with the Supreme Brahman and characterized as the Supreme Self—that form comes into being. What is that form? It is that form which "remains"; this is the sense of the word *śeṣa*. It remains, meaning it persists as the witness to its own destruction. Of what [does it remain]? Of the mind (*manas*). Having done what? Having caused its own self to perish within pure consciousness alone (*śuddhacinmātra*).

"Having brought [the mind] to dissolution. Under what condition? "When there is the cessation of mental fluctuations," meaning when the fluctuations have perished. What is that form? It is that which becomes "inexpressible"; the meaning is that due to its extreme purity, it is no longer fit for expression.
This is the point: according to the principle of "cutting the mind with the mind itself," by means of right knowledge, [the mind] has emerged even slightly from the conceptualizations of saṃsāra.

The pure mind, by the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—acting as the cause for the cessation of both pure and impure mental modifications (*vṛtti*)—destroys its own pure-impure form. Thereupon, that mind, having dissolved into some indescribable state that is even more pure, becomes indescribable itself.
This very state is experienced by everyone in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), yet it is mixed with delusion (*mūḍhatā*). And when that mind...
At that time, such a state of being the Supreme Self arises for him; therefore, the yogi should remain attentive to that very state.
There is no visible world, nor a seer; because of the absence of the visible, it is as if dissolved. That which appears as "it shines" is the very nature of that reality.

Of that reality characterized as the Supreme Self—that reality—there occurs its very form. What is that? It is this: there would be a manifestation, a radiance. What is this? The world, which is the object of the act of seeing, does not exist, because it is established merely as a mental representation (*pratīti*). The seer, the agent of the act of seeing, is as if dissolved, like one who has vanished, due to the absence of the seen.
"It shines" (bhāti) means this: first, the absolute non-existence of the object of perception must be ascertained through reasoning by means of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).

Thereafter, due to the absolute non-existence of the object of perception, the perceiver also becomes, as it were, dissolved. Consequently, it flashes forth that neither the perceiver nor the object of perception exists. And that flashing forth, because it is devoid of any stain of perceiver or perceived and is of the nature of "nothingness," is inexpressible.
And that very thing is the nature of the supreme self; therefore, the yogi should cultivate that state with full attentiveness.

If that which is the very nature of the individual soul (jīva) is turned toward the object of cognition, it is the body; yet that which is pure consciousness—stainless and tranquil—is the cause of all causes.

That is well-known; that pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is the cause of causes, the fundamental cause, the very nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). What is that pure consciousness? It is the body—the essential form—of consciousness, which is the material cause of the individual soul (*jīva*); for consciousness has the nature of pure consciousness alone. Furthermore, how is it characterized? It is stainless (*vimala*), being undefiled by the impurity of the object of thought (*cetya*).

Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "peaceful" (*śāntam*), meaning free from the agitation of objects of cognition (*cetya*). What is that pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)? It is that which is the "nature of the individual soul" (*jīvasvabhāva*), the very form of the individual soul (*jīva*).

The masculine gender of the word *yaḥ* is used in relation to the word *svabhāva*. Now, one might ask: when does this become the nature of the individual soul? To this he says: "if" (*yadi*). That is, if it should be directed toward objects of cognition (*cetyonmukha*). [This refers to] the consciousness (*cit*) that is oriented toward objects of cognition.

Because it is thus living. This is the meaning: that which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), when directed toward an object of cognition (*cetyonmukha*), attains the state of being a living soul (*jīvatā*); yet, when that very same [consciousness] is purified by ascertaining through perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) the non-existence of the object of cognition, it becomes inexpressible (*anākhyeya*). And that alone is the form of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). In this regard, the yogi should remain vigilant. Furthermore, consciousness (*cit*) functions by means of self-reflection (*svaparāmarśa*).
It exists in two ways: as the agent of reflection and as the object of reflection. Of these, the first is named "pure consciousness" (cinmātra), and the second is "consciousness" (cit).
Furthermore, when there is contact with wind or other elements by means of the thumb or a finger, that form which appears to the mind of a living being is the supreme Self.
"Form" (*rūpa*) is the understood subject. That is the supreme, most excellent reality; it is the form of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). What is that?

It is the form which belongs to the mind (*cetas*), that is, the intellect (*manas*). Of what kind of mind? Of one that is living, capable of its own activity; not, however, of one that is incapable, such as in states of fainting and the like, for at that time it is in a state of delusion (*mūḍhatva*).

Thus it is; there is no state of being the supreme self. Under what condition? When there is no touch by the thumb or, alternatively, by a finger. This is an illustration; it applies to all parts of the body when there is no touch by wind and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), fire and the other elements are included. "Asparśana" means lack of touch. The meaning is this: in whichever part of the body of a person [there is no touch]...
When there is no contact with any object whatsoever, then that consciousness pervading the parts would be entirely without support (*nirālamba*).

At that time, for one who is intent upon the contemplation of those very parts alone, the mind—even though capable of grasping external objects—remains as the Supreme Self itself, whose nature is pure, supportless, and non-objectifying consciousness-only (*cinmātra*). It is at that very moment that the yogi, being attentive, should examine [the state] after abandoning all mental fluctuations (*manovṛtti*).
O sinless one, that form which remains after long contemplation upon the dreamless, infinite, and non-inert state of dense abiding—that alone is what is left.

"O sinless one," [meaning] free from defects such as passion and the like; "that object" remains at that time, during the moment of the dissolution of the Great Self. What is that? It is the form which comes to be. Of what? Of long-continued reflection (*cintā*). "Long" means throughout the entire night. That reflection which has been performed is a meditative absorption (*ādhyāna*) upon a desired object. Regarding that reflection, he states its qualifications, beginning with "dreamless" (*asvapnāyāḥ*). "Dreamless" means not having undergone transformation into the state of a dream.

A thought being performed while awake transforms into a dream. Since it has transformed into a dream, it may—due to its lack of control—be directed toward other objects; thus it is rightly said, "not of a dream. "Endless" means proceeding with an uninterrupted continuity.
The meaning is that no other thought enters into the midst of it. For some thoughts, indeed, [proceed] without interruption in a non-inert state.

When performed [while awake], it brings about a state of fainting; therefore, the qualification "of one who is not dull-witted" (*ajaḍāyāḥ*) is added for the sake of preventing that. "Of one whose state is dense" (*ghanasthiteḥ*): "dense" (*ghanā*) means compact or thick. It is that which does not allow entry even when being contemplated. "State" (*sthitiḥ*) means abiding. She who possesses such a state—of her, that is the meaning: "of one who is without support" (*nirālambāyāḥ*). This is the intended sense: when performed while awake, it is severed and free from the defect of dullness.

Thought, when defiled by the touch of the object of thought, is severed from its nature as consciousness and becomes non-consciousness itself; yet that which is non-consciousness is precisely the nature of the supreme self. Therefore, the yogi should remain vigilant therein.
That which is the heart of space, or that of stone and wind—that form of the supreme self, the inconceivable sky of consciousness (cidvyoman), is such.

Of that well-known, unperceivable, and untainted by contact, of the sky of consciousness whose nature is the space of manifestation, the form—that is, the true nature—is that which becomes it. What is that? It is that which is the heart of the void, known as the "emptiness" (śūnya).
Or else, it is that which is the heart of stone and of wind; therein, the heart of stone is [distinct] from the other.

It becomes a form that cannot be entered and is pierced by subtle parts. When the heart of the wind is sought, it comes to rest in emptiness itself. If it is argued that by this its insentience follows, no; for that is precluded by the mention of its name, "the sky of consciousness" (*cidvyoman*). When investigation is performed, the heart of the sky and so forth [is found] accordingly.
The form of emptiness is worthy of entry by others; and since such indeed is the form of the Supreme Self, the yogi should cultivate that [form] with focused attention.
The state of one who is without ego-conception, without mental activity, yet living and acting—that is the supreme, peaceful existence of that primordial reality.

"Supreme" means most excellent; "tranquil" means free from agitation. It is the state of existence (*sattāvasthiti*) of that primordial reality, the reality characterized as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). That [state] would be it. Which one? That state which is existence. Of what? Of a living person, one endowed with life, but not of one who is dead. Of what nature is he? Of one who is "without an object of thought" (*acetya*), because through right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) the absence of any object of thought has been ascertained.

Therefore, it is devoid of an object of thought (*cetya*) and thus devoid of mind (*amanaska*), meaning it is free from mental activity. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "possessing action" (*kriyāvat*), performing actions such as movement. The underlying point is this: just as a person who does not direct the mind toward an object of thought—and is therefore entirely devoid of mental synthesis—yet performs actions such as movement, exactly so is the Supreme Reality (*paramātmatattva*), which performs the activities of creation and so forth.
Thus it is said; in this regard, the yogi should practice with vigilance.
That which is the center of the light of consciousness and of dense light, and that which is the center of vision—that they know to be the form of Brahman.

O wise ones, they know—that is, they understand—the form of Brahman, the Supreme Self, who has expanded through the state of various objects. What is that? It is the middle state, which exists between the light of consciousness (*cit*) that has arisen and the light in the form of the manifestation of the object of cognition (*cetya*). Likewise, it is the middle state between dense, thick light, such as the solar orb and so forth, and [the aforementioned consciousness].

That which is the middle, the intermediate state, of that which has arisen; likewise, that which is the middle, the intermediate state, of seeing—the act of seeing—which has arisen from the seer: this is the state of being. There are three states of the light of consciousness, the external light, and the act of seeing: the initial state, the intermediate state, and the final state. Among these—

At the time of the arising of external light such as the sun, there is an initial state which is defiled by contact with the sun; and at the time of illuminating objects, there is a final state which is defiled by contact with those objects. However, the intermediate state is of the nature of pure light and is inexpressible (*anākhyā*). The nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is exactly like that; therefore, the yogi should remain attentive toward it.

The same should be applied to consciousness (*cit*) and light (*prakāśa*), as well as to seeing (*darśana*). One should understand that the distinction between consciousness and light, and between seeing and consciousness, is based solely on their being limited (*parimita*) or unlimited (*aparimita*).
The experience of sensation, of light, of the visible, and likewise of darkness—that which is without beginning or end is the form of the Supreme Self.

That is the form of the Supreme Self. What is it? It is that which is experience and continuity. Of what nature is it? It is without beginning or end, proceeding without interruption. For only in the midst of that which has intervals does there repeatedly occur the state of having a beginning and an end. Of what? Of the light, which is the nature of the manifestation of objects; that is, of experience, which is knowledge.

Furthermore, of what? Of *tamas*, which has the singular nature of being the object of apprehension; of some particular deity imagined as the visible that must necessarily be seen. This is the meaning: when the concentration on knowledge (*jñāna-dhāraṇā*) and the concentration on the deity whose form is identical with the object of knowledge (*jñeya-ekarūpa-devatā-dhāraṇā*) proceed uninterruptedly, they transform—by virtue of consisting solely of knowledge and consisting solely of the deity—into the form of the Supreme Self, which is of a single nature.
Thus it is said. In this regard, the yogin should practice with vigilance. Alternatively, it refers to *vedana*, that which produces knowledge;

to *prakāśa* (light); to the visible object (*dṛśya*), which is graspable by the eye through the appearance of illumination; and to *tamas* (darkness), meaning external darkness—so it should be construed.
For some have stated that there are meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) upon both external light and external darkness.
That supreme self-nature, though eternally unarisen in form, seems to arise as the world; though non-different, it appears as if different—that is the nature of the Absolute.

That is the supreme, pertaining to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); it is the form (*rūpa*). What is it? From which, because of which, the world seems to arise—that is, it appears to emerge—due to its being manifest. Of what nature is it? It is "of a nature that is eternally non-arisen" (*nityānuditarūpi*);

that is to say, it possesses a form that is eternally unarisen in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), since, by virtue of its nature as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), it has not appeared in the form of the world.

Even such [a thing], moreover, of what nature is it? It is "undivided" (*abhinna*), meaning "consisting of that" (*tanmaya*). Again, of what nature is it? "Abiding"—this is the ellipsis. "Abiding" means existing in the present. How so? "As if divided" (*vibhinnavat*), i.e., as though divided. The suffix *-vat* is employed to exclude actual division from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). This is the intended meaning: because this [thing] arises from a subtler entity...
The world emerges like a mass of ripples from water; that indeed is the form of the Supreme Self. In this regard, the yogi should remain attentive.
Even for one intent on worldly affairs, that state of sitting like a stone, which is the very sky-like nature of that which is not the sky—that is the form of the supreme Self.

That is the supreme self-nature, belonging to the Supreme Self; it becomes his form. What is that? It is that which, even for one intent on worldly activity—even while performing worldly activities—is a state of sitting or remaining like a stone. What is that sitting? It is the state of being space (*vyomatva*), which belongs to one who is indeed not-space because of being devoid of the qualities of space such as insentience, and who is thus distinct from the very nature of space.

This is the meaning: even while engaged in worldly activity, a person who is devoid of concern for success or failure therein remains in the very nature of the Supreme Self; therefore, a yogi should remain vigilant in this regard.
Furthermore, that wherein these three forms—the object of knowledge, the act of knowing, and the knower—arise and set, that is the supreme, most excellent reality.

That which is well-known, supreme, most excellent, unsurpassed, and characterized as the Supreme Self—that reality exists. What is it? That in which this being experienced—the object of the act of knowing (*vedya*), the act of knowing (*vedana*), and the knower (*vettṛ*)—exists; the state of these three is "the condition of the object, the act of knowing, and the knower," and that is its designation.

The threefold form—consisting of the nature of the object of cognition (*vedya*), the act of cognition (*vedana*), and the cognizer (*vettṛ*)—arises and sets. This is the meaning: the triad beginning with the object of cognition, as that which is being conceptualized, arises and dissolves within some reality called pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). That alone is the form of the Supreme Self; thus, the yogi should remain attentive toward that.

That in which this state of the object of knowledge, the act of knowing, and the knower is reflected within the great mirror of the non-intellective [unmanifest]—that is remembered as the supreme form.
By the wise, that supreme, most excellent form—the essential nature characterized as the Supreme Self—is remembered.

What is it? That in which, within a great mirror, the state of being the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and the knower—the triad beginning with the "object" (vedya)—is reflected, manifesting as a reflection. In what kind of mirror? In one that is devoid of intellect and the rest (*abuddhyādau*), meaning free from intellect and so forth. And it is logical that a mirror is devoid of intellect and the like.

The distinction is that while a mirror possesses insentience (*jāḍya*) and is devoid of intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, this [consciousness] is free from such limitations. This is the intended meaning: the triad beginning with the object of knowledge (*vedya*), manifesting for a mere moment and dissolving in the very next moment, does not impart any impurity to the substrate of its own manifestation; it shines solely as a reflection. For even a reflection lasts but a moment.
In one very moment it flashes forth, and in another very moment it dissolves; it does not impart its own impurity to its substratum, such as a mirror.
Therefore, some entity distinct from the triad must be accepted as the substratum for the reflection of the triad consisting of the knower, the known, and the act of knowing.
Otherwise, the reflection of the triad would be impossible. And that entity, when so accepted, is precisely the "Inexplicable" (anākhyam).
And that very thing is the reality of the supreme self; therein, the yogi should remain attentive.
That form of the Great Consciousness which transcends the six senses, including the mind—whether in the moving or the stationary—remains at the end of the creation.

That reality remains at the end of creation, during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). What is it? It is that which is the form of the Great Consciousness (*mahācit*), of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) alone.
Of what nature is it? It is beyond the six organs with the mind as the sixth.

Those of which the mind is the sixth are the "mind-sixth" ones; these, being the organs, are the "organs with the mind as the sixth" (*manaḥṣaṣṭhendriya*); that which transcends them is "beyond the six organs with the mind as the sixth" (*manaḥṣaṣṭhendriyātīta*).

The meaning is that this is beyond its scope. Where? In both the moving and the stationary. This is the point: the fact of being mind (*cittatva*) is indeed beyond dispute in the case of the moving; it is likewise so in the case of the stationary, such as grass and even mountains. It is not determined by the mere sprouting of grass and the like. No, for it is not logical that anything should sprout from that which is devoid of consciousness, since we do not observe the growth of hair and so forth from a dead body.
And thus, in whatever form consciousness exists everywhere, that is indeed the inexpressible; and that alone is the reality of the supreme self (paramātmatattva).
In this regard, the yogi should remain attentive.
For if the form of immobile beings were to consist of consciousness, being free from mind, intellect, and so forth, it would be equal to the Supreme.

The inclusion of the word *hi* is for the purpose of completing the meter. *Tat* means by that; *pareṇa* means by the Supreme Self; *samam* means equal; *bhavet* means it would be; *tat* means then; *kadā* means when? *Tat* refers to that which consists of consciousness (*bodhamaya*), whose nature is awakening; *cet* means if; *tat kim* means what is that? It is the form which belongs to immobile beings (*sthāvara*). This is the intended meaning: is the form of immobile beings necessarily devoid of agitation?

However, it is corrupted by dullness (*jāḍya*). Therefore, having abandoned dullness, one should make one's own essence of consciousness (*jñānatattva*) free from agitation by simply not touching the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). From that, the attainment of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) occurs; thus, the yogi should remain vigilant in this regard.
And so, these meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) have been clearly explained as being individually means for attaining the Supreme Self.
He concludes what was stated previously with a verse at the end of the chapter:

When Brahmā, Arka, Śakra, Hara, Viṣṇu, Sadāśiva, and the rest have attained peace, this one supreme Śiva alone remains here. He is the taught, the undecaying, the effortless, the desired; he is both mixed and unmixed, yet not dependent even upon the atom, nor dependent by anyone. (MU 3.10.54)

This exists as one's own self; it is Śiva, whose nature is supreme bliss; it is the ultimate, most excellent reality. It abides, remaining exactly as it is in its own essential form, and does not perish. Under what condition? When there is the cessation of Brahmā, Arka, Śakra, Hara, Viṣṇu, Sadāśiva, and the rest. By the word "and the rest" (ādi), all beings from the gods down to the grasses are included. [This refers to] the cessation of Brahmā and the others, who are the lords of their respective worlds.

When the time of the great dissolution (*mahākalpānta*) has arrived in the form of quiescence (*śānti*), Hara is the agent of withdrawal (*saṃhārakārī*). Sadāśiva is the one who produces bliss by bringing everything into his own nature.

Alternatively, the meaning is: when there is quiescence—known as the fourth state (*turya*)—of the mind and other faculties of those such as Brahmā, who are the agents of the arising of volitions (*saṅkalpa*) and so forth. Of what nature is he? He is "remnant" (*śiṣṭa*), meaning he is declared to be the residue, existing as the witness of all quiescence.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is undestroyed, being beyond the sphere of destruction. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is effortless, being easily understood.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is desired, being most dear to all. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is mixed, having the essential nature of various existents and non-existents.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is unmixed, having the form of pure consciousness alone. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is not dependent upon anything limited or minute.
It has become the very nature of reality (dharma) and is relied upon by the world as its foundational support. Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the tenth canto in the "Section on Origination" within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. Śrī Rāma asks:
"This form, this visible world called the 'shining universe,' where does it go, O Brahmin, upon the occurrence of the great dissolution?"

This world—this object known as the "world" (*jagat*), which is the visible realm appearing before one and the objective field of the act of seeing—exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*) alone; otherwise, its appearing in such a manner would be impossible. Of what nature is this? It is "of this form" (*idam-rūpa*); that is, its own nature (*svarūpa*) consists of existence and non-existence as they are presently being experienced. What follows from this? To this, he says: "At the time of the great dissolution," etc. O! [Listen.]
O Brahman, where does this very world go when the great dissolution occurs? The meaning is: to what place does it go?
The venerable Vasiṣṭha also asks something similar to this:
"From where does he come, or what is the son of a barren woman like? Where does he go? Tell me, where does the forest of the sky go, or from where does it come?"

From where does it come? This means at the time of its arising. Or of what kind? Of what nature? Where does it go? This means at the time of its destruction. The sense is that your question is similar to this.

Śrī Rāma gives the following reply: "The son of a barren woman and the forest of the sky do not exist, nor will they ever exist. What kind of visibility could he have, and what kind of non-existence could he have?"

By the negation of the present and the future, the negation of the past is also implied. To the question "What follows from that?", he replies with the word "of what kind" (*kīdṛśī*). "Visibility" (*dṛśyatā*) means fitness for being seen; by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it means existence.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha, taking Śrī Rāma’s statement as an illustration, gave this reply:
"Just as the son of a barren woman and the forest in the sky never exist at any time, so too the entire visible world, beginning with the universe, never exists."
By the word "beginning" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the beginning of the world," dissolution (*pralaya*) is included; "at any time" (*kadācana*) means "at some time."
He states the conclusion:
"That which neither arises nor perishes because it did not exist at the outset—what kind of arising could there be for it? What talk can there be of the word 'destruction'?"

The word *kila* indicates certainty. As for that entity which, in the beginning—that is, previously—has not arisen, nor does it perish, nor even undergo destruction; likewise, it does not exist and does not enter into the state of abiding—for such a thing, what kind of production could there be? What form could it have? And in the absence of production, what talk can there be of the word "destruction"? This is what is being stated.
The sense is that even this is not tenable.
Śrī Rāma asks again:
"The conceptualization of the son of a barren woman or a tree in the sky certainly exists; just as it is devoid of birth and destruction, why should this [world] not be the same?"

The word "tāvat" indicates the absence of any contradiction; "hi" signifies certainty. The sense is that if there were no conceptualization of things such as the son of a barren woman, even the very mention of "the son of a barren woman" would be improper. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "sā" (that). That is, the conceptualization of the son of a barren woman and so forth, even though it is unreal, is "nāśajanmāḍhyā"—meaning it is possessed of destruction and birth—just as it occurs.
Likewise, this visible world—though unreal—is rich in birth and destruction; why should it not be so? The meaning is: let it be so.
And thus, the question "Where indeed does it go? is entirely appropriate; such is the sense.

The response is stated by Śrī Vasiṣṭha in another manner: "It is indeed appropriate to imagine the son of a barren woman by superimposing upon him a son seen elsewhere in a woman; however, since there is no existence whatsoever for that which is perceived, such an imagination is not appropriate. He says: "Just as one might properly pluck the blossoms from a tree with its incomparable branches and leaves, so too is the existence of the world; it is indeed a baseless statement."
The word *hi* indicates certainty. The existence of the world (*jagatsattā*) is likewise—in that very same manner—without continuity (*niranvayā*), meaning it proceeds without aiming at any object;
that is to say, it is futile (*vyarthā*). How so? It is as stated in the passage beginning with "of the blooming [flower]" and ending with "the crushing," wherein it becomes without continuity.
He establishes the very absence of continuity through other examples:

"Just as the state of being a bracelet, though clearly visible in a golden bracelet, does not exist at all [as a separate entity], so too does the state of being the world not exist in the Supreme. (MU 3.11.8)

Just as the state of being a bracelet does not exist in a golden bracelet from the perspective of ultimate reality—even though it is clearly perceived—because it consists solely of gold; so too, the state of being the world does not exist in the supreme pure consciousness (cinmātra). Just as emptiness does not exist in space as something distinct, so the state of being the world does not exist at all in Brahman, even though it is perceived.

The word *ca* (and) is used for conjunction. "Possessing a negative concomitance" (*vyatirekavat*) means being endowed with a negative concomitance; the meaning is that no negative concomitance is perceived between space and emptiness.

He states the application to the subject (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "the nature of the world" (*jagattvam*). "The nature of the world" (*jagattvam*) means the state of being the world. "In that manner" (*tathā*) means by that method.
[It] does not exist at all in Brahman, which is all-pervasive and of the nature of consciousness; the meaning is that this is because it cannot withstand critical analysis.
Of what nature is it? It means that even though it possesses perception—that is, even though it is perceived by way of appearing.
Just as blackness does not exist apart from collyrium, nor whiteness apart from snow, so too the world is not perceived as separate [from it] in the supreme state.

Just as blackness—the state of being black—cannot exist apart from soot, and just as whiteness—the state of being white—cannot exist apart from snow; so too, the world is determined by the Buddha to be, in the ultimate sense, within the supreme state, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Thus, it does not exist separately from that supreme state. Here, the two locative endings (*pare pade*) should be understood as standing in the place of the ablative.
Just as coolness is not distinct from the moon, so too creation does not exist as something separate from Brahman.

The word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction. Just as coolness (*śaityam*) is not distinct from—that is, it does not exceed—coldness (*śītatā*), [which comes] from the cold *hima* or from the moon (*śaśin*); likewise, creation (*sargaḥ*) does not possess distinction—that is, it does not possess difference—from Brahman.
Having stated the oneness [of the Self] by way of illustrating the qualities and the possessor of qualities, he now declares the oneness of the world as being established through delusion:

"Just as there is no water in a mirage-river, and just as there is no moonhood in the second moon, so too the world does not exist; though it is seen, it does not exist within the stainless Self. (MU 3.11.12)

The Dārṣṭāntika explains with the word "evam" (thus): in the stainless Self, which is the pure nature of consciousness, the Supreme Self; "evam" means in that manner. The meaning is that the world, though seen and though appearing, does not exist. If it is objected: "But previously, bracelets and the like were employed as examples, whereas here the water in a mirage and so forth are used; thus a discrepancy has arisen," we reply: No. By the previous examples, the oneness of Brahman [was established].

It has been stated that the world is unreal; however, in terms of the ultimate result, the intent of all these examples is precisely the oneness of Brahman, so there is nothing contradictory whatsoever.
Furthermore, he confirms this very point by means of another illustration:
"The light of the eye of consciousness shines within the sky of consciousness, like a string of pearls in the stainless firmament called the world."

This light of the eye of consciousness stands as the self within direct perception. "Consciousness" (*saṃvit*) is indeed *cit* (pure awareness). The "eye" (*vilocana*) is the organ of sight, by virtue of its similarity in being a manifestor; its "light" (*āloka*) is its radiance. It shines—that is, it vibrates—as the nature of objects. Where? In that which is called the world, in the sky of consciousness, the space of *cit*. What is it like? It is like a pearl necklace of vision.

The meaning is: "just as," that [light] shines in the stainless sky, which is the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*). This is the intended sense: just as rays of light emerging from the eyes are seen shining in the sky in the form of strings of pearls, so too the rays called "cognitive luminosity" (*cidāloka*), arising from consciousness (*cit*), shine within the sky of consciousness known as the world in the form of various objects.
"They are seen. // MT_3,11.13 //
In the space of consciousness, that which shines by itself through its own consciousness is that very same self-form which is perceived as the world.

The space of consciousness (cidākāśa) shines and vibrates within the space of consciousness—upon its own wall called the space of consciousness—by virtue of being consciousness, that is, through its nature as consciousness;

this means it becomes the object of the self-reflective awareness "I. For in the absence of such reflective awareness, its very status as consciousness would not exist. By means of each respective space of consciousness, its own nature—which is called "shining"—is understood as the world.
It is known [to be so], because the world has the nature of mere appearance.
He returns to the subject at hand:
For that which does not exist from the very beginning because of the impossibility of a cause, that does not exist even when present; what kind of destruction could there be in that case?
Indeed, as for the certainty: whatever thing is called "the world," since its cause is impossible, it does not exist by itself even at the outset;

therefore, it does not exist even in the present. Regarding that very thing, the notion of "destruction" is raised by way of the analogy of the son of a barren woman—what kind of destruction could it be? What would its form be? It would not exist, because it is untenable due to the absence of an object; such is the meaning.
[Objection: But surely, since the Supreme Self, characterized as the cause, exists, how can the impossibility of a cause arise? To this he says:
"Where could insentient matter, such as earth and so forth—which is born of insentient elements—be capable of being a cause, just as sunlight cannot be the cause of shade? (MU 3.11.16)

The "inertness of the elements" (*bhūtajāḍya*) is the dullness observed in the elements. That which possesses such impossible inertness of the elements is "that which has impossible inertness of the elements" (*asambhavadbhūtajāḍya*);
this refers, by implication, to the reality called Consciousness (*cit*). Where would it be capable of being the cause of earth and other insentient things?
The meaning is that it is not so capable. Here he states an illustration: "of a shadow," because a shadow cannot destroy sunlight.
It is clear that [the reflection] cannot serve as an example, because it is impossible for it to be the cause of the shadow.

[Objection: "But surely the world could exist even in the absence of a cause. To this he says: "Due to the absence of a cause, this effect has not arisen as anything at all; that which exists is the cause itself, and it is simply situated in this manner. (MU 3.11.17)

That [is so] because of the reason previously stated; due to the absence of a cause, that is, from the non-existence of a cause, this being experienced—the effect known as the world—is not arisen, meaning it has not been produced. How so? Not even in the slightest degree—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, if one asks, "What then is this that is seen? he says here: "that which," namely that very entity, exists in this manner in the form of the world.

It exists as the present. What is that? It is the very entity—that entity which was suspected to be the cause of this world by virtue of being its cause; it is precisely that, and nothing else—this is the meaning.
That which appears as unarisen is indeed the manifestation of consciousness; that which is seen as the world in a dream is likewise the radiance of consciousness.

Whatever object appears even while being unborn—that is, for consciousness (*saṃvid*), which is knowledge (*jñāna*), its very appearance is its manifestation as suchness; that is, it exists solely as a flash of radiance. Regarding this, he states a corresponding illustration with the word "that" (*yat*). By the word "that" (*tat*), there is a reference to the world.
Since it is established by universal experience that a dream consists of the nature of the radiance of consciousness, it is taken as the illustrative example.
Just as the delusion of the dream-world is merely the internal manifestation of consciousness, so too at the beginning of creation, the manifestation of the world is extended within Brahman.

"Within the mind" means in the internal consciousness. "The delusion of the dream-world" refers to the delusion consisting of the form of a dream-world; that is to say, the dream-world itself. "At the beginning of creation" means at the commencement of creation, superimposed by the intellect. By the word "thus" (tathā), the manifestation of consciousness is implied. "Extended" means broad and vast.
Whatever is seen here exists indeed within the Self; this world never sets nor does it ever rise.

Whatever object is being experienced and is seen here, that is indeed real; it is a real entity alone. It remains established within its own self, which is of the nature of consciousness and its own essential form. The result of this is stated as "it does not set. The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is to be supplied [from the context]. The sense is: because it exists eternally in the form known as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
Just as liquidity is water, as movement is wind, and as radiance is light, so too the three worlds are Brahman alone.

The point is that no one is able to separate fluidity and so forth from water and the like and demonstrate them [independently]. *Prakāśa* is the light of the sun and so forth; *ābhāsa* is the manifestation of an object.
Just as the internal knower alone exists within the consciousness of a dream as if it were a city, so too one's own self alone shines forth within the Supreme Self as if it were the world.
