Just as in the consciousness of a dream—that is, in dream-cognition, meaning during the state of dreaming—the internal organ alone shines forth and plays like a city; so too, one's own self alone shines forth within the Supreme Self—within that which is designated as the "Supreme Self" and serves as its own ground—as if it were the world. The sense is that there is no other thing called "the world" apart from this.
In this regard, Śrī Rāma asks:
"If it is so, then O Brahmin, tell me how this poison of the visible world has arisen with such firm conviction, like the experience of an unreal dream?"

O Brahmin, you speak thus: "If it is so"—that is, if the manner previously described is indeed the case—then how, by what cause, has this which is being experienced come to be? This visible object (*dṛśya*) is poison; because it produces delusion, the visible itself is poison, a poisonous substance. It is characterized by a very solid conviction (*sughana-pratyaya*); that is, it is that in which there is a very solid conviction or reassurance. How, for what reason, has such a thing arisen or been produced?
How so? Like the experience of a non-existent dream. That which is the experience of a dream—an experience having the form of a dream; that is to say, a dream—just like that.
Not considering liberation possible without the absolute non-existence of the visible, he asks about that very point in detail:

"If indeed there is a seer when there is something visible, and visibility exists when there is a seer, then for a single being there is bondage for both; liberation occurs upon the destruction of one of the two."

The word "kila" indicates certainty. The existence of the seer occurs when there is the existence of the seen; and the existence of the seen occurs when there is the existence of the seer—this is the sense, namely, that it is by you yourself [who have stated this]. He states the conclusion: "In the case of the existence of one of two. Between the two, when one exists, there is bondage; between the two, when one perishes, there is liberation. Therefore, for the sake of liberation, there must indeed be the destruction of one.
The sense is that it is the probandum (*sādhya*).
"Is it not the case that even there you are asking again and again about the absolute non-existence of the visible? To this he replies:

"As long as the absolute impossibility of the visible has not been realized by the awakened one, so long the state of being a non-seer—which bestows liberation—is not possible for the seer. (MU 3.11.25)
The Buddha is perfectly known as inexhaustible and uninterrupted. "Non-seeing" (*adraṣṭṛtva*) is the state of being a non-seer; that is to say, pure consciousness alone (*śuddhacinmātratā*).

The sense is that because the absolute non-existence of the visible (*dṛśyātyantābhāva*) is easily accomplished, whereas the negation of the state of being a seer (*draṣṭṛtānirāsa*) is difficult to accomplish without the absolute non-existence of the visible, there is a repeated inquiry into the absolute non-existence of the visible.

"Surely, what purpose do you have in the absolute non-existence of the visible? For the goal is accomplished even by the destruction of the visible. To this, he replies: "If the visible were possible at first and later underwent destruction, then bondage—in the form of the uselessness of remembering that visible—would not cease."

That [bondage] at that time consists of the recollection of the perceived object as an unreal thing; "recollection of the perceived" itself is the "unreal thing. That which has this as its form—that is such a bondage. It does not perish; it does not go to destruction. For the recollection of an object previously known as real and subsequently lost is indeed unavoidable, just as in the case of one's mother and so forth—this is the sense. When is that? If, at the beginning...

Previously, the visible object exists as a reality and possesses logical justification; subsequently, it undergoes decay and destruction. Therefore, the meaning is that non-existence must be accepted here as pertaining to all three times.
[Objection: But how can there be a memory of an object that has perished? To this, he says:
"Wherever it may be situated, just as in one's own mirror, a reflection indeed adheres to the movement of consciousness; for this [world] consists of the memory of creation. (MU 3.11.27)

"Hi" indicates certainty. This [reflection], which was just mentioned, consists of the memory of creation—that is, its nature is the recollection of creation. It "adheres," meaning it necessarily adheres. To what? To a certain movement of consciousness (*cit*), that is, a particular mode of consciousness. Like what? Like a mirror.
Just as a reflection adheres to a mirror situated anywhere when there is the proximity of an object, so too [does this reflection adhere] wherever [consciousness is].

The meaning is that, because the movement of consciousness (cidgati) remains in some place, a reflection adheres to it due to its proximity to the perceived object (dṛśya) that exists there by virtue of its subtlety.
If that is so, when does liberation become possible? To this he says:
"If, from the very beginning, the visible object has not arisen and does not exist by itself, then liberation becomes possible because of the absence of the delusion of seer and seen. (MU 3.11.28)

The "visible" (*dṛśya*) is the collection of entities that are the objects of the act of seeing (*dṛśikriyā*). If, from the very beginning—that is, at the outset—it is itself unarisen, being unborn by its own nature (*svabhāvena*), and thus does not exist at all; then, at that time, liberation (*muktatā*) is possible, meaning it becomes logically consistent. Why? Because of the absence of the delusion (*bhrama*) regarding the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) and the seen (*dṛśya*). This is the point: when there is the absolute non-existence of the visible, this [liberation] belongs to the person (*puruṣa*).

The delusion that "there is something visible" subsides; when that has subsided, the delusion that "I am the seer" also necessarily subsides. Consequently, only that which is the nature of pure consciousness alone remains, and that indeed is liberation.
He concludes the question:
"Therefore, O best among the knowers of the Self, tell me how liberation—which is impossible for me due to my being filled with enthusiasm—is absolutely impossible regarding the visible world."

O best among those who know the Self! Therefore—for that reason—tell me of the absolute impossibility of the visible world existing [for me], since liberation is impossible without the knowledge of the absolute non-existence of the visible. Why? Because it must be done with great effort; that is to say, by applying intense exertion.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha spoke this reply:
"Just as that which is non-existent appears as the entire world, listen, O Rāma, as I relate it to you through a long discourse."

Listen! I shall tell you that manner in such a way—by means of a long and detailed discourse, by a continuous flow of words—and how: how the world, which consists of all things and has the nature of every visible object, appears as if it were non-existent, shimmering with unreality like bubbles.
"Now, why do you speak with such a long discourse? To this he replies:
"As long as that [reality] has not been described through sentences of decisive discourse, so long will it not find rest in your heart, just as silt does not settle in a lake."
By means of sentences that constitute discourse on determination (*vyavasāya*). Discourse on determination is discourse that produces a specific, certain conviction;

by means of the sentences that express that, namely, "sentences of discourse on determination. That non-existence of the perceptible will not find rest in your heart—that is, it will not take its stand—as long as it has not been fully described. How so? Just as dust [does not settle].
The meaning is: "Just as dust and grit do not settle in a lake, so too [is it with him]."
[Objection: "But what will be achieved for me by the knowledge of the absolute non-existence of the visible world? To this he replies:

"Having realized the absolute non-existence of this delusion of the creation of the world, you, with your self established in one-pointed meditation, shall carry out your worldly affairs. (MU 3.11.32)

You will carry out the worldly affairs that have come down through tradition—the affairs consisting of kingship—just as one carries out the business of counterfeit coins; you will not turn away from them like one in a state of dispassion (*vairāgya*), nor will you be attached to them like one in a state of delusion (*mūḍhatva*). In what state will you be? With a self established in single-pointed meditation (*ekadhyāna*) upon that one reality called pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
One whose culmination is in meditation and reflection—such a one, whose self is the mind in the form of a sentient being—he will be thus:

fixed solely in the internal meditation on pure consciousness, even while remaining engaged in external worldly affairs; this is the meaning. Having done what? Having [abandoned] this persisting delusion of world-creation that is currently being experienced—[the delusion] which consists of the creation of the world, the manifestation of the universe.

The meaning is: having understood—that is, having known—the absolute non-existence, which is the non-existence throughout the three periods of time, of that state of delusion, which is the firmness of delusion.
Now, in response to the inquiry "What follows from that?", he states another result:

"Views characterized by grasping and abandoning existence and non-existence, as well as being gross or subtle, moving or stationary, shall pierce you, just as arrows do not pierce a great mountain. (MU 3.11.33)

When there is the knowledge of the absolute non-existence of the visible, the perceptions—whether gross or subtle, moving or stationary, consisting of grasping at existence and non-existence or rejecting them—will not pierce You; they do not inflict the "wounding" that consists in the production of joy or anger. Existence (*bhāva*) is manifestation; non-existence (*abhāva*) is disappearance.

Grasping (*graha*) is seizing; rejection (*utsarga*) is abandonment. This is because even existence and the other states are, by their very nature as objects of perception, absolutely non-existent [in You].
Because it is perfected, no blow caused by them shall befall you; for no one is ever struck by the son of a barren woman—this is the sense.
What are they like? Like arrows. Just as arrows do not pierce a great mountain, so it is here—the meaning is that.
He makes a formal declaration regarding the absolute non-existence of the visible world:
"This Self alone exists; there is no second conceptualization. O Rāghava, I shall explain to you how the world has arisen herein."

He is well-known; he exists as something directly manifest to all. He is one alone. [The author] clarifies the meaning of the word "alone" with the word "not. There is no second conceptualization—that is, no conceptualization consisting of the visible world. Thus, the sense is that the absolute non-existence of the visible is indeed clear. [An objection: "In that case, how does the appearing world exist? To this, he says: "the world. In this regard, within this non-dual reality—
I shall explain to you how the world arises within Brahman; the intention is that by this very means, the absolute non-existence of the perceptible will become clear.
He summarizes this with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"Therefore, from that Supreme Self, who is the material cause characterized by the Great Soul (Mahātman), all these manifested forms have emerged; for he, O dear one, being the abode of the treasury of light that perceives forms and conceives them through the mind, himself arises and dissolves within the All.
From that Supreme Self, which is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), these perceived manifestations have unfolded as visible forms.
The playful manifestations—meaning, like pots emerging from clay—issue forth. Why is that? Indeed (*hi*), for certain;

O dear one (*aṅga*), he who, having become the entire manifold of all visible phenomena (*dṛśyaprapañca*), arises by himself and through himself alone, and sets, and dissolves; who is that Great Self (*mahātman*)? He is the perception of forms, the mental ideation, and the act of attention (*manaskāra*).
"Manifestation" (prakāśa) is the flashing forth of a form perceived by the sense organ within the pure consciousness that serves as the witness, by means of the mind's reflection.
Their "sheath-form" (kośarūpa) is their abode or locus; the meaning is that these [sheaths] abide in that very place and emerge from it alone. Thus, all is auspicious.
Thus ends the eleventh canto in the "Chapter on Origination" within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.

Oṃ! Having made the promise "I shall speak," he fulfills it from this supreme, most peaceful, and most purifying state: listen with the highest intellect to how this entire universe has arisen from it. MU 3.12.1.

Immediately after this—that is, from that which has just been described as its true nature—from the supreme, the most excellent; from the peaceful, devoid of the agitation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);

from the supremely purifying, which is the unsurpassed purifier even among all purifiers; from the state, the locus characterized as the Supreme Self—in whatever manner this perceived universe has arisen, has come into manifestation.
Listen to that manner with the highest—that is, the most excellent—intellect. By this, it is stated that only one possessing the highest intellect is qualified [for this].
He explains that very point:
deep sleep appears like a dream, and Brahman alone appears like a creation; all is one and that is peaceful—listen now to the sequence regarding that.

Deep sleep (*suṣuptam*) is the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). It appears, that is, it manifests, like a dream (*svapnavat*); for a dream arises only for one who has awakened from dense slumber. Brahman alone—Brahman itself, which is the reality called pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), expanded in the form of creation (*sargabhāvena bṛṃhitam*)—appears as if it were a creation (*sargavat*). [Objection: In that case, does not Brahman, being the material cause (*upādānabhūta*) of the world, become insentient (*jaḍa*) just like the world?

It may be argued: "Because a cause endowed with a deficiency in its effect is not observed. To this, he says: "All" (*sarvam*). That is Brahman. It becomes all; it becomes one; and it becomes tranquil. The sense is that it is indeed a marvel in every respect. [The opponent asks: "But how does it arise? To this, he says: "Therein" (*tatra*). The word *tāvat* signifies totality.
He explains the very sequence:
"The manifestation, which consists of mere existence, that belongs by its very nature to that gem of consciousness whose essence is infinite light, occurs incessantly."
Therefore, within the self, something itself appears as if it were becoming an object of cognition; though its nature remains ungrasped, it indicates effort, impatience, and the desire for inquiry.

That gold, by some slight degree, as it were, undergoes the state of being an object of cognition (*cetyatā*); yet in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), it does not do so—this is why the word "as it were" (*iva*) is employed.

How so? By itself, through its own nature, and not by the instigation of another, because no other exists therein. In what? In the self, which is the very essence of consciousness known as radiance (*sphuraṇa*). For at that time, nothing else exists apart from that. What is that?

Whatever flickering [manifestation] there is—meaning, the reflective awareness of "I"—it exists perpetually and continuously by its very nature. Of what? Of that which is well-known as appearing as "I" in all things, whose essential form is infinite light;
he whose nature and essential constitution consist of that very thing—that is, whose self is that infinite, undivided light.

Of that [Self] whose nature is infinite light—meaning, of the pervasive jewel of consciousness (*cinmaṇi*). "Pervasive" (*ātata*) means it is omnipresent everywhere; such is the jewel of consciousness. Of what nature is its manifestation (*kacana*)? It is "of the nature of pure existence" (*sattāmātrātman*), having existence as its sole essence. For it is only within manifestation, which is the form of radiance, that the conventional usage of "existence" occurs. This is the intended meaning: [it is] pure...

And being an object [of knowledge] consists in being an object of consciousness (*cit*). And that [objectivity] is a relation with consciousness. Furthermore, a relation between consciousness and that which is of the nature of the non-conscious (*acid-rūpa*) is not tenable because of their opposition;

for a relation between light and darkness is never observed anywhere. Moreover, the tranquility of consciousness is established by the aforementioned reasoning precisely through the impossibility of there being an object of cognition (*cetya*).

Thus, Brahman alone shines forth clearly as the Self by means of the Self within the Self; because of its consciousness, it manifests within itself like water in the form of whirlpools due to its fluidity.

Thus, in the form of the world, that which is transparent and free from the stain of the object of thought (*cetya*) shines and manifests as Brahman alone—by itself, through itself, within itself as its own foundational ground, and as the Self that has become the Self of all. Why? Because of its nature as consciousness (*cittva*), because of its being the state of consciousness (*cidbhāva*).
The sense is this: if it were to manifest as the world in the form of objects of thought, its very nature as consciousness would cease to exist. Regarding this, he provides an illustration:
"Because of fluidity": just as water, due to its fluidity, vibrates in the form of whirlpools within its own nature called "water," so too [does this]; such is the meaning.
This world appears as if it were real, yet it is experienced here as something unreal; in the end, it perishes as something unreal, just like one's own death in a dream.

This world appears and manifests as something non-existent; yet it is experienced by us here, within the nature of the Supreme Self, as if it were existent. At the end, at the time of dissolution, it perishes as something truly non-existent. Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "like a dream."

Having explained at length the absolute non-existence of the world, he now declares its nature as consisting of Brahman, which is the established conclusion: "Moreover, because it has the nature of pure consciousness (*vāja*), this [world] is always free from affliction, undivided, without beginning or end, and has the interior of the sky of mere cognition as its belly. (MU 3.13.53)
Alternatively, this world is always free from affliction (*anāmaya*), because it is by nature unborn and because its nature is pure consciousness devoid of birth;

it is free from the diseases such as being a substratum or a superstratum mentioned previously. However, it is not characterized by non-existence. And that [notion of] non-existence is stated only with respect to those whose intellects are occupied by it and who do not perceive its true form. Of what nature is this? It is undivided (*akhaṇḍita*).
Its nature is complete; it is without beginning or end, devoid of beginning and end. It is the interior of the sky of mere consciousness (*jñātamātra*).

It is indeed mere consciousness itself, not something destroyed by blows from a mallet or other such instruments. When the world is scrutinized through perfect knowledge, it becomes nothing but the interior of the sky.
He summarizes what was previously stated with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"In the supreme ether alone, the first Lord of Creatures shines eternally by himself, identical with emptiness; for he possesses a subtle, transportable body and not a form composed of the elements such as earth; therefore, that which has not been born does not exist as a reality. (MU 3.1.54)

The first is the primordial one; the Lord of Creatures is Brahmā. In the supreme, which transcends all, in the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), he shines and vibrates eternally, always, by himself and through his own nature. Thus, the entire process previously described is intended for those whose minds are not yet satisfied without the commencement of creation. Of what nature is he? He is identical with emptiness, by way of the state of voidness.

By virtue of its purity, it is equal to that [the Supreme], but it is not of the same nature as it, for that would entail the consequence of insentience (*jaḍatva*). Indeed (*hi*)—this being certain—he, the Lord of Creatures (*prajeśa*), possesses a subtle body (*ātivāhikavapuḥ*), consisting of a subtle form; he does not, however, possess a form composed of the gross elements (*bhūta*). The word "but" (*tu*) serves to specify: he does not have the form of gross elements such as earth and the rest. Therefore, by that reason known as "not having the form of those elements," earth and the others do not exist [as ultimate reality]. Now, one might object: since the Lord of Creatures does not have the form of earth and the other elements...

How is it that earth and the other elements do not exist as real? To this he says, "When... (yadā), which has the sense of "since" (yataḥ). Since [they] have arisen—that is, been produced—they do not exist. For earth and the rest could only be said to have arisen through the Lord of Creatures (Prajeśa) assuming their form, provided he were of the nature of pure mind; however, according to the previously stated principle, it is impossible for the Lord of Creatures to assume such a form. Therefore, [earth and the rest...]
The sense is that even "the state of being born" is not possible. Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the thirteenth canto in the "Chapter on Origination" of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.

Oṃ! Having thus repeatedly stated that the world is absolutely non-existent and consists solely of the one Supreme Self, and having understood that only this much remains to be established, he speaks of that very same point once more: "In this way, the world—the visible objects such as the ego and so forth—has arisen as nothing at all; because it is unarisen, it does not exist, and that which does exist is the Supreme alone. (MU 3.14.1)

"Beginning with 'I-ness' (*ahantā*) and so forth—the world of the visible (*dṛśya-jagat*)—in this manner, according to the previous mode, has not arisen even in the slightest degree (*kiñcana*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says here: "Because it is unarisen. Since the world is unarisen, [it does not exist]. The word *ca* is for the purpose of completing the meter.
[It] simply does not exist. [Objection: But how do you establish the non-existence of the world by its being unarisen, given that it appears to exist?
Thus [it is said]. Here he says: "And that which... That is precisely the supreme, the transcendent, pure consciousness alone; it does not become the world.
What is that? The meaning is: that which exists, which cannot be denied because of its manifest nature.
"But if that is so, how can it be said that the living state was previously established? To this he replies:
"This very Supreme Space itself experiences the living state; it is like water within the womb of the motionless ocean that possesses movement. (MU 3.14.2)

That which was previously mentioned is the supreme space (*paramākāśa*), which is indeed the space of pure consciousness (*cinmātrākāśa*). By itself, through its own nature, it perceives—that is, experiences—the state of being a living being (*jīvatām jīvabhāvam*). How so? Like water. Just as water situated within the belly of the motionless ocean—in the midst of the waveless sea—possesses motion; for here, by the word "motion" (*spanda*), that which is endowed with motion is indicated, namely, the state of being possessed of motion.

It intends; and here, "intention" (cetanā) is merely the capacity for that [action]. For in that case, the water is not endowed with movement in any part whatsoever. Likewise, in Brahman as well, there is merely the capacity for being a living soul (jīvatva); however, there is no such thing as "being a living soul" therein at all. Just as in the case of water, where there is a cognition of capacity because it will later be joined with movement, so too in the case of Brahman, [there is a cognition of capacity] by way of its being in the form of a living soul.
The distinction lies in the fact that it is by means of manifestation.
He explains this very point through various modes of expression:

"Let it be seen that consciousness, without ever abandoning its nature as space, appears as if it perceives; for the internal activity of consciousness is like that in dreams, mental constructs, mountains [in the mind], and so forth. (MU 3.14.3)

Let this supreme space be seen as having the nature of the visible; it knows, as it were, it experiences, as it were. In what state? Without ever abandoning its form—that form called the space of pure consciousness (cinmātra-ākāśa). For the sense is that if it were to abandon that, it would have no cognition at all. It is like a modification of consciousness (cid-vṛtti) within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is the essence of the "I-reflection" (ahaṃ-parāmarśa).

The meaning is as follows: just as in a dream or a mental construction (*saṅkalpa*), when one's own object—such as a mountain that is one's own nature—is present, one perceives its visibility, thinking, "This is a mountain. It is just like that.
That great body of the Virāj-ātman, which is devoid of earth and the other elements, is indeed the subtle body (ātivāhika), consisting of pure consciousness and the ether of space.

Devoid of earth and the other elements, and untainted by contact with gross earth and the rest; belonging to the Virāṭ Ātman—that is, the Supreme Self who exists in the form of the Virāṭ; that body which exists is indeed *ātivāhika*, that is, subtle.
He states a qualification as the reason for this: "consisting of pure consciousness" (*cinmātra*). For it has the nature of the stainless ether known as pure consciousness.
It has not been laboriously argued that the subtle, transportable nature of a body consisting of pure consciousness is observed in dreams.
It resembles a mountain in an imperishable dream, like a city in a stable dream; it has the appearance of an army depicted in a painting situated within the mind of a painter.
It is like a multitude of statues on great pillars that have not been fixed in the ground; it is the unattached self within the space of Brahman, like a statue upon a firm pillar.
In the beginning, the first Lord of Creatures was renowned as Svayambhū; because he lacked prior actions of his own, he was without a cause.

The first is the causal source; he is renowned as the Self-Existent (Svayambhū), famous by that name. He is Prajāpati. At the beginning of the previous creation, he exists without a cause, being devoid of a cause. Why? Because of the absence of his own prior effects—the actions performed in a previous kalpa. And the fact that actions are the cause of birth is established in all the scriptures.

This is indeed well-known. Furthermore, the non-existence of his effects should be understood as arising immediately from pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). What is its nature? It is "indestructible" (*akṣaya*), and so forth. "Indestructible" means free from the defect of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), like a mountain in an ordinary dream;

that which has an appearance like such a dream-mountain is "one whose appearance is like an indestructible dream-mountain. It is comparable to a stable dream-city, being distinct from other dream-cities.

"Stable" means having a stable form. That which has a dream-city as its simile is [the city]; by these two qualifiers, its stability even in its state of being a *ativāhika* (transmigratory) body is expressed. "Citta situated in a painted creation" (*citrakṛtsthitacitta*) refers to the mind situated in a painting;
that which has a form similar to the painted army appearing before one—that is, the army depicted in the drawing—is its own nature (*svarūpa*).

He has the appearance of an army of figures situated within the mind of a painter; he is neither dug in nor carved out. He is like a multitude of large pillar-figures that have not been fixed in the ground nor carved from it. In the firm pillar of the space of Brahman, his self is not dug in and his true nature is not carved out. A *sālabhañjikā* is a large figurine. "Not dug in" means...
This is the explanation of the qualification itself; by these two qualifications, its state of being solely composed of Brahman is stated.
At the conclusion of the great dissolution, it is said that even the primordial Grandfathers are liberated; therefore, what prior karma could there be for them?

All indeed those primordial Grandfathers (pitāmaha) [are liberated] at the conclusion of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). Here, by the word "conclusion" (*paryanta*), intensity is intended. They are released; that is, they dissolve into their own essential nature (*svarūpa*) called pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). He states the result [of this]: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). For this reason, regarding all those primordial Grandfathers, what becomes of their prior karma? The meaning is: nothing at all.
And thus, the meaning is that all of them are indeed without cause.
The very nature of the wall must be released; it exists as both visible and invisible. There is neither the visible, nor the seer, nor the creator, and indeed, everything is thus.
This very desire is the essence of all things; from it arises the series of living beings, just as a row of lamps arises from a single lamp.

This is that very Prajāpati mentioned previously; he is the reflection, the collective totality (*samaṣṭi-rūpa*), of all objects. This is because he is the essential nature of all reflections. Of what nature is he? He is "capable of being released" (*moktavya eva*), meaning he is capable of being liberated or of passing through the middle. He is "of the nature of a wall" (*kuḍyātmā*); for a wall, by virtue of its obstructive nature, [prevents one from] passing through the middle.

It cannot be [otherwise]. However, this is indeed a wall that was not there before; for it is to be released because it possesses the magnitude of the entry and exit of all perceived movements. Its nature as a wall, moreover, is due to its being the support of all things. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It exists as visible, established in the form of the visible; and it exists as invisible, established in the form of the seer, because it has the nature of Prajāpati, whose form is the mind purified by the radiance of pure consciousness alone (*cinmātra*).
Regarding the seer and the seen: what further [is said]? It is neither the seen nor the seer, neither the creator nor the agent of the act of creation, because its nature transcends everything.
What further? And yet, it is indeed everything. [Objection: But how can this reflection exist? To this he says: "From this.
Because from this Prajāpati, the series of living beings (*jīvālī*) arises—that is, it manifests. [Objection: But is it not like the series of pots arising from clay, or a collection of ropes?

Or, a snake-line arises in that same manner; yet, no state of being a reflected image (*praticchanda*) and a reflecting object (*praticchanda*) is seen between those two. To this, he says "lamp-line" (*dīpālī*):
the meaning is that here there exists a distinct mode of being a reflected image and a reflecting object, characterized by transformation (*vivarta*) and evolution (*pariṇāma*).

Indeed, by virtue of its own volition, it moves from one volition to another, devoid of earth and the other elements, yet appearing as if possessing them—just like one who passes from one dream to another without any walls or boundaries.

"Kila" indicates certainty. "Devoid of earth and the rest" means being free from gross earth and so forth, because its nature is that of a mere appearance (*ābhāsa*). "Appearing as if possessing earth and the rest" means appearing as if accompanied by them due to the manner of its manifestation. "Without walls" means being devoid of mountains and the like that appear in the form of walls. "The volition" refers to the volition known as the world. [It] "proceeds" from Brahman, which is of the nature of pure mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*).
It manifests. Regarding this, he provides an illustration with the words "from a dream. From a dream, which is of the nature of conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*);
"another dream," meaning another dream that is likewise of the nature of conceptual construction. "Just as" means "in the same way."
From this very reflection, these individual souls emanate; and due to the absence of auxiliary causes, that [reflection] alone is what they are.

From this [source] named Prajāpati, from this reflection, from this appearance, these living beings (jīvas), manifesting before our eyes, proceed forth—that is, they undergo movement. If that were so, one might ask: since they are produced from that, would they not be distinct from it?
To this, he says: "The co-operative causes. Those living beings are that very [Prajāpati] himself; they are not distinct from him. Why? Because of the co-operative causes.

Because of the absence of the auxiliary causes that consist of past karma; for it is a well-established principle that in the absence of auxiliary causes, the effect is of the very nature of its cause.
In the absence of auxiliary causes, this cause and effect is one; therefore, there is no other delusion of creation arising from another.

The "effect-and-cause" refers to that which is both the effect and the cause; from the Supreme Prajāpati, who is superior in relation to the visible world, there arises the delusion of creation, the playful manifestation of creation.

Brahman alone is the primordial Virāṭ Self; the state of emanation is the Virāṭ Self itself. That very one exists thus as the space of the individual soul (jīvākāśa), since the earth and other elements are unreal.

Brahman alone—that is, the very reality of Brahman—is the primordial Virāṭ-Ātman, the Supreme Self in the form of Virāṭ. The Virāṭ-Ātman itself becomes "sargatā," which means creation (sarga); here the abstract suffix (*bhāva-pratyaya*) is used for the sake of filling the meter. He provides the conclusion with the word "jīva": that aforementioned Jīvākāśa—consisting of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) enveloped by everything from the state of being an object of cognition (*cetyatva*) down to the subtle elements (*tanmātra*)—is indeed the Jīvākāśa.
Thus, in this manner, he exists in the form of the creation beginning with Prajāpati. Here, he states the reason: "Because [the earth] and so forth.
That is to say, for which reason, the earth and the rest become non-existent.
Having heard the term "living space" (*jīvākāśa*), Śrī Rāma, having fallen into some doubt, asks:
"Is the mass of living beings limited, or is it infinite? Or rather, does there exist an infinite aggregate of souls, as immovable as a mountain?"
The "mass of living beings" (*jīvarāśi*) is said to be the "space of living beings" (*jīvākāśa*), which is a collection of souls. Is it limited, or rather infinite and immeasurable?

Or is the aggregate of souls (*jīvapiṇḍa*) infinite in nature, like a mountain, resembling a peak? It exists. A "mass" (*rāśi*) is a collection of things existing as distinct entities; a "lump" (*piṇḍa*), however, like a lump of clay, refers to a single, unified mass consisting of souls—this is the distinction.
Anticipating the objection, "But why do you ask about your being a heap or a mass?", he says:
"Why do individual living beings issue forth like streams from a rain-cloud, like droplets from the ocean, or like sparks from heated iron? (MU 3.1.6)

"Streams" (dhārā) are streams of water; "sprays" (śīkara) are droplets of water. "Heated iron" (taptāyasaḥ) refers to iron ignited by fire; "particles" (kaṇāḥ) are minute fragments consisting of fire. Why? The sense is that if a mass of living beings (jīvarāśi)—or a collection of individual souls—is not admitted, the departure (niryāṇa) of these [beings] would be impossible.
He concludes the question:
"O Blessed One, tell me this: the definitive determination regarding the web of living beings. This has been mostly understood by me; please make that very thing manifest."

"O Blessed One, you have been asked: 'Tell me the definitive resolution regarding the net of living beings. Having said this much, was it not heard by you? To this he replied, "It is known. [The meaning is: "This has been known by me mostly—that is, for the most part—but not in its entirety; therefore, reveal that very thing so that I may know it completely."
The venerable Vasiṣṭha replied:
"There is not even a single living soul; how then can there be the existence of multitudes? Your words are like saying that a hare's horn has flown up and departed."

From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), there is not even a single living being (*jīva*). How, then, could there be the existence of the multitudes you have asked about? He states that this question is devoid of meaning by using the word "hare" (*śaśa*). Your words are like the statement: "The horn of a hare flies up into the air. Since the horn of a hare does not exist even at the outset, what talk can there be of its flying? In the same way, the living being itself does not exist.
The meaning is: what need is there to mention its mass and so forth?
All this that was asked is refuted [by the following]:
"O Raghava, there is no individual soul (jīva), nor are there multitudes of souls; nor does there exist any single mass of soul resembling a mountain."

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because everything consists solely of pure consciousness (*śuddhacinmātra*), the individual soul (*jīva*) does not exist. O Rāghava, there are no multitudes of souls, nor is there any single mass of soul (*jīvapiṇḍa*) resembling a mountain. Therefore, the implication is that this question of yours is not appropriate.
By way of a benediction, he declares the certainty that must be established:
"Let your firm conviction be this: that all conceptual constructions associated with the meaning of the word 'jīva', along with every other conceptual construction, do not exist at all."
"This certainty that 'it is yours'—let this certainty be immovable and firm. What [is it]? It is the conceptualizations of the meaning of the word "jīva.
Those [conceptualizations], accompanied by all conceptualizations—that is, endowed with all conceptualizations such as the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva)—do not exist.
[Objection: "But since the individual soul (jīva) and so forth manifest through direct perception, how can this certainty be appropriate? To this, he says:
"For here exists the pure, stainless Brahman, which is mere consciousness and all-pervading; because it possesses all powers, it assumes whatever form it chooses of its own accord. (MU 3.14.21)
Indeed, by means of the sequence of pure consciousness alone, one quickly beholds that very [reality], whether embodied or unembodied, like a creeper in full bloom.

The word *hi* indicates certainty. Pure consciousness alone (*cinmātra*) is the very nature of pure consciousness; for this reason, there exists the stainless Brahman. Of what nature is it? It is all-pervading (*sarvaga*), meaning it extends through all space and time. What follows from this? To this he says: "That" (*tat*). That is Brahman. Because it possesses all powers (*sarvaśaktitvāt*), since it has every power, [it manifests] whatever portion (*kalā*) consisting of individual souls (*jīva*) and so forth.

"In what manner" means by which mode; "by itself" means by its own nature, and not through dependence on another. It "perceives," that is, it makes its own perception the object. Of what nature is this *kalā*? By the sequence of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), that is, by the progression of pure consciousness; "like a creeper" means like a creeping vine; "fully blossomed" means expanded. For this is the very progression of pure consciousness itself, that it causes the various mental constructions (*kalanā*) to blossom.

Indeed, in the case of certainty, one perceives that conceptualization—whether embodied or unembodied, gross or subtle—in that very moment as already fully accomplished. And thus, the meaning is this: since the individual soul (*jīva*) is not established by itself in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), how could there be for it any state of being a heap or a mass?

Now, one might object: "If Brahman perceives the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth, then these must be distinct from It, because only that which is different from oneself can be an object of perception. To this, he replies:

"The individual soul, the intellect (*buddhi*), the vibration of activity (*kriyāspanda*), the mind (*manas*), and even duality and unity—all these direct their own manifesting existence toward that [Brahman] as its object of cognition. (MU 3.14.23)

That is Brahman; that well-known [Brahman] impels its own existence and its own radiance toward cognition, making them the objects of cognition—that is to say, one perceives them. Of what nature is this own existence? It is the individual soul (*jīva*), the intellect (*buddhi*), the vibration of activity, the movements for the sake of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, and the mind (*manas*). And that duality and unity—duality-unity—in this form as well, it shines forth.

"Throbbling. And likewise, the sense is that even though it falls within the range of vision, it is not logical for the living being (*jīva*) and so forth to be distinct [from the body]. // MT_3,14.23 //

Now, one might ask: "How does the existence of Brahman manifest itself in the form of the individual soul (jīva) and so forth? To this, he says: "It is indeed Brahman alone that becomes thus through awakening; it would be Brahman alone by virtue of being awakened. Ignorance perishes upon investigation, yet that [Brahman] is not itself awakened [by that investigation]. (MU 3.14.24)

That Brahman-existence, though awakened, being unknown in its nature as Brahman-existence, appears precisely in this way—in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth. Through awakening—that is, through knowing it in its nature as Brahman-existence—it becomes Brahman itself, because there is no difference between existence (*sattā*) and that which possesses existence (*tadvat*). [Objection: Even if the individual soul and so forth consist of Brahman by virtue of having Brahman-existence as their nature, they remain objects of the knowledge of Brahman-existence.

But that which was non-conscious, being known as such, remains exactly like a jar or other objects; and thus, the state of being solely composed of Brahman is not established. To this, he says: "Non-consciousness. Non-consciousness goes to destruction through the observation of consciousness. But in the alternative case, that non-consciousness is not perceived; it does not become an object of consciousness.
Because it is contradictory [to light], it perishes at the very moment it is stimulated; for darkness cannot be an object of light—this is the sense.
He confirms this very point with an illustration:
"Just as darkness perishes when it is confronted by a lamp, yet its true nature is not known [by the lamp], so indeed is it with non-awakening."

Just as darkness, when illuminated by a lamp, begins to be seen and then perishes, yet the true nature (*tattva*)—the essential form (*svarūpa*)—of this darkness is not known; the phrase "by the person" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. He applies this to the case at hand with the words "of non-awakening" (*abodhasya*).
For (*hi*) signifies certainty; the meaning is that in exactly this same way, the true nature of non-awakening—that is, of ignorance—is not known.
He concludes that the individual soul is Brahman:
"Thus, the individual self is indeed Brahman—undivided, continuous, omnipotent, without beginning or end, and bearing the form of the essence of the great Consciousness. (MU 3.1.4.26)

In this way, according to the manner previously described, the individual soul (*jīvātman*) becomes Brahman itself. He states its qualifying attributes that bring about this state of being Brahman, beginning with "undivided" (*nirvibhāga*). "Undivided" means devoid of division; for there is no division whatsoever within the nature of the individual soul, because it is partless (*niravayava*). "Uninterrupted" (*nirantara*) means devoid of any intervening space, being entirely filled with light. It is "all-powerful" (*sarvaśakti*).

His possession of all powers is indeed directly perceived in dreams and similar states. His being without beginning or end—that is, his freedom from limits of beginning and end—is established precisely by the fact that he is the delimiting agent; for the object to be delimited cannot effect the delimitation of its own delimiting agent. He assumes the form of the essence of the Great Consciousness (*mahācit*). "Great Consciousness" is the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*); its "essence" is luminosity (*prakāśa*).
He assumes his form, bearing the essence of the Great Consciousness; the meaning is that he is of the nature of luminosity.
In every way, it negates the conceptualization of difference;
yet, because of its absolute infinity, no conceptualization of difference exists within it. For whatever conceptualization there may be, that is itself [the reality] through direct experience.

But in the case of this Brahman, because it is "all-infinite"—that is, it is both everything and infinite—the state of being all-infinite is "sarvānantatā. By virtue of that, there is no conceptualization of difference (*bhedakalanā*), which is to say, no conceptualization in the form of distinction; that is, there is no such thing as "difference. This is because difference is impossible for that which is both of every form and infinite. Indeed, infinity does not exist in relation to things such as jars.

It is logical that there is a distinction between the jar and such things, and the clay and such things from which all those forms arise. Now, one might object: "Is not 'allness' (*sarvatva*) and 'infinitude' (*anantatva*) precisely what distinguishes [the whole] from the non-all and the finite? Thus, its distinction from them is established by those very two qualities. To this, he says: "It exists" (*vidyate*). The word *hi* signifies "because. That conceptualization (*kalana*), namely the conceptualization of difference, exists; it is that very thing.

It becomes Brahman itself. Why? Because of being experienced—that is, because its very nature is experience. This is the point: whatever conceptualization exists, is it experienced or not? If it is not experienced, then being unestablished by itself, how could it produce differentiation within Brahman? If it is experienced, then it is of the very nature of experience; and since experience is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), its identity with Brahman is already established.
"That would indeed be Brahman itself."
In this regard, Śrī Rāma asks:
"O Brahman, how is it that all the living beings of the world do not act in accordance with the will of a single soul, given their subjection to the unity of the Great Soul?"

"O Brahmin, what has been stated by you is so; it is indeed true—this is the meaning. One might raise the doubt: how can it be that all living beings follow the will of a single living being? [The text answers: 'All world-living beings' (*akhilā jagajjīvāḥ*).

'World-living beings' refers to those living beings situated within the world. This occurs by virtue of their oneness with the Great Living Being (*mahājīvaikatāvaśāt*). By the 'Great Living Being' is meant that which is called Pure Consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is enveloped by the phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) beginning with the object of cognition and ending with the subtle elements (*tanmātra*)."
"Unity" (*ekatā*) means oneness; "by its power" (*vaśāt*) means by its influence. "By the will of one living being" (*ekajīvecchayā*) means by the will of any single, universal living being.

How could they not be joined? This is the sense: since all living beings consist of the one Great Living Being (*mahājīva*) whose nature has been described, it is logical that when a desire arises in one living being, there is a union with all living beings.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha replied:
"That Great Soul, which is Brahman, consisting of all powers, remains here exactly as it desires—undivided and continuous."

The Great Living Self is the Great Life. That Brahman remains here according to its will, in accordance with its own desire. Of what nature is that Brahman? It consists of all powers (*sarvaśaktimayātmaka*). "Consisting of all powers" means filled with all powers;
that whose self (*ātman*) is such—that is how it is. Furthermore, the fact that Brahman consists of all powers is because all powers [originate] from it.
Thus, from its arising; furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "undivided" (*nirvibhāga*), meaning it has emerged beyond all divisions because its essential nature is indivisible.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "uninterrupted" (*nirantara*), being filled with the essence known as light (*prakāśa*).
"Let Brahman remain as it pleases; what follows from that? To this he says:
"Whatever that Great Soul desires, that comes to him immediately. But first his desire perishes, for consciousness is non-dual; thus, duality arises from that. (MU 3.1.4–5)

That is Brahman; whatever He desires, He makes that very object of His desire, and nothing else. Of that Great Self, of Brahman whose nature is all-pervasive, [the effect] comes into being—that is, it is accomplished—swiftly, at the very moment of His will. By the phrase "previously" (*pūrvam*), he explains the arising of duality through the destruction of the single will. *Cit* is will; it is a will qualified by consciousness, as in the expression "a blue lotus."

It is to be known that here, being "qualified by consciousness" (cid-viśeṣitatva) means being the object of consciousness (cid-viṣayatva). The word "yataḥ" (since/from which) is to be supplied. Therefore, the meaning is as follows:

since consciousness (cit) has a desire—namely, a singular desire in the form "May I exist as the very nature of consciousness"—at the beginning, at the start of the first creation; "ataḥ" (from this) is used in the sense of the locative case, meaning "in this Brahman"; the particle "tu" (but/however) has the sense of "iva" (as if); and [that which was previously unmanifest] perishes in the form of not being an object of clear manifestation.

It appears to go to destruction; however, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), it does not perish, because it is all-pervasive—this is the purpose of employing the word "but" (*tu*). Furthermore, the destruction of the desire for objects of consciousness (*cid-viṣaya*) should be understood as occurring precisely through the arising of the desire for objects of the cognized (*cetya*). For that reason (*tat*), duality—the state of being divided into two forms, such as the nature of the cognized and the form of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth—arises or manifests, by virtue of being the cause for the destruction of the desire for unity.
The intended meaning is that duality arises precisely through the desire for duality.

Immediately after the emergence of duality, he describes the process of the sequence of powers and actions: "Thereafter, for those powers divided by duality, a sequence of action is fashioned by him [the Lord] in this manner, such that 'by this, it becomes thus. (MU 3.14.31)

Afterwards, by that Brahmā, a sequence of actions was conceived in this manner: "of the powers divided into duality"—that is, divided by way of being twofold, established through partition; "of his own powers"—in this way, indeed, [the process] is accomplished by this. How so? It is thus. //MT_3,14.31//

Whatever rule has been established by that power of Brahmā through which one’s own desired goal is accomplished according to one's capacity—without that, there is no arising of other [powers]; it is the will of the Pradhāna alone that flourishes.

By that well-known primordial power belonging to Brahman (*brāhmī śakti*), which serves as the fundamental cause, a certain regulation (*niyama*)—a destiny corresponding to His own will (*svecchā*)—has been fashioned. Without that regulation, there would be no emergence of other states of existence for living beings (*jīvasthāna*). The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is to be supplied [as a conclusion]: therefore, it is the will of the Pradhāna alone that comes forth; [the will] of the Pradhāna, which has become the Great Soul (*mahājīvātman*).

[The opponent argues: "It is the will of Brahmā alone that grows; it transforms into the form of the individual soul's (jīva) will. Thus, it is simply the conformity to the will of Pradhāna. It was not stated that she [the will] exercises restrictive control. But here, it is said 'by her power'—is this not so? [The author replies: No, because there is no difference between the power and that which possesses the power.
He explains this very point through various formulations:
that which bears fruit as the will of the power called *jīva* does so not without the performance of the regulation of the primary power (*pradhāna-śakti*).

Of that power called *jīvā*, or of that individual soul (*jīva*) which is of the nature of power—of her, [the word] "whose" (*yasyāḥ*) must be supplied; of that power, this is the desire. Without the performance of the regulation of the primary power—that is, without the performance of the regulation, the act of imposing restraint, of the primary power, the power of Brahman. Without that.
It does not exist; it does not even obtain its own nature. What, then, can be said of its fruit? Such is the meaning.
If the regulation of the power of the Pradhāna were not well-established, then the fruit of undertakings would never occur anywhere, due to the presence or absence of that power.

The "regulation of the power of Pradhāna" (pradhānaśaktiniyamaḥ) refers to the regulation of the power of Brahman (brahmaśakteḥ). It is "well-established" (supratiṣṭhaḥ), meaning well-firmly rooted. "If it were not so" (na ced bhavet) means if that [regulation] did not exist; then (tat), at that time, there would be no fruit (phalam) of the red-colored things (rohitānām) anywhere, in any place or time. Why? Because of the presence or absence of power (śaktyaśaktatvāt). By "power" (śaktyā) is meant the power of Brahman (brahmaśaktyā); by implication, it refers to its regulation.

Capability with respect to a result is efficacy; the absence of that is incapability. Therefore, from this capacity and incapacity, it is inferred that there exists some rule by which actions possess the efficacy to produce a result—this is the intended meaning. Since various kinds of red-colored actions have results, it follows that there must be a certain principle governing the power of actions to bring about their effects.

Returning to the subject at hand: thus the Great Soul (Mahājīva), Brahman, exists, devoid of end, beginning, and so forth; it becomes millions upon millions of individual souls, or else it is nothing at all.
In this way, according to the manner previously described, there exists the Great Life (mahājīva), which is devoid of beginning and end—free from extremes, middle, and so forth.
He provides the answer to the question previously asked, "From where do living beings emerge? by saying, "The millions of lives" (jīvatkoṭi). That is Brahman.
"The millions of lives, the great millions" (jīvatkoṭimahākoṭī) refers to the millions and great millions in number of those who possess life—that is, of those who perform the activity of living.

He becomes that very form himself; the sense is that no individual souls (jīvas) emerge from him. Or, even so, nothing at all occurs, because he remains exactly as he is in his own nature consisting of consciousness.
Now, one might ask: "By what means does Brahman become a living soul? To this it is said:

Through the non-perception of the object of thought, it becomes a living soul and enters into the cycle of transmigration; through the non-perception of that [object], its form attains peace from transmigration.

Due to the non-perception of the object of consciousness—that is, due to the failure to reflect upon the multitude of entities that have become objects of consciousness—the Brahman becomes the individual soul (jīva). From that, it enters into transmigration;

it becomes a participant in the cycle of existence characterized by the taint of pleasure and pain. Now, one might ask: "Is its transmigration ever terminated or not? To this, he says: "That [due to the non-perception of that]. This means: due to the non-perception of that, i.e., due to the failure to reflect upon the object of consciousness. The word "asya" (of this) is to be supplied [as the subject].
The form of this living being—that is, of transmigratory existence—attains tranquility, which is peace.
Now, one might ask: "What is accomplished for the individual soul (jīva) by the cessation of transmigration? To this, he says:
"In this way, through the sequence of activities of the elder souls, the state of being the primordial soul (ādyajīvatva) arises for the younger souls, just as the state of gold arises for copper."

This being so, when there is the cessation of saṃsāra, through the sequences of activity of the eldest living being—that is, through the sequences of activity of the eldest living being—the state of being the primordial living being, which is Brahmanhood, arises or manifests for the youngest living beings. In this context, the "sequences of activity of the eldest living being" should be understood as the sequences of activity performed by Brahman; for it is precisely through the sequence of activity performed by Brahman that living beings attain the state of Brahman.

Because of its capacity. Regarding this, he provides an illustration with the words "of copper. The meaning is: just as the state of being gold arises from copper through the successive processes of a goldsmith's work, so it is here.
He remembers what was stated previously:

"In this infinite supreme space, even though this group of elements is non-existent, it arises as if existent, being essentially the self of the void and consisting of the wonder of consciousness. (MU 3.14.38)

In this way, according to the sequence previously described, here—in the infinite, well-known, and immeasurable supreme space (*parākāśa*), which is the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*)—this aforementioned multitude, the phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) consisting of the nature of the objectified (*cetyatva*) and so forth, arises as if existent even though it is non-existent. Of what nature is it? It is of the very nature of the void (*khātman*), being essentially nothing at all. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It consists of the wonder (*camatkaraṇa*) of consciousness; that which is the wonder of consciousness...

The act of tasting by means of one's own power—that which has this as its self (ātman) or essential nature—is that which consists of the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkaraṇātmaka*). For independent consciousness cannot be directed toward an object of cognition (*cetyonmukhatā*) without such a wonder.

[Objection: Since there must necessarily be a dependence on something else for the sake of producing wonder (*camatkāra*), how can this [consciousness] be called "independent" (*svatantra*)? To this, he says:
"That which is experienced as a wonder by consciousness itself, prior to the future body, name, and so forth—that the wise know as the state of *ahaṃbhāvanā* (the sense of 'I'). (MU 3.14.39)

The wonder (*camatkāra*) which is encountered by consciousness itself—along with its own substratum and its own object—without effort, and which spontaneously attains the state of being the object of that encounter; the wise know that to be the "I-feeling" (*ahambhāvana*), the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).

Since even the ego-sense is nothing but the wonder of consciousness, what need is there to mention the individual soul (*jīva*)? This is the intended meaning of the term "I-feeling. Of what nature is it?
"Future name, body, and so forth" means that which has a future name and a future body and so forth. "Name" (*nāman*) refers to designations such as "I-conceit" (*ahaṃkāra*).

"Body" (*deha*) refers to the gross and subtle forms. The expression of the object and the agent—as in "is brought together" (*samāgamyate*)—is used to illuminate the independence of consciousness (*citi*). 39. MT_3,14.39.

He explains at great length the subject at hand—the unity of consciousness: "That which is the light of consciousness, being infinite due to its identity with that [consciousness], this very expanse of the worlds is reflected within it. (MU 3.14.40)

Of consciousness (*citaḥ*), which has an infinite nature and is the light of awareness (*citprakāśasya*); that light (*ālokaḥ*)—which is the cause for manifesting phenomena and a particularity of its own nature—exists. How is it? Because it consists of that; because it consists of consciousness (*cinmayatvāt*). It is infinite (*anantakaḥ*), immeasurable like consciousness itself.
And this immeasurability of consciousness should be understood from the absence of a measurer and because it is impossible for it to be a measurer of itself.

This aforementioned light of consciousness (*cidāloka*) regarding the object distinct from itself— that is, this expansion of the world (*bhuvanābhoga*) belonging to that consciousness— reflects; it manifests as a reflection by not assuming the impurity [of the object].
By means of words such as "transformation" and "modification," that very same immutable consciousness, though indivisible due to its uniform nature, is awakened by its own power alone.
By her own power alone—that is, by her innate power which manifests as the state of the subject—she is the imperishable (avyayā), meaning devoid of destruction;

she herself, as Consciousness (cit), is understood through such terms as "transformation" (pariṇāma) and "modification" (vikāra). It is well known that a word serves as the cause for the cognition of its meaning, so no further effort is required [to prove this]. Of what nature is she? She is of such a form, because of her nature as consciousness (cidrūpatā).

"Indivisible" means that it is incapable of being divided. If it is asked: "But if it is non-different from its own nature (*svarūpa*), how can it be denoted by words such as 'transformation' (*pariṇāma*) and so forth?"—the answer is:

True. Just as water, though non-different from its own nature, is described by the term 'transformation of water' and by terms for its modifications when it attains the state of waves, so too is this [consciousness]; thus there is no contradiction.
The self-sustained savoring of consciousness, which is itself of the nature of uninterrupted play, is that very manifestation of the non-objectifiable light which stands as the world.

The tasting—which is the relishing by its own power—of this consciousness (*cit*), which is non-objective light and whose nature is a luminosity free from the stain of objectivity, occurs spontaneously and without effort. Of what nature is it? It is "of the nature of uninterrupted play" (*avicchinnavilāsātman*). That whose essence (*ātman*) is characterized by uninterrupted play—that is, by a vibration (*sphuraṇa*) devoid of interruption—is "of the nature of uninterrupted play. That tasting is the world.
Thus, it remains established in the very nature of the world.
This power of consciousness, which is more subtle than even space and is all-pervasive, perceives this "I-ness" by its very nature.

That which is subtler than even space, indivisible, spread everywhere, and all-pervasive—that is the power, the capacity of consciousness (cit). That is consciousness itself. By its very nature, by its own existence alone—and not through effort or the like—it perceives this aforementioned qualified [reality] as "I-ness" (ahantā); it cognizes it through the state of ego (ahaṅkāra).
That which manifests within this Self by the Self alone, like water, as far as the end of the world—that very thing He perceives as the subtle atom of egoity (*ahantā*).

Of this consciousness (*cit*), the self (*ātman*) is its essential nature (*svarūpa*) known as vibration (*sphurattā*). Within the self—that is, within its own essential nature known as vibration—it manifests by its own being (*svabhāva*), and not through effort. That which vibrates and shines forth—how? Like water, like a liquid.
That very vibration is this consciousness; it perceives the atom of "I-ness" (*ahantāṇu*), grasping it in the form of limited egoity (*parimitāhantā*).
Of what nature is the atom of ego? It is that which reaches the end of the world, the limit of the universe.
That which causes wonder and is beautiful—the consciousness that manifests within itself—it is that very [consciousness] which has fashioned this extended thing called the "world."

It is the cause of wonder for that which produces wonder; it is "tataṃ," meaning expanded. "Jagannāma" means that which is named "jagat" (the world); it was "kṛtaṃ" (created) by her alone—this is the ellipsis.

The state of being consciousness is the intellect (*citta*), and that very thing, O Rāghava, is the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*); it is mere conceptual construction. Therefore, since it is only consciousness from the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) onwards, where could duality and unity possibly reside?
The state of consciousness (*cittva*) becomes the ego (*ahaṅkāra*); the meaning is that it is through the transformation of consciousness itself into the state of ego.
O Rāghava, that very [consciousness] becomes the ego. It becomes "imagination" (*kalpanā*); the feminine gender is used in dependence upon the word *kalpanā*.

Therefore, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and so forth are produced from the ego; they are the subtle elements and so forth. Consciousness itself becomes [the ego], for the ego is the cause of the subtle elements.
Because it is mental. Where could duality and unity reside? The implication is that they do not exist. If it is argued: "Let there be no duality;

why should unity not exist?"—do not say so. For without its opposite, duality, even unity is unestablished. Indeed, light does not become manifest without shadow, because it is indefinable [without its counterpart].
Having thus established that everything consists of the one consciousness, he enjoins upon the disciple the abandonment of duality as something to be practiced:
"Abandon both 'you' and 'I' so long as the cause of the individual soul (the ego) is not relinquished; remain in the midst of existence and non-existence, and become the essential Self."

The "Person" (puruṣa) is of the nature of the meaning [of the word]; that is, he is of the nature of the meaning of the sentence of the Guru's instruction implied by the word "iti. This is what is meant by "intent upon that" (tatpara). He states the Guru's instruction implied by the word "iti": "Abandon both 'you' and 'I'"; the sense is that by means of which, while living, one goes far away. Furthermore, as for the form [in which one asks], "How shall I remain?", he says here: "the remainder" (śeṣa), [referring to] existence and non-existence.
Abide in the middle, which is indefinable as either being or non-being; remain as pure consciousness alone, the witness that remains pure even when all conceptual proliferation has been sublated.

Having thus stated non-difference to the disciple as that which is to be practiced, he speaks again of non-difference alone out of compassion for him: "Just as consciousness first assumed its own existence, so it has arisen; it is seen as non-different from space. Now I realize both existence and non-existence. (MU 3.14.48)

"At the beginning of creation," such as that of the *cit* (consciousness), "one's own existence" (*svasattā*)—which is one's innate nature in the form of the intuition "I am"—is "assumed" (*kalitā*) "in whatever way" (*yathā*), that is, in the form of individual souls (*jīva*) and so forth. The word "of this" (*asyāḥ*) is to be supplied; [the meaning is: "that existence of this *cit*. Having thus arisen or manifested in that form, it is seen as non-different from the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*). The words "by the knowers" (*jñānibhiḥ*) are to be understood as the ellipsis. By the term "I" (*aham*), the subject of universal existence (*sattāsāmānyapramātā*) is indicated.
It has been explained. Now, I perceive and know existence and non-existence; however, the sense is that they do not exist in that manner [as independent entities].

The sky of consciousness, the void, the movements of the world, the void, the oceans, the gods, and the mountains—because they are of the nature of the wonder of consciousness in the form of the void, there is indeed nothing else that exists.

The consciousness-space (*citkha*) becomes the void (*kha*), the sky (*ākāśa*). The activities of the world—meaning the efforts of living beings for the sake of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful—become the void.
The oceans, the gods, and the mountains—they too become nothing but the void. Regarding this, he states the second half [of the verse] as the reason:

"having the form of the void" (*khākāra*). For the word *hi* signifies "because"; because that which has the form of the void is precisely the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*). That very thing is its form.
Its state is its *tattva* (reality). Therefore, because it has the nature of the wonder of consciousness in the form of space (*khākāra*), nothing else exists.
The meaning is that everything, being the very nature of space, consists solely of the wonder of consciousness.
Whatever is a manifestation of something is never distinct from it; this holds true even for that which possesses parts—what then need be said regarding that which is partless?

Whatever is the play (*vilāsa*) of something, that is its manifestation (*sphuraṇa*); it is never—not at any time—different from that reality (*tattva*), even though that reality possesses parts (*sāvayava*). For no one says that a wave is different from water; such is the sense. [This applies] to that which is partless (*anavayava*), devoid of parts;
the sense is that this should be stated even in the case of a dream.
[Objection: "But even if consciousness (*cit*) has the world as its form, since there exists another consciousness that perceives it, it cannot consist of non-duality. To this, he says:

"For consciousness, which is eternally unobjectifiable, there is no other consciousness whose nature is not [itself] manifest; whatever is the form of the world, that is the form of that which consists of its own radiance. (MU 3.14.51)

"Always" means [of that] which is unperceivable, that is, unfit to be perceived. "Cognition" (cit) refers to cognition that grasps itself; the sense is that there is no loss of its nature as consciousness. Of what kind is this cognition? It is "of unextended form" (*avitatākṛti*). That is, it is that whose form—its nature—is unextended due to its subtlety, not situated anywhere.
Of that [cognition]. Now, is this not unproven? Because it is endowed with the nature of the manifestation "I am shining forth."

Regarding this, he says: "That which is form" (*yad rūpam*). That which is form—that which [appears] as "I am vibrating" (*sphurāmi*) and so forth—becomes form. The word "that" (*tat*) is to be supplied [in the text]. That is the form of the world alone, and not of consciousness (*cit*). For, primarily, the state of being consciousness belongs only to that consciousness which apprehends "I am vibrating. However, for that which has the nature of the object of apprehension in the thought "I am vibrating," the state of being consciousness exists only in a secondary sense.

The state of being the world (*jagattva*) does not deviate [from that]. Of what kind of world? Of that which has the nature of various manifestations (*tattatsphuraṇarūpin*). "Various manifestations" refers to such things as the thought "I am manifesting. That which has this as its nature is "that which has the nature of various manifestations. The meaning is that whatever comes within the range of being an object of cognition (*cetyatā*), all that is indeed the world.

The mind, the intellect, the ego, the elements, the mountains, and the directions—such is the arrangement of synonyms for the consciousness that constitutes the existence of the world according to its true nature.
The continuous stream of words expressed in such forms as "mind" (*manas*) and "intellect" (*buddhi*) constitutes a series of synonyms for consciousness (*cit*). Why?

Because of the nature of the world's existence—that is, because the existence of the world takes the form of mind, intellect, and so forth—and because of its reality, which is the nature of consciousness. The underlying sense is that all words are indeed expressive of consciousness alone.

Know that the world is the consciousness of consciousness; for there is no non-worldly consciousness. Since it would be non-conscious due to being non-worldly, how could there be a world if there were no distinction between existence and consciousness?
The "cittva" (consciousness-ness) belonging to consciousness is that certain quality by which it becomes fit to be named "cit" (consciousness);
know—that is, understand—that very thing to be the "jagat" (the world). He states the reason for this with the word "na" (not): for indeed, because of that cause, "cittva" is not non-worldly;
it does not exist apart from the world. For in the absence of the world—which is of the nature of the object of cognition—the indefinable consciousness would clearly [not manifest].

Because of the unfitness for consciousness (*cittva*). He states the intermediate conclusion: "not the world" (*ajagat*). The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is to be supplied. Therefore, for this reason; because consciousness (*cit*) is not the world, for that reason, it would be non-conscious (*acit*), meaning it would be unfit to be called consciousness. The point is that if there were no world, even consciousness—which is otherwise indeterminable—would lack the quality of being conscious. He states the ultimate conclusion: "because of the non-difference of existence" (*bhāvābhedāt*). Because of the non-difference of existence.

Because the non-difference of the categories [of existence] is established by the non-difference of consciousness and the world, which is proven by the logic previously established, how and from where could the world exist?

The sense is that since there is no difference between consciousness and the world, and since consciousness consists solely of the one consciousness (*cidekamaya*), consciousness alone exists in every way; therefore, the world does not exist.

To cite the innate, wondrous power residing at the end of the seed-syllable *marīca*: that very power remains as this world, which consists of nothing more than the subtle element of the living soul (*jīvatanmātra*).

Within—that is, in the middle of—the seed-syllable *marica*, which is called *citi*, there occurs a sense of wonder (*camatkṛti*); that is to say, by its own power, there is a marvelous experience known as the relishing of its own energy. That very [wonder] exists in the form of this world (*jagat*), abiding as the world itself.
Of what nature is this world? It consists solely of the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) of the individual soul; it has the essential nature of the five subtle elements of the living being alone.
But it is not composed of gross elements, because grossness is unreal according to the analogy of a dream.

Because it possesses consciousness, that manifestation of its own power which is the consciousness's sense of "I" is the *jīva*; for it consists of the activity of vibration and is indeed designated by the name "the future."

The manifestation of one's own power (*svaśaktikacana*), which consists in the vibration of one's own power (*svaśaktisphuraṇarūpa*)—that which exists as the sense of "I" (*ahambhāvana*)—from what [does it arise]? From consciousness (*cittvāt*), that is, from the cause known as the state of consciousness (*cidbhāva*). Indeed (*hi*), for certain; this vibration of one's own power becomes the individual soul (*jīva*). The masculine gender is used here in relation to the *jīva*. Of what nature is this *jīva*? It is of the nature of pulsation (*spandātman*), having the form of a slight vibration. That which is action (*karma*), that is it.

The self is one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Whose [nature]? It means that its essence consists of vibration (*spanda*), that is, its nature is the vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*). Furthermore, of what kind is it?
It is "that which will have a name," meaning it is the manifestation of *vaikharī* speech.

Whatever conceptualization occurs through the nature of consciousness regarding the meaning of designations and so forth, that is differentiated by exclusions and modifications; therefore, it does not truly exist.

The elision of the genitive case [in the compound *cit-ārṣa*] is Vedic; thus, it is *citaḥ*. By being conscious (*cittvena*), that is, by the state of consciousness (*cidbhāvena*). "Apprehension" (*kalana*) means delimitation (*pariccheda*). It exists. Of what nature?

That by which the direction of the meaning of the denotation (*abhidhārthadik*)—that is, a mere fraction of the meaning of the name (*nāmārthaleśaḥ*)—is easily accomplished (*susampādyā*), meaning it can be brought about with ease.

That is "that by which the direction of the meaning of the denotation is easily accomplished. For it is only of a delimited entity (*paricchinnasyaiva vastunaḥ*) that there is a name and its status as the denoted object.

It is possible [to do so]. That [consciousness] is differentiated; it remains as something distinct from consciousness (*cita*). By what means? By means of delimitations and modifications (*vyavaccheda-vikāra*). This means that [consciousness] does not touch the mind. Let there be the production of difference from insentient things; those very things are the modifications. By them—meaning, because of being conjoined with them—it is distinct from consciousness. What loss is there [in this]? To this, he says: "Therefore. Thus.

Because it is distinct from consciousness (*cit*), it does not exist; for that which is distinct from consciousness cannot be an object of cognition (*cetyamānatā*). And even if it were to exist, since it lacks such an object, it would be devoid of conceptual construction (*asaṅkalpa*).
