Due to the absence of mental activity (*kalanā*) by virtue of its nature as pure consciousness, even the state of being a "mind" (*cittva*) is rendered void and thus non-existent.

In the absence of the state of being a mind, the world (*jagat*) is non-existent. And in the absence of that [world], there is the sovereignty of pure consciousness alone (*cinmātra*); this is the intended meaning.

[Objection: "Granted that everything consists of the one consciousness (*cit*), yet the mutual difference between the agent and the object, which are its constituent parts, is difficult to avoid. To this, he says:

"There is no difference between the agent and the object, both of which consist of the vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*). The object is merely vibration; that very [vibration] is traditionally known as the person (*puruṣa*). (MU 3.14.57)

There is no distinction between the agent and the object, both of which consist of the vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*) and possess the form known as the manifestation of consciousness (*citsphūrti*). To the question "How is this so?", he says here: "Vibration" (*spanda*). Merely the vibration would be the object (*karman*), because it is observed that only external vibration constitutes the state of being an object. That very [vibration] is traditionally known as the person (*puruṣa*); the words "by the wise" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. This is the intended meaning: knowledge, when investigated within, is...

Nothing whatsoever is obtained without [consciousness]; moreover, objects such as pots and cloths exist externally. Therefore, there is no connection whatsoever between consciousness and them; thus, pure consciousness remains. And that alone is the vibration of the intellect (citta) known as its radiance (sphuraṇa). That itself is action (karma), because even external action in the form of bodily movement and so forth is preceded by it.

That is indeed reality, and that alone is the person (*puruṣa*). Since nothing else is perceived within [it], and since it is impossible for the external body, which is like a lump of clay, to possess the nature of a person, it is established that action (*karman*) is the person.

It establishes the unity of the entire class of living beings and so forth: "The soul is consciousness; movement belongs to persons, and that very [consciousness] is the mind. But the mind, being in the form of the senses, moves through various objects. (MU 3.14.58)

The *jīva*—that is, in its state as consciousness (*cit*), meaning its very nature is consciousness—possesses vibration (*parispanda*). For men, that very vibration becomes the mind (*citta*), which is synonymous with karma; for there exists no *jīva* or mind distinct from the vibration of consciousness. However, specifically, the mind (*manas*) itself, in the form of the vibration of consciousness, constitutes the mind (*citta*) and takes on the form of the sense organs (*indriya*).

Being (*sat*), it does not undergo diversity (*nānātva*). Of what nature is the mind? It is precisely non-diverse (*anāna*); because it is one from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is devoid of diversity. This is the intended meaning here: the living being (*jīva*) is, first of all, merely the vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*);
that mind is likewise of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). And that very mind transforms into the form of the sense faculties (*indriya*). And therefore—
Having gone out through the doors of the senses, which are its own transformations, it assumes the form of objects consisting of the fivefold [group] beginning with form (*rūpa*).
Thereafter, it attains the state of the pentad that serves as its substratum, and subsequently transforms into the nature of its effects;

thus, the vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*) alone exists in the form of gross and subtle entities. And since that [vibration] is non-different from consciousness, everything [is consciousness].
It remains as nothing other than the very nature of consciousness.

For the world is indeed a flash of the radiance of consciousness, in which all particularity has been stilled; therefore, nothing other than this exists, such as the relationship of cause and effect or the like.

For this reason—that is, because the entire world without exception is a mass of the radiance of consciousness (*citprakāśa*), since it consists of a series of established objects within the radiance of consciousness; it becomes a series of the radiance of consciousness. Of what nature is it? It is that in which all particularities (*viśeṣa*) are stilled—that is, all particularities, which are entities, have dissolved into pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Therefore, for that reason, there is no state of being cause and effect, and so forth.

Nothing else exists apart from pure consciousness (cinmātra), because even the relationship of cause and effect does not deviate from being the very radiance of consciousness (citprakāśacchaṭā) insofar as it constitutes the world.

"I am uncuttable, I am unburnable, I am indeed unmoistenable and undryable; I am eternal, all-pervading, fixed, and immovable"—thus it is established. Since the entire world, including all living beings, consists of the nature of conscious light (*citprakāśa*), this remains the case; this very certainty becomes firmly established. Why so? Because "I" am of the form of conscious light.
I am indivisible; like that which has no body, I am not subject to being cut. In this same way, [the attributes] "this is unburnable" and so forth are also to be connected.

I am eternal. Regarding this eternity, he states the reason by way of a qualification: "ever-moving" (satataga), meaning existing at all times. Furthermore, of what nature am I? I am a pillar (sthāṇu), firmly established in my own essential form. Here too, he states the reason as a qualification: "immovable" (acala).
Thus; the meaning is that he is unwavering.
"But if all is composed of the one Consciousness, for what purpose do the disputants argue? To this he says:
"For just as they argue here, so do they wander through delusions; we, however, have become free from delusion, whereas these others are wandering."

The word "of the disputants" (*vādinām*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis; "disputants" refers to logicians and others. Here, in this light of consciousness (*citprakāśe*), in whatever manner they dispute—that is, engage in controversy—so too do they dispute through delusions (*bhramaiḥ*), which are false cognitions (*mithyājñānai�*). This is because there is an absence of dispute among those who have realized the true nature of reality (*jñātatattvānām*). For instance, logicians describe the self (*ātman*) as possessing the quality of knowledge (*jñānaguṇam*) and as being subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāriṇam*).
The Sāṅkhyas [describe it] as indifferent, though its nature is knowledge, yet in the form of atoms; the Cārvākas as the form of the elements; the Buddhists as the form of emptiness;

the Vedāntins as the peaceful essential nature; and others likewise describe it as something else entirely. Although these [disputants] contend solely out of compassion for those qualified [for liberation], nevertheless, for the sake of those qualified persons who are established in their respective stages, so that they may abandon a lower stage and proceed to a higher one—

The delusion of disputants has been described. If disputants debate out of delusion, then how do you stand? To this he says: "We are wandering," but the word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction. We here are free from delusion, because we have accepted pure consciousness alone—which transcends the various qualities asserted by disputants—and thus false knowledge has been cast far away. How are we? The meaning is: "we are not wandering. Now, [one might ask], was this not said by the venerable Vasiṣṭha?

[Objection: "By one intent on refuting their doctrine, a dispute has been created. [Reply: Not so; for even in refuting their doctrine for the sake of awakening [others], all doctrines are already accepted by virtue of accepting pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) alone. Indeed, everyone accepts pure consciousness; however, they dispute regarding its specific attributes.
Furthermore, he explains that it is indeed of the nature of pure Consciousness alone:

"In the visible, embodied form superimposed by the ignorant, modifications and the like may exist as distinct; but not so in the formless, conscious Intellect—the sky of consciousness whose self is both being and non-being. (MU 3.14.62)

"In the embodied" means in the gross, visible collection of entities that are objects of the act of seeing. In what state? "Deeply rooted in the ignorant"; that is, firmly established among the ignorant or fools—meaning, known by fools. "Transformation and so forth": by the word "and so forth," transformation (*pariṇāma*) and the like are included. "It would exist separately": this is because the gross, visible [entity] possesses the fitness to be the locus of properties such as transformation.

The meaning is as follows: in that which is formless and subtle; in the consciousness of those who know it, which flashes forth among the knowers of reality; in the space of consciousness (*citkha*), the space of the intellect—there, modifications and the like do not exist separately. In what kind of space of consciousness? In that whose nature is both being and non-being (*sadasadātman*). The sense is: if a modification and so forth exists, even then it is composed of that [consciousness] alone; if it does not exist, even then it is likewise [composed of that].

The essence of consciousness, through its savor of the object of thought, expands its own clusters of blossoms—powers named Time and so forth—which are as pure as space and possess the beauty of the honey of pure awareness.

The splendor of consciousness is the beauty of spring known as Consciousness (Cid). She spreads forth—meaning she expands—her own clusters of blossoms, which are the powers (śaktis) designated by names such as Time and so forth, that is, those associated with time, space, and other categories. Why? Because it is joined with the essence of the object of thought (cetya-rasa); for it is fitting that the beauty of spring should produce clusters of blossoms through its own sap. What are these powers? They are the reality of consciousness (cittattva), whose nature is pure consciousness alone.

Thus, because of the non-difference between the power and that which possesses the power. Furthermore, of what nature are they? They are as clear as space; they do not possess a gross form that appears [to the senses].
It describes how consciousness-in-itself manifests as the form of the object of cognition by its own nature:
"The unstruck sheath of consciousness flashes forth of its own accord in manifold ways; the jewel of consciousness shines of its own accord in manifold ways, being without cause. (MU 3.14.64)

The "garment of consciousness" (*citkañcukam*): by metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇayā*), "garment" means a cloth; thus, it is a cloth called consciousness. "By itself," that is, by its own nature (*svabhāvena*), it vibrates diversely, like a painted canvas;

the meaning is that it becomes possessed of manifold variety. This manifold variety should be understood as being produced by objects and the cognitions thereof. Likewise, the jewel of consciousness shines forth by itself in diverse ways; and such shining forth is entirely appropriate for a jewel.
He himself explains the meaning of the word "svayam" (himself) by saying, "without a cause."
The wind of consciousness, being non-inert by nature, possesses an inherently distinctive vibration; the water of consciousness, possessing an inherently manifold movement, does not remain stagnant.

"Distinct vibration" means possessing a vibration distinct from that of external air. Regarding this, he states the qualification "of a non-inert nature" as the reason; the implication is that the vibration of the inert and the non-inert must necessarily be distinct. Water, when buried underground, undergoes various undulations—that is, various pulsations—but the water of consciousness (cid-vāri), even when buried...
Being existent, it does not undergo various transformations.
The lofty peak of consciousness, fashioned from various elements, has been manifested by itself; the moonlight of consciousness, shining with the splendor of diverse flavors, is perpetually risen.
The lofty peak is uncreated and devoid of fabrication; it consists of various elements (*vicitradhātu*). "Various" means manifold;

"elements" refers to the causal substances known as the primary elements (*bhūta*). That [peak] possesses such [elements]. Even a peak may consist of various elements, being endowed with diverse minerals such as red ochre and the like; however, this one is uncreated. It is itself the lunar radiance of consciousness, overflowing with the essence of manifold wonders.

Endowed with the radiance of the essence of various objects of perception, she is ever-arisen by means of that [consciousness]. External moonlight, too, is endowed with the radiance of the essence of diverse ambrosial flavors;
however, it arises only during the bright fortnight.
The light of consciousness, which is pure by nature, is always manifest of itself; yet to the ignorant, it seems as if it has set, while for the wise, consciousness arises through knowledge.

The sense is that light possesses the quality of manifestation (*prakaṭatā*). Regarding the word "itself" (*svayam*): consciousness (*citi*) itself, in the case of an ignorant or foolish person, becomes as if it has set. Its state of having "set," even while it remains present, is simply its not being an object of knowledge; hence the employment of the word "as if" (*iva*). Consciousness itself, in the case of a wise person endowed with knowledge, arises from knowledge, just as [light does] in the sky.
The meaning is that even though the sun is blazing, it is as if unrisen for one who is blind, yet it is risen for one possessed of eyes; so too is this [knowledge].

In the insentient things, it has itself arrived at the state of deep sleep through its own inertia; likewise, as consciousness, the great sky of the intellect is both vibrating and non-vibrating by its very nature.

Consciousness (*citi*) [becomes] inert within insentient things such as stationary objects; by means of inertia, that is, through the state of being insentient, it itself arrives at the state of deep sleep (*sauṣuptapada*), the locus of *suṣupti*. The great sky of consciousness (*citimahānabhaḥ*), the vast space called *cit*, itself becomes vibrating, endowed with the quality of throbbing; likewise, in that same manner, it becomes non-vibrating, endowed with the quality of stillness. However, for the external sky, [this occurs] by way of wind.
The state of being with vibration [is defined by] its own nature as being without vibration.
In the virtuous one who is consciousness endowed with qualities, [the sage] declares the existence and non-existence of the world;

for the world both exists and does not exist by virtue of being illumined by the light of consciousness. The world both exists and does not exist because it is the singular voidness of the space of consciousness.

"Hi" signifies certainty. It is the manifestation of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*). Of this light of consciousness—of that radiance called *cit*—the "manifestation" is its quality known as illumination.
The world both exists and does not exist. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that existence and non-existence are of equal importance.
This is the intended meaning: just as in the case of a luminous substance (*guṇin*), the quality known as light exists because it appears as distinct [from the substance].

Because it cannot be apprehended as separate from that, it does not exist. Likewise, the world also exists because it appears within the substratum called consciousness (*cit*), which is its possessor of qualities; yet, because it cannot be apprehended apart from that, it does not exist. This same logic should be applied to what follows as well. Regarding "the single voidness of the space of consciousness" (*cidākāśa*): the single voidness of the space of consciousness is the quality (*guṇa*) known as voidness. Thus, it is "the single voidness of the space of consciousness."
The world exists and does not exist as the great form of the light of consciousness; the world exists and does not exist as the dense vibration of the wind of consciousness.
The great form is radiant and possesses the quality known as white. Regarding "consciousness and wind": it is well established that vibration is indeed a quality of wind.
The world exists and does not exist due to the blackness of the darkness of the density of consciousness; the world exists and does not exist on the day of the light of the sun of consciousness.
And the blackness of darkness is its quality. Regarding the term *cidarka* (the sun of consciousness): because the day conforms to the light of the sun, that [light] is its quality.

To further solidify what was stated previously, he declares that the world is in every respect nothing but a quality of consciousness: "The delusion of the world is a single atom from the mountain of soot-dust that is consciousness; the world-lineament is the heat of the fire of consciousness; the world is the whiteness of the conch-shell of consciousness. (MU 3.14.72)

Consciousness itself is the mountain of collyrium dust, the Añjana mountain; its atom (paramāṇu) should be understood as having the quality of a mountain through metaphorical attribution based on its being supported by that [consciousness]. The "form of the world" is the delusion of the world—meaning, the world itself. The "line of the world" is the series of worlds.

The world is the interior of the mountain of consciousness; the world is the fluidity of the water of consciousness; the world is the sweetness of the sugarcane of consciousness; the world is the richness of the milk of consciousness.

The world is the interior of the mountain of consciousness; it is an internal constituent part whose nature is essence. Fluidity is the state of being liquid; viscidity is the quality known as *sneha* (moisture).

The world is the coolness of the snow of consciousness; the world is the blazing of the flame of consciousness. The world is the oil within the ghee of consciousness; the world is the wave of the river of consciousness.

The flame of consciousness (*cijjvālā*) is the crest of the fire called consciousness (*cidākhyāgniśikhā*). Its "blazing" (*jvalana*) is the act of flaming. Because vibration (*vīci*) consists of a structural arrangement, it possesses the quality of water (*jalaguṇatva*).

The world is the sweetness of the honey of consciousness; the world is the golden armlet of consciousness; the world is the fragrance of the flower of consciousness; the world is the fruit at the tip of the creeper of consciousness.

Color possesses the quality of being a quality (*guṇatva*). The creeper possesses the quality of being the fruit, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) because the fruit is dependent upon it.
He states the conclusion:

"The existence of consciousness alone is the existence of the world; the existence of the world alone is the body of consciousness. Herein, no distinction, modification, or the like exists, just as no impurity exists in the sky. (MU 3.14.76)

Therefore, the existence of consciousness itself is the existence of the world; the existence of the world itself is the embodiment of consciousness. The point is that the existence of a quality is not distinct from the possessor of the quality, nor is the existence of the possessor of the quality distinct from the quality. Here, regarding consciousness and the world, [terms such as] "difference," "modification," and so forth—by the word "and so forth" (ādi), "transformation" (pariṇāma) and the like are included—do not exist. Like what? Like impurity in the sky, in space.
as it were. //MT_3,14.76 //
He summarizes the world's nature as consisting of both the existent and the non-existent:

"Thus, this triple world is both existent and non-existent by virtue of its being composed of the existent; or rather, because its essence is that which is beyond conceptualization, it is both existence and non-existence. (MU 3.14.77)

"In this manner," as previously stated; "the three worlds" refers either to the triad of worlds known as Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar, or to the triad of states beginning with waking. "It becomes existent and non-existent" means that, by virtue of being composed of *sat* (Being), it is a modification of the consciousness whose nature is *sat*. Anticipating the objection that there might be a distinction between the root cause, consciousness (*cit*), and its effects based on the support of existence and non-existence, he says, "without conceptualizing. The word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative position.

That very [reality], which is indeed the three worlds, becomes existence and non-existence. Why? Because its nature is non-conceptualizable (*avikalpyatadātmatvāt*). "Non-conceptualizable" means unfit for the conceptualization of existence or non-existence. That which is its nature is the conscious self (*cidātman*); the state of being that is its reality (*tattva*). Therefore, this is the point: the two terms "existent" and "non-existent" denote the agent of the actions of "being" and "not being. And thus:

The conceptualization of agent and object is difficult to avoid; however, when [the scriptures] speak of existence and non-existence as pure, supportless expressions for the acts of "is" and "is not," they describe nothing other than the nature of consciousness itself, which is free from conceptualization. Since the three worlds are non-different from that [consciousness], it is logical that they too possess only the nature of existence and non-existence [as consciousness], and not the state of being both existent and non-existent.

"Is it not possible that there exists a relationship of part and whole between the world and Brahman? To this, he says: "Woe to those by whom the meanings of the words 'part' and 'whole' are imagined—like the horns of a hare—for the sake of denying direct experience! (MU 3.14.78)

By those dull-witted ones who, in order to deny experience—that is, to deny the experience known as the identity of the world and consciousness—have imagined (kalpitau) both the term "part-whole-ness" (avayavāvayavitā), which signifies the relationship between parts and a whole, and its referent (artha), which is that specific relation; how were they imagined? Like a hare's horn, just as someone [might imagine such a thing].

It imagines even a hare’s horn, though it does not exist externally; such is the meaning. "Woe to them" means they are indeed objects of reproach. And their being objects of reproach is due to their cognition of the whole as distinct from its parts.
The point is that there is no such thing as a whole that is separate from its parts.
Where the world—including mountains, heaven, earth, and rivers—does not exist because of the oneness of consciousness, what occasion for the delusion of "otherness" could there be therein?

In that place called *cidrūpa* (the nature of consciousness), the world—along with its mountains, sky, earth, rivers, and oceans—does not exist because of the oneness of consciousness (*cidaikya*). Here, the locative case is used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe*) regarding "other delusion" (*itaravibhrama*); for what possibility is there for the delusion of "other," which consists of its effects?
He explains the all-pervasiveness of consciousness through the analogy of stone:
"Though dense as the heart of a stone, consciousness is as clear as its own space; it holds within it the entire tranquil configuration, just like a stone. (MU 3.14.80)

The consciousness, which is peaceful in the ultimate sense and free from the agitation of existence, non-existence, and so forth—entirely and completely—bears within itself, in its very midst, that which is called "structure," a specific kind of arrangement. How is it? Though solid as the heart of a stone;
for, by being filled with the essence known as light, it is as solid as the heart of a stone, yet it remains as clear as its own space. Truly.

It is indeed as clear and stainless as space, yet it is not capable of containing the world within itself. Regarding this, he provides an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as): just as a stone, though filled with its own essence, contains within it a structural arrangement known as a multitude of engravings;
such is the meaning.
"Even so, am I not still a distinct questioner? Otherwise, questioning would be impossible. To this, he says:
"In the space that encompasses the multitude of objects, you are like a mere fragment of space; for you, there exist no delineations of 'I-ness' or 'otherness,' nor of 'selfhood' or 'non-selfhood.'"

"In the space of the collection of objects" (*padārthanikarākāśe*): the "collection of objects" (*padārthanikara*) is an aggregate; that itself is the "space" (*avakāśa*) because it is of the nature of nothingness.
"In that" means in the midst of that. You are the questioner; you are like a mere fragment of space. He states the conclusion with the words "from you":

therefore, from you—the questioner—there arise "the delineations of 'you-ness,' 'not-me-ness,' 'selfhood,' 'you-ness,' 'not-me-ness,' and 'I'. This is by way of "you-ness," "not-me-ness," and "selfhood," that is, by way of having the form of your state and my state.

The delineations (*ullekha*) are situated as follows: the delineations of "thou-ness" (*tvattā*) and "I-ness" (*mattā*) are conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of the nature of "thou" and the nature of "I. Those delineations of "thou-ness" exist as having the form of the nature of "thou," and those delineations of "I-ness" exist as having the form of the nature of "I. They do not exist [as independent entities], because their nature is that of space (*ākāśa*).
By means of the analogy of a sprout, he explains the fact that the consciousness (cit) under discussion consists of everything:
"Like the arrangement of a multitude of lines within a sprout, this consciousness naturally contains within itself that which is both different and non-different [from it]. (MU 3.14.82)

Consciousness (*cit*) holds this object of consciousness (*cetya*) within itself (*antaḥ*). Why? By its very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*). [Objection: Is it not rather by some specific purpose? Of what nature is it? It is of the nature of being both other and non-other (*anyānanyātmaka*). "Other" (*anya*) means distinct from itself; "non-other" (*ananya*) means not distinct from itself. That which has such a nature is "of the nature of being both other and non-other. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is extended (*ātata*), possessed of expansion.
How does it hold? It stands within the sprouts, that is, in the midst of the sprouts. It is like the arrangement of a multitude of lines within the sprouts;
for since the multitude of lines appears within the sprout, their distinctness cannot be grasped by separating them, and thus their non-distinctness remains clearly established—this is the simile.
Know that consciousness, by its very nature, is without cause; it is the primordial grandfather of all streams of causes, being itself uncaused, as is known through direct experience.

Know—that is, understand—that you are consciousness (*cit*), the state of consciousness, by your very nature, by your own form, through experience, that is, by your own direct realization; and not merely by my word, for you are without cause. "Without cause" means one whose self, or essential nature, is devoid of a cause. Know it to be such. Of what kind?
It is the primordial grandfather who exists as the cause and so forth of all causes; know its nature to be that of the grandfather of all causes. Of which causes? [Of all things.]
Of all the multitudes of causes, of the entire visible world—whatever those multitudes of causes may be, this is their nature:
the causes of the entire visible world are the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*); their cause is the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*); and its cause is the intellect (*citta*).

"Surely, like the world, consciousness too must be unreal. To this he replies: "Unreality cannot be established even by words for consciousness that is beyond being an object of cognition; for it is observed that only that which exists arises, just as a sprout from a seed. (MU 3.14.84)

The meaning is that the non-existence of the *cit*—which is beyond objects of thought (*acetyā*) and untainted by the impurity of the objectifiable (*cetyamala*)—cannot be established even by speech; it is not even fit to be spoken of. He states the latter half [of the verse] as the reason for this, beginning with "that which" (*yat*). The ellipsis is: "Because we have observed that whatever exists arises and manifests as something other [than its prior state]. Here he provides an example: "from a seed... [and so forth].

Thus, the meaning is as follows: just as a sprout existing in the form of a seed arises from the seed, so too does the object of cognition (cetya) exist in the form of pure consciousness (cinmātra). And thus, since the existence of objects of cognition would otherwise be inexplicable, it is not logical to claim that pure consciousness is unreal.
With a verse at the end of the chapter, he summarizes what was previously stated:

"O dear one, within this Great Consciousness there exists the three worlds, possessing distinctions like the vast emptiness of the sky; yet, through experience, you should possess the certainty that all this which is visible is composed of the Supreme State. (MU 3.14.85)

My dear friend, the three worlds exist within—that is, in the midst of—this Great Consciousness, which is pure consciousness alone. It is "of the nature of absolute void," meaning its differentiation (*bheda*) is an absolute void;
that is to say, it is entirely devoid of any internal differentiation of its own nature.
What is it like? It is like the sky. Just as the sky exists devoid of differentiation, so too does this [Great Consciousness] exist. This is the meaning.
He states the result with the word "parama" (supreme). Therefore, being one who possesses certainty, you should become thus endowed with certainty. Why?

Because of experience—that is, through your own direct experience (*svānubhava*), and not merely by my words or by faith alone. How so? Because the entire visible world is composed of the supreme state; it is nothing other than the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*) which transcends all.
The venerable Vālmīki describes the end of the day to Bharadvāja with a verse at the conclusion of the chapter:

"When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites; the assembly, having offered salutations, departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun"—this was stated previously. "When the sage" refers to the venerable Vasiṣṭha. "When he had spoken" means while he was speaking. "Then" means immediately after the instruction mentioned in the preceding verse.

The day passed; that is, it went away. He states the reason for this with the word "astam": because the sun (ina) had gone to its setting (asta). The assembly (sabhā)—the gathering of listeners—went to bathe for the sake of the evening rites (sāyantanavidhi), such as the evening *agnihotra* sacrifice, since there is no entitlement to perform any ritual act without bathing. That assembly [reconvened] at the end of the night (śyāmākṣaye), when the darkness had subsided.

"At the beginning of the day" means at dawn. "Together with the rays of the sun" means with the sunbeams. "She came again" means she arrived; the words "for the sake of hearing" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. May there be auspiciousness! (MT 3.14.86)
Thus ends the fourteenth canto in the "Chapter on Origination" within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. The venerable Vasiṣṭha offers praise at the beginning of the day to that which is being described:
"Just as a pearl shines within the pure sky, so too does this world, which is of the nature of space, shine within the sky of consciousness."

This world, as it is being experienced, becomes nothing but space itself. To provide a supporting illustration for this reason, he says "yathā hi" (just as). The word "hi" is used in the sense of "because. Because the world shines forth in that manner within the stainless sky of consciousness (*cidgagana*), the sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*); in what way? It is of the very nature of the void (*khātman*), that is, its essential form is the sky of consciousness itself. And how so? Just as...

In the sky—that is, in the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*)—a cluster of pearls (*mauktika*) shines. This is the intended meaning: just as a pearl seen in the sky through the vision of one who is deluded is nothing but the sky itself, so too the world seen in the sky of consciousness (*cidgagana*) is nothing but the sky of consciousness itself.
The statue of the three worlds appears as if carved, yet it is not carved upon the pillar of consciousness; nor is there any carver to be found here.

In the pillar of consciousness—known as the pillar of *cit*—the statuette of the three worlds, known as the triple world, appears as if it were carved out, though in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*) it does not appear at all; this is why the word "as if" (*iva*) is employed. Now, one might ask: for what reason is it not actually carved?
To this he says: "And not... That statuette called the world is not carved; here, the meaning of the suffix *-arha* (denoting fitness) is implied by itself.

It is to be understood that it is not capable of being cut away, because it is of the nature of nothingness (*nakiñcidrūpa*). Furthermore, no cutter—that is, an agent of cutting—exists here, due to the absence of duality (*dvaitābhāva*).

Just as within the ocean, waters that are motionless and by their very nature unchanging appear as if they were being known when perceived, so too do those who know the supreme appear as if they were perceivers of the visible world.

The word "yathā" (just as) is to be supplied [at the beginning]. "Situated within the ocean" means existing inside the ocean. "Motionless waters" refers to waves. "Even though not fallen from their own nature" means even though they have not deviated from the essential form called water. "In the domain of knowledge" means in the sphere of cognition. "Objects of knowledge" means they become fit to be known as waves. The use of the word "iva" (as if) indicates that, in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), they do not actually exist.

Likewise, when the other has crossed over into the nature of consciousness, those who know the visible—the cognitions whose form is the visible, that is to say, the objects of perception—seem to come into being.
Even the arrangements of the lattice-like reflections of the sun within water are gross in relation to the appearance of the world, yet they are as immovable as mountains in relation to an atom.
The reflection of the sun within water is "the reflection of the sun within water"; its lattice-like arrangements are "the lattice-like arrangements of the reflection of the sun within water.

Furthermore, this nature of the reflection of the sun within water results in the form of a lattice. With respect to the perception of the world, these appear as gross as immovable mountains; they appear gross with respect to the minute atom.
The aforementioned grossness of the illustration is reinforced:
the appearance of the world has no appearance of its own because it is non-different from Brahman; however, the mass of rays from the sun reflected in water provides an experience of differentiation.
The appearance of the world becomes an appearance that is non-appearance. Why? Because it is not distinct from Brahman; the meaning is that it has the nature of Brahman.
But in the case of distinction—as in the case of the sun’s rays reflected in water—the network of rays provides an experience of distinction and causes the manifestation of duality.
Therefore, the sense is that in that [latter] case, grossness is appropriate.
Even these things experienced in this world—earth and the rest—do not exist at all within that which has the nature of space, just as in dreams and mental constructs.

In the world, which has the nature of space and consists of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), [the elements] are like what? Like a dream and a mental construction (*saṅkalpa*). Just as the earth and other elements, though experienced in a dream and in a mental construction, do not exist—such is the meaning.
The grasping of a solid mass in this [reality], which consists of consciousness and space, is nowhere possible, just like water in a mirage-river.

*Grahaṇa* means grasping (*grāha*). Grasping [something] as a solid mass is *piṇḍagrāha*. "Being existent" is a grasping as a solid mass; it is a grasping as a solid mass that serves as the cause for the conventional usage of "existent. While this, which has the nature of consciousness and space, is being experienced, it occurs—somewhere, in some place—it arises even in a slight degree. Regarding this, he states an illustration: "in a mirage" (*marunadyām*).
"Now, how can the appearance of visibility shine forth in a world whose very nature is non-existent? To this he replies:
"In this world, which cannot be grasped as a solid mass and is like a city of one's imagination, visibility appears in the form of an illusion, like a river in a desert. (MU 3.15.8)

In this world—which is like a city of imagination, resembling a city sketched by the mind—in which there is no grasping at a solid mass (*piṇḍa*), the state of being an object of perception appears; it shines forth as a delusion, consisting of false knowledge. Like what? Like a river in the desert, in the land of Maru.
He explains that because the world is unreal in nature, being of the form of an illusion, it does not fill the scales of a balance, just like a dream:
"By a dream-mountain, as by the world, no two scales of a balance are filled; when freed from mental construction, the splendor of the visible is merely the void. (MU 3.15.9)

Like a dream-mountain—that is, like a mountain in a dream—the world does not fill the scales or occupy space. Because its weight is unreal in nature, it does not fill the scales; because its extension is unreal in nature, it does not occupy space. And since this is established by universal experience in dreams and the like, it serves as a valid example. He states the conclusion: "free from conceptualization" (kalanonmuktā)—that is, free from the conceptualization known as "visibility."

Excluding the conceptualization of the meaning of the word "world" as something distinct from the Self and the Knower, there is indeed no difference in the meaning of the words "world," "Brahman," and "space."

By the ignorant—those devoid of knowledge of the nature of consciousness—the conceptualization of the meaning of the word "world" (jagat) has been made an object of their own experience. This conceptualization refers to the continuous mental engagement with both the word "world" and its referent. Having abandoned and relinquished that conceptualization of the meaning of the word "world" as understood by the ignorant, there is indeed no difference or distinction whatsoever among the meanings of the words "world," "Brahman," and "space."

The meaning is that these words are merely synonyms. Since for an ignorant person, whose true nature is unknown, the world's nature as space is not established, it is said that one must abandon the conviction in the reality of the world and the mental cultivation thereof.
But this manifestation of the sun of pure consciousness, which is devoid of objects of thought, is so subtle toward the sky that it is like a cloud of volition compared to an actual rain-cloud.

But in the case of the specific instance: for the sun of consciousness, which is pure awareness (*cinmātra*) and devoid of objects of thought (*acetya*), and whose solar light is untainted by objects of thought (*cetya*), its "appearance" (*bhāna*)—that is, its manifestation—is subtle in relation to the sky, meaning in comparison to the external ether. It is in that manner, by that method, subtle.
Just as a cloud perceived in the waking state is subtle in relation to a [mental] cloud; a "cloud of volition" (*saṅkalpavārida*), a cloud delineated by one's own mental construction, is subtle.
it occurs.
Just as a dream-city appears clear in relation to the excellent city of the waking state, so too does this world appear clear in relation to the world imagined [in the mind].

Just as, from the perspective of worldly intellect, the dream-city appears clear toward the excellent city of the waking state— being of the nature of a mere manifestation and devoid of the impurity called grossness— so too, from the perspective of the wise, this world being experienced in the waking state appears clear toward the imagined world, because it is of the nature of pure consciousness alone, devoid of the impurity called conceptualization.
It becomes stainless. Although even a city in a dream is exactly like that for one who possesses knowledge, it was stated in this way solely for the purpose of instructing the ignorant.

Therefore, the world, being of the nature of the non-conscious and devoid of consciousness, is nothing but the void alone; know that the words "void" and "world" are synonymous, both consisting of pure consciousness.

Therefore, for the reason stated above, the world—which is of the nature of non-objective consciousness (*acidrūpa*) and consists solely of pure consciousness (*śuddhacinmātra*)—becomes nothing but empty space.
He states the conclusion: "They are void" (*śūnyau*). Thus, being void due to the absence of grasping as a solid mass (*piṇḍagrāha*), they are of the nature of nothing whatsoever;

yet they are composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), having the very essence of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*). Know that the words *vyoma* (space) and *jagat* (world) are synonyms, because they denote the same meaning.
With a desire to explain the events that are about to be described, he concludes what was previously stated with three verses:
"Therefore, nothing whatsoever has arisen here as this visible world; it remains exactly as it is—unnameable, unmanifest, and established in its own state. (MU 3.15.14)
Therefore, because it consists solely of consciousness (*cidekamayatva*), no visible object such as the world arises even in the slightest degree.

Of what nature is it? It is "inexpressible" (*anākhyam*), meaning unworthy of a name. Regarding this, he provides a qualifying attribute as the reason: "unmanifested," which means beyond the range of the senses.

For indeed, a name is inappropriate for that which is unmanifested by way of another form. [Objection: In that case, would it not follow that the world is something previously non-existent (*apūrva*)?
Anticipating this objection, he provides the qualification "abiding" (*avasthitam*). It means "it remains. How? "As it was situated" (*yathā-sthitam*);

that is, exactly as it was before, and not by way of being something new. Just as a rope previously known as a snake, when subsequently known as a rope, remains exactly as it was before; it does not attain a different form.
The meaning is "so it is."
The world itself is the great space, the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) which is without walls; it does not fill even an atom of space or the weight on a scale.

The world becomes the very expanse of consciousness (*cidākāśa*). Of what nature is this expanse of consciousness? It is called the "great expanse" (*mahākāśa*) because of its vastness in comparison to external space. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "without a wall" (*abhittimat*). The phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) of living beings and so forth constitutes a "wall" (*bhitti*) by virtue of being the substratum for their respective attributes; [the expanse of consciousness] is devoid of that. He states the conclusion: "Therefore, that [world] consists of the expanse of consciousness. Thus, it is composed of the expanse of consciousness.
The world, due to the absence of weight and the absence of magnitude, does not fill even an atom-sized space or a scale;
it does not act as a filler.
He further qualifies that very [reality]:
it is indeed of the nature of space, transparent, devoid of any grasping at a solid mass; it is variegated, consisting of space within space, and exists like a city of one's imagination.

It is indeed of the nature of space, being of the nature of nothing at all; it is transparent, the very essence of pure consciousness, and devoid of grasping as a solid mass. "Grasping as a solid mass" refers to the apprehension of something as a compact body; it is free from that. And it is fitting that space should be devoid of grasping as a solid mass.

In the sky—that is, in the sky of consciousness—it is composed of space, meaning it consists of the sky of consciousness. It is a manifold painting, like a city drawn by mere conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*).

Since it is logical that the city of conceptual construction (*saṅkalpapura*) consists of space and does not occupy any physical location such as a scale-pan, the intended absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the entire world is established. Furthermore, as for the "origination" mentioned previously, since it is of the nature of non-origination, it serves only to prove absolute non-existence; thus, there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows.
Now, out of compassion for those who desire to hear his life story, he tells this great narrative which establishes that the world is not filled by the scales and other measures:
"In this regard, listen to this account of the pavilion, an ornament for the ears, so that this matter may find rest in your mind beyond all doubt. (MU 3.15.17)

You—here, regarding the fact that [the Lord] does not fill the space of this world—listen to the *maṇḍapākhyāna*. *Maṇḍapākhyāna* means the narrative well-known by the name *maṇḍapa*. How is it? It is "an ornament for the ears," meaning it is worthy of being heard.
To the question "What comes of that?", he says here: "without doubt. *Yathā* means "in such a way that" one becomes *niḥsandehaḥ*, i.e., one who has emerged from doubt.
This aforementioned meaning will find rest in the mind—that is, in your own mind.

Overcome with urgency, Śrī Rāma requests Śrī Vasiṣṭha regarding the narrative of Maṇḍapa for the increase of true awakening: "O Brahmin, tell me briefly and quickly the entire narrative of Maṇḍapa, by which my awakening may flourish."

The knowledge that [the Self] fulfills the world’s measure and its location is true awakening (*sad-bodha*). For the sake of its increase, he states the result with the words "by which" (*yena*); the meaning is "by which [knowledge] having arisen."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha relates the narrative of Maṇḍapa:
"On this surface of the earth, there was a king named Padma, a glorious sovereign with many sons and vast treasuries, who was like a blossoming lotus of his lineage."

On this earth there was a king named Padma. He describes his various specific qualities with the word "kula" (lineage): he was a "family-lotus" (*kulapadma*) who was full of blossoming. And it is appropriate that a lotus should blossom. Here, the word *padma* is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) to signify excellence.
He possessed an exceeding treasury, being endowed with many storehouses.
He is an ocean in the maintenance of his boundaries, a sun to the darkness of his enemies, a moon to the night-lotus of his beloved, and a fire to the thirst for faults.

It is well known that he maintains the boundaries of the ocean; he is the moon to the night-lotus of his beloved. His status as the moon is due to his power to cause her to bloom. He is the fire that consumes the thirst for vice, because he burns away such cravings.
He is Mount Meru to the hosts of the learned, an ocean from which the moon of their fame arises. He is a lake for the swans of virtuous qualities, and the sun to the lotuses of the arts.

The wise (*vibudha*) are the learned; they themselves are the gods (*vibudha*). Of them, he is like Mount Meru because of his bestowing of much gold and because of being their refuge. Regarding "fame" (*yaśas*): it is an ocean arising from the moon of fame;
it is a lake for the swans that are the forms of his excellent qualities; and it is a sun because it causes the blossoming of the lotuses that are his artistic skills (*kalā*).
He is a wind to the ocean of his enemies, a lion to rutting elephants; he is beloved by all branches of knowledge and a mine of every wondrous virtue.
"Śātravam" refers to a multitude of enemies; that itself is the "ambhoda," or cloud. He is its "pavana," or wind, because he causes its destruction.

Here, "mātaṅgas" refers to the enemy army intended [by the poet]. "Samastā" refers to those heroines who are the embodiments of knowledge (vidyā). Their "dayita" is their beloved husband. And "sarve" refers to all those qualities which are marvelous; he is their "ākara," or source of origin.

He is the mountain Mandara sporting in the agitation of the ocean of Śūrāri; he is the honey from the clusters of flowers of his own play, and the flower-weaponed god of love for his own good fortune.

And those enemies are heroes; he is like the ocean. Upon its agitation, Mount Mandara shines forth; its playful movements (*vilāsa*) are indeed its *vibhrama* (graceful tremors), which are the flowers. The spring (*madhu*) is the season of their abundance, because it causes them to blossom.
By virtue of his good fortune—the state of being blessed—he is the flower-armed one, Kāma.
He is the breeze that causes the play-lotus to dance, the Keśava who celebrates the festival of daring, the moon for the white water-lily of goodness, and the fire for the creeper of wicked conduct.

His grace is like a creeper; in its dancing, he is the wind—the meaning being that he is endowed with playful charm (*līlā*). His very audacity (*sāhasa*), which is action regardless of what is beneficial or harmful, is his festival (*utsava*); Viṣṇu, the slayer of Hiraṇyakaśipu and others, serves as the point of comparison because of his performance of such audacious deeds. His goodness alone is the night-lily (*kairava*); because it causes that [goodness] to blossom, he is the moon. [He is the moon] for the creepers of wicked playfulness...
It is called *anala* (fire) because of its burning nature.
He had a fortunate wife named Līlā, a playful woman endowed with every charm, like a lotus risen upon the earth.

That King named Padma had a wife named Līlā; she was his wife called Līlā. He states her qualifications: "fortunate" (*subhagā*), meaning endowed with praiseworthy beauty; "graceful" (*vilāsinī*), meaning possessed of charm; "filled with all good fortune" (*sarvasaubhāgyair valitā*) upon the earth; and "arisen like a lotus" (*kamalevoditā*).
Adorned with every excellence, speaking with playful sweetness, moving slowly with joy, her smile was like the rising of a second moon.
"Līlā" means she who speaks sweetly with playful charm. "Sānandā" means she whose slow movements are full of joy. "Dvitīyā" means she whose smile is like the rising of a second moon.
Possessing a lotus-face as enchanting as a braid of hair, with cool limbs and fair as a *karṇikā* flower, she was like a moving lotus-pond.

She is graced by that lotus-face which captivates the mind of Alakā; she possesses cool limbs, meaning her body is cold. She is like a *karṇikā*, meaning she is fair-skinned like a pericarp. Like what? Like a moving, wandering lotus-pond (*sarojinī*).
A lotus-pond, too, captivates the bees with its lotuses, possesses cool limbs, and is fair with its *karṇikā*. // MT_3,15.27 //
Laughing like a mass of jasmine blossoms with the playful grace of creepers, full of aesthetic flavor, with sprouts for hands and rich in flowers, she was like the embodied splendor of spring.

"Śālinī" means she who is beautifully endowed with erotic passion (*śṛṅgāra*). "Prabālā" means she whose hands are like young sprouts (*prabāla*). "Puṣpā" means she who is richly adorned with flowers serving as ornaments. Like what? Like the embodied splendor of spring (*madhuśrī*) personified.
She too smiles with clusters of *kunda* flowers; she is endowed with "rasa," meaning the essence of spring; and she is likewise "śālinī. The rest is the same.
His pure and auspicious body brings delight to the people; like the celestial river Gaṅgā descending to earth, it is graced by swans.
Her body is pure white and her limbs are bright; she is meritorious and fortunate. She is "of the people" (janatā), meaning she bestows joy upon the multitude.
She is like a "swan" (haṃsa), being endowed with grace like that of a swan. Like what? Like the celestial river Gaṅgā, which has gone to the earth (gāṃ gatā);
for she too is exactly like that.
To perform for a long time the service of that god whose arrows are flowers of the earth and who bestows all delight, another woman appeared, as if she were Rati herself.
This was said because it is appropriate for her to perform service for Rati, the wife of the Flower-Arrowed One (Kāmadeva).

With a verse at the end of the chapter, he describes her virtuous qualities: "When he was anxious, she was deeply anxious; when he was joyful, she was joyful; when he was agitated, she was agitated; like a reflection, the beloved was identical to him; only when he was enraged was she afraid."
She was his beloved; [the word] "of him" is to be supplied as the object. She was like a reflection of that king. Of what nature was she?

When he was agitated, she was agitated; when he was joyful, she was joyful; when he was distracted, she was distracted; when he was enraged, she was merely afraid. It was by this much alone that she was entirely in opposition to him.
Such is the intended meaning. May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the fifteenth canto in the "Chapter on Origination" within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. It is said that the king, whose consort was none other than the Apsaras Bhūtalā, sported with that queen; he took delight with his beloved in the flavor of unfeigned love.

That king, together with his beloved named Līlā, in which there was an unfeigned essence of love, took delight in the places to be described by means of the specific sports to be described. Of what nature was she? She was a celestial nymph (apsaras) upon the earth.
How was he? He was a husband who had no other woman; the meaning is that he was devoted to her alone.
He describes the places for play:
"In garden groves and thickets of *tamāla* trees, upon couches within flower-pavilions, and in dwellings formed by circles of creepers. (MU 3.16.2)

In the garden groves, in those arbors and dwellings that have been constructed; "with flowers" means in those pavilions and couches made of flowers; a *maṇḍapa* is a shelter for people; and in the "houses formed by the coils of creepers," that is, in the dwellings consisting of circles of vines.
Upon flower-beds in the inner apartments, on pathways strewn with heaps of blossoms, on swings in the spring gardens, and in the pleasure-pools;

In those bedchamber beds fashioned with flowers; "with flowers" means in those pathways or streets provided with an abundance of flowers, a collection of blossoms; "in spring" means in those garden swings constructed during the springtime.
In groves of sandalwood trees and beneath *santānaka* canopies, in dwellings of *kadamba* and *nimba* trees, and within the heart of *pāribhadra* trees;

*Ṣaṇḍāḥ* are groves; *santānakāḥ* are specific types of trees. Regarding *kadamba*: it refers to the houses constructed at the bases of *kadamba* and *nimba* trees. Regarding *pāribhadra*: it refers to specific types of trees found in mountain caves, marshy lands, and window-towers, as well as on the banks of rivers, in thickets, and upon the dwellings atop elephants.
In mountain caves; in marshy lands; in cities and upper chambers provided with windows; on the embankments and thickets along the banks of rivers; and in dwellings constructed upon elephants.
In summer, however, [he dwells] in houses of snow, in bowers of creepers, under trees that are golden palaces, and in walls made of pearls and rubies.

"In the palaces of frost" means in cool houses. "In gold" refers to those golden palace-trees planted upon the golden palaces; in them. "With pearls" means those houses whose walls are fashioned with pearls and rubies. In them. (MT 3.16.6)
In the groves of the spring forest, fragrant with the nectar of blooming *kunda* and *mandāra* flowers, where rows of cuckoos were warbling; MU_3,16.7 //

Regarding the phrase "in those clusters of forest flowers blooming in spring": the two adjectives *vikasat* ("blooming") and *kūjat* ("warbling") qualify this very term *vasantavanajāleṣu* ("in the forest clusters of spring").
And upon patches of various jewel-like grasses with soft luster, and at waterfalls raining down dense showers of shimmering spray; //MU_3,16.8//

And those various jewel-like grasses—on what kind of surfaces? On soft-glittering lotuses; this is the meaning. Regarding "in the waterfalls" (*nirjhara*): on what kind of waterfalls? "Tarat" means those prominent, rising droplets (*śīkara*, drops of water) that are like stars; their *āsāra* refers to a downpour of showers, which they rain down.
In such cases.
And upon the surfaces of golden and ruby slabs on the mountains, in the dwellings of divine sages and seers, and in hermitages of long-accumulated merit;
Upon those stone slabs which serve as the source of the production of gold and rubies among the mountains.
When the night-lotuses had blossomed, when the day-lotuses were smiling, when the forest glades were in bloom, and when the water-lilies were fully opened;
When the *smerā* flowers have blossomed.
Having described the places for play, he now describes the modes of play:

"By means of riddles (*prahelikā*), narratives (*ākhyāna*), and likewise by 'fistfuls' of syllables (*akṣaramuṣṭi*); by *aṣṭāpada* games, by many bright [puzzles], and likewise by those with a hidden fourth line (*gūḍhacaturthaka*)."
By means of narratives, which are accounts of events; and by means of "syllable-fists," which are specific types of games.
And by means of dramas and narratives, verses containing wordplay on the letter *bindu*, distinctions between regional dialects, and the activities of cities and villages.

By those narratives (*ākhyāyikā*) mentioned in the dramas; by *bindumatī* and *bhrama*, which are specific types of games; by "regional" (*deśa*), meaning by the divisions—that is, the distinguishing features—of regional dialects (*deśabhāṣā*); and by "urban" (*nagara*), which should be construed as "by the activities of cities and the activities of villages."
With wreaths, garlands, and strings of flowers, adorned with various ornaments, their movements were playful and graceful, and they were vessels for diverse aesthetic sentiments.
"With movements" means with turnings. "Various" means by means of the arrangements of various ornaments, that is, by their mutual combinations.

"Graceful" means those playful, swaying motions and gait; by what kind [of motions]? "Variegated," meaning of various kinds; "receptacles of sentiments," meaning vessels for the erotic and other aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*).
By chewing betel leaves with fresh areca nuts and camphor, and by hiding their bodies within bowers of flowering creepers; MU_3,16.14.

*Carvaṇaiḥ* means by those that have been chewed. *Phullā* means flowering creepers; *kuñjāni* refers to the bowers formed by them; *in those*. *Dehagopanā* is the act of concealing the body; for that purpose, there are *kharvaṇāni*, which are acts of shrinking or becoming small;
[it is] by means of those.
With the playful application of unguents, the graceful sport of swinging on swings, and the sequence of mutual tossing upon flower-adorned swings within the house;
*Samālambhana* means the application of body-paint (*aṅgarāga*). *Anyonya* means one another, mutually. *Āndolana* is the swinging of a swing; [it refers to] by means of its various sequences.
By means of the coming and going of boats, vehicles, elephants, horses, tamed camels, and other such transport; and by the playful sport of water-sports, splashing one another with water.

And by means of boats, as well as by means of draft-animals serving as vehicles—such as tamed elephants, horses, and camels—and by their coming and going; "tamed" refers to a herd of oxen; "mutually" means one another; "sprinklings" means acts of sprinkling;
by those [acts].
Through the modes of dance, song, and the arts of *lāsya* and *tāṇḍava*, through musical performances, conversations, and the playing of the *vīṇā* and the *mṛdaṅga* drum; MU_3,16.17 //
"Dancing and so forth" refers to those intense (*udbhaṭa*) or exuberant (*udrikta*) "functions" (*vṛtti*), which are activities; [the Lord is worshipped] by means of them.
Furthermore, he describes the places of sport:
"In gardens, on trees by the banks of rivers, in forest groves, in inner apartments, and in palaces—in those various places, in such and such ways."
In such and such a manner, by means of the various kinds of specific sports previously mentioned.
That young woman, raised in comfort, was his beloved and dear companion; once, being possessed of auspicious intentions, she reflected.

The beloved wife of that king named Padma was she called Līlā. She was young; one day, on a certain occasion, she reflected—that is, she gave rise to a thought. Of what nature was she? She was nurtured in happiness. Furthermore, of what nature was she?
She was "Śubhā" (Auspicious), meaning she was endowed with a praiseworthy resolve (*saṅkalpa*) to be described below.

"What was she thinking? To this he replied: "This lord of the world, my husband, is dearer to me than even my own life; endowed with the splendor of youthful exuberance, how might he become free from old age and death?"

"This husband of mine is ageless and immortal," meaning he is free from the defects known as old age and death. "How could he be?"—the logical connection (*anvaya*) is: "By what cause could he be so? [The phrase] "from the vital breaths" (*prāṇebhyaḥ*) means "from living beings."
How might I, with my high breasts, sport for long centuries at will with this husband of mine in houses of flowers?
The meaning is: "How might I enjoy myself for hundreds of years with this beloved husband? By what means could I engage in play for hundreds of years?"
One should strive accordingly through the sequence of austerity, recitation, and self-restraint, so that one may become a king with the luster of the moon, free from old age and death.

The word "ataḥ" (therefore) is to be supplied. Therefore, by means of these—asceticism, recitation, and self-restraint—I make this effort so that [the world] may become like the moonlight of the night-lord, free from old age and death.
"I shall therefore question the twice-born who are advanced in wisdom, advanced in austerity, and advanced in learning, as to how death might not come to men."

"I shall ask the twice-born who are advanced in knowledge, advanced in austerity, and likewise advanced in learning. What was it she asked? "By what means might death not occur for men; by what cause might it not happen?
Having stated her intention, she spoke of external effort:
"Then, having quickly summoned and honored the twice-born, Sāṇḍilī questioned them again and again: 'O Brahmins, how might immortality be attained? (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.6–7).

Now, immediately after the resolve; regarding the word "having summoned" (*ānāyya*), the word "by the attendants" (*parijanaiḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The phrase "again and again" (*punaḥ punaḥ*) is intended to indicate the intensity of her desire.
The Brahmins declare, O Goddess, that through austerity, recitation, and self-restraint, all the perfections of the Siddhas are attained; yet immortality is never obtained.
"Siddhasiddhayaḥ" means the accomplishments (siddhis) of those who are accomplished (siddhas), that is, those endowed with success. The word "tu" (but) indicates a distinction.

Having heard from the mouths of the twice-born that her desired goal would be accomplished, she reflected once more; having heard this, she, terrified of separation from her beloved, pondered again by means of her own wisdom.
By one's own wisdom alone, and not by following what has been said [by others].
"What was she thinking? To this he replied: "If, by fate, my death should occur before that of my husband, then, liberated from all suffering, I shall abide happily within myself. (MU 3.16.27)
The meaning is: because of not seeing the suffering caused by the death of her husband.
Now, if my husband should die first after a thousand years, I shall act in such a way that his life-force (jīva) will not depart from this house.

The phrase "in a thousand years" indicates a blessing. Now, if the husband should die at the end of those thousand years, then I shall employ such a means that the life-force of the husband will not depart from the house.
"What follows from that? To this he says:
"Due to that delusion, I shall dwell at my ease, constantly gazed upon by my husband, in this very private inner chamber belonging to my husband's life."
"Out of that delusion—that is, out of the delusion that 'my husband is looking at me'—I shall always, at all times, return according to my pleasure.

In what state am I? While this husband of mine, my own person, remains alive in this inner apartment pavilion by means of the stratagem accomplished by me, I have been observed—that is, looked upon—by my husband."
Starting this very day, for the sake of this purpose, I shall worship the goddess Jñapti Sarasvatī with recitations, fasts, and observances until she is fully propitiated.

"Right now, and not tomorrow"—that is, for the purpose of ensuring that while her husband is alive, she does not depart from her own home. "The Goddess Jñapti" refers to the goddess who is one's own intuitive insight (*pratibhā*). "Until satisfaction" means until the limit of her grace. But why is it heard [in scripture] that [liberation] comes through the propitiation of Jñapti? We say: solely from the grace of Jñapti, because the grace of Jñapti alone is the cause in all cases.

Furthermore, the instruction for making known that will be explained further on should be understood as being produced by one's own intuition (*svapratibhā*). For whatever is performed or heard as a play (*līlā*) is done solely through one's own intuition; even that which is heard through the mouth of a teacher and others is likewise through one's own intuition alone, because one's own intuition is present everywhere.

Having decided that she would speak of her efforts immediately after her reflection, that excellent woman, without even telling her lord, undertook a severe penance according to the scriptures, remaining steadfast in her observances.
She is one who has taken refuge in and relies upon the observance (niyama), because without it, ascetic practice (tapas) is in vain.
He describes that austerity by way of its specific characteristics:
"At the conclusion of every three-night period, having broken her fast, she was devoted to the worship of gods, twice-born brahmins, gurus, the wise, and the learned. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.6)
In the expression "trirātrasya trirātrasya," the doubling [of the word] indicates distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).
Her body was constantly engaged in bathing, giving, austerity, and meditation; she practiced all forms of faith and right conduct, yet she caused herself great suffering.

She whose body is constantly engaged in bathing and other such acts, and is endowed with purposeful exertion—she is [described as such]. "Sarva" refers to one who is fit for faith (*āstikya*). "Kleśa" refers to austerity (*tapas*) in its essential form.
In accordance with the proper time, the proper effort, the proper scriptures, and the proper sequence, she gratified her husband, whose own state of mind remained unknown to her.
Uncomprehended is that play; his state consists in the thought, "I am performing this triad of asceticism," by means of which he [acts].
In this manner, for three hundred nights, that young woman, steadfast in her observances, remained engaged in arduous effort, devoted to unceasing asceticism.

"Anārata" means that in which there is unceasing dedication to ascetic practice (*tapas*). This is an adverbial modifier. It refers to an arduous exertion consisting of activities such as breaking the fast after three nights, which is painful in nature.

Then, regarding the attainment of knowledge, he said: "After she had worshipped the image for a hundred three-night periods, the blessed goddess Gaurī, the Mistress of Speech, being pleased, spoke this to her."

Now, immediately following the observances (niyama): Vāgīśī is the personification of knowledge; Gaurī is of pure nature. Her status as Vāgīśī is to be understood through her being the root cause of all speech. "Having gone to the image" means she has resorted to an image made of stone or other materials;
the sense is that by means of her own creative power (*pratibhā*), she appeared within the image and granted him a vision of herself.
Speaking words of formal declaration, she said:
"O child, I am well-pleased with you because of your uninterrupted asceticism and your extraordinary devotion to your husband; choose a boon as you desire."
Uninterrupted and continuous.
Having heard the formal proclamation, the queen praised her:
"Victory to you, O moonlight that dispels the defect of the burning heat of the flames of birth and old age! Victory to you, O solar radiance that wards off the mass of darkness within the heart!"
It is well known that the light of the moon wards off the affliction of burning heat, while the light of the sun dispels darkness.
O Mother, O Mother of the three worlds, protect me, this wretched one; grant these two auspicious boons that I here entreat.
"Pitiable" means miserable; "auspicious" (*śubha*) is an adjective qualifying the two boons.
Between the two boons, she spoke one:
"O Mother, let the life-force of my husband, the lord of Videha, depart from this very pavilion of his own inner apartments."
"Between these two boons, grant me this one boon. To the question "Which one?", he says: "videha," meaning of the one who is bodiless—that is, of the deceased—let him not go, let him not depart.
The second [request] he says:
"O Great Goddess, I entreat you for a second time: whenever I desire to see you for the sake of a boon, then grant me your vision."

"Give me this second [boon]. To the question "What [is it]?", he says: "Thee. O Goddess, when I pray for the sight of you, then, for the sake of a boon—that is, out of compliance with my request—grant me that sight.
Having accepted the two boons, [he] made it known.
